01-01.t: Death of Saint Basil the Great
01-01.x: By tradition Basil, Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, died on this day. He defended the faith of Nicaea against the Arians, wrote a rule that still shapes Eastern monastic life, and built a great hospital for the poor.

The Jewish philosopher Edith Stein was baptised in the parish church of Bad Bergzabern in Germany, after reading the life of Saint Teresa of Ávila. She became a Carmelite nun and was killed at Auschwitz in 1942.

01-01.t: The first World Day of Peace
01-01.x: The Church kept the first World Day of Peace, which Pope Paul VI had asked for a few weeks earlier. Each pope since has marked 1 January with a message on peace addressed to the whole world.

01-02.t: A pope takes a new name
01-02.x: The Roman priest Mercurius became pope and chose to be called John II, since he bore the name of a pagan god. He was the first pope to change his name on election, a custom that later became usual.

Saint Marcellin Champagnat, a young curate at La Valla in France, gathered his first two recruits in a small house to teach country children. From them grew the Marist Brothers, who now run schools across the world.

01-02.t: Birth of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux
01-02.x: Thérèse Martin was born at Alençon in Normandy, the youngest child of Saints Louis and Zélie Martin. She entered the Carmel of Lisieux at fifteen, and her “little way” of trust and love made her a Doctor of the Church.

01-03.x: Pope Leo X issued the bull Decet Romanum Pontificem, which excommunicated Martin Luther after he refused to withdraw his teachings. The break that followed divided Western Christians, and the Church still prays and works for that wound to be healed.

01-03.t: Birth of Saint Damien of Molokai
01-03.x: Jozef De Veuster was born at Tremelo in Belgium. As Father Damien he went to Hawaii and asked to serve the leprosy settlement on Molokai, where he lived among the sick for sixteen years and died of the disease himself.

01-03.t: Death of Saint Kuriakose Elias Chavara
01-03.x: Kuriakose Elias Chavara died at Koonammavu in Kerala. A priest of the Syro-Malabar Church, he helped to found the first religious congregation for men begun in India and opened schools beside parish churches. He was canonised in 2014.

01-04.t: Death of Saint Angela of Foligno
01-04.x: Angela of Foligno died in her Umbrian home town. A wife and mother who turned to God in middle life, she became a Franciscan tertiary, and the account of her inner life made her one of the great medieval mystics.

01-04.t: Death of Saint Elizabeth Ann Seton
01-04.x: Elizabeth Ann Seton died at Emmitsburg in Maryland, aged forty-six. A widow and convert, she founded the first American congregation of religious sisters and opened a free school for girls. She was the first person born in the United States to be canonised.

01-04.t: Paul VI arrives in the Holy Land
01-04.x: Pope Paul VI landed in Jordan and entered Jerusalem the same day, the first pope to visit the Holy Land since Saint Peter left it. He was also the first pope to travel by aeroplane, and the first to leave Italy for a century and a half.

01-05.t: Death of Saint Edward the Confessor
01-05.x: King Edward of England died at Westminster, a week after the consecration of the abbey church he had built there. Remembered for his prayer and his care for the poor, he was canonised in 1161 and lies buried in the abbey.

John Neumann, the Bohemian-born Redemptorist who became Bishop of Philadelphia, collapsed and died in the street while running errands. He had built up a system of parish schools and learned many languages to hear his people’s confessions.

01-05.t: Pope and Patriarch meet in Jerusalem
01-05.x: Pope Paul VI and the Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras embraced on the Mount of Olives. It was the first meeting of a pope and a patriarch of Constantinople for more than five centuries, and it opened the way to lifting the excommunications of 1054.

01-06.t: Death of Saint Raymond of Penyafort
01-06.x: The Dominican friar Raymond of Penyafort died in Barcelona at a great age. He gathered the laws of the Church into the collection that served for nearly seven centuries, and his guide for confessors shaped the care of souls.

An eighteen-year-old Loreto postulant from Skopje, later known as Mother Teresa, reached Calcutta by sea. She taught in the city for many years before leaving the convent to serve the poorest of the poor in the city’s streets.

Brother André, doorkeeper of a Holy Cross college in Montreal for forty years, died aged ninety-one. Thousands credited their healing to his prayers to Saint Joseph, and about a million people filed past his coffin at the Oratory he built.

01-07.t: Election of Pope Saint Pius V
01-07.x: The Dominican cardinal Michele Ghislieri was elected pope and took the name Pius V. He put the decrees of the Council of Trent into practice, issuing the Roman Catechism, a revised Breviary and the Roman Missal of 1570.

Bernadette Soubirous was born in a mill at Lourdes, the eldest child of a miller who later fell into poverty. At fourteen she saw the Virgin Mary at the grotto of Massabielle, and she ended her life as a nun at Nevers.

01-08.x: Cardinal Lotario of Segni was elected pope at the age of thirty-seven on the day his predecessor died. As Innocent III he approved the way of life of Saint Francis and called the Fourth Lateran Council.

The council summoned by Pope Eugene IV opened at Ferrara, and moved to Florence the following year. There the Greek and Latin bishops met to seek the reunion of East and West, which was proclaimed in 1439 but did not last.

Raymond Kolbe was born at Zduńska Wola in Poland. As the Franciscan friar Maximilian he spread devotion to Mary Immaculate through the press, and at Auschwitz in 1941 he gave his life in place of a fellow prisoner who had a family.

01-09.x: Adrian of Utrecht, a Dutch cardinal then governing Spain, was elected pope in his absence. An austere reformer who openly admitted the faults of the Roman court, he reigned less than two years. No other non-Italian was elected until 1978.

In Venice a young Sudanese woman who had been kidnapped and sold as a slave was baptised, confirmed and given her first Holy Communion by the Patriarch. She took the name Josephine, and later entered the Canossian Sisters who had sheltered her.

01-10.x: Pope Agatho died in Rome while the Third Council of Constantinople was still sitting. The council fathers received his letter teaching that Christ has both a divine and a human will, and declared that Peter had spoken through him.

Pope Gregory X died at Arezzo. Chosen after a vacancy of nearly three years, he called the Second Council of Lyon and laid down that cardinals should be shut in a conclave until they had elected a pope.

01-10.t: The first printed Greek New Testament
01-10.x: At Alcalá in Spain the printers finished the New Testament volume of the Complutensian Polyglot Bible, a work sponsored by Cardinal Ximénez de Cisneros. It was the first Greek New Testament ever printed, though it was not published until some years later.

01-11.t: Death of Saint Thomas of Cori
01-11.x: The Franciscan friar Thomas of Cori died at Bellegra, in the hills east of Rome. He lived there for decades in a strict house of retreat, preaching in the villages around and spending long hours before the Blessed Sacrament. He was canonised in 1999.

01-12.t: Death of Saint Aelred of Rievaulx
01-12.x: Aelred, abbot of the Cistercian monastery of Rievaulx in Yorkshire, died after years of painful illness. Under his gentle rule the community grew to some 140 monks and 500 lay brothers. His book on spiritual friendship is still widely read.

Marguerite Bourgeoys died in Montreal, where she had arrived from France in 1653. She opened the settlement’s first school in a stable and founded the Congregation of Notre-Dame, whose sisters taught without being enclosed. She was canonised in 1982.

Richard Challoner died in London aged eighty-nine, after guiding English Catholics through decades of the penal laws. His revision of the Douay-Rheims Bible was the Scripture that English-speaking Catholics read for the next two centuries.

01-13.t: Eugene IV condemns slavery in the Canaries
01-13.x: Pope Eugene IV issued the bull Sicut dudum, ordering that the people of the Canary Islands who had been enslaved be set free within fifteen days. Those who refused to release them were to be excommunicated.

At its sixth session the Council of Trent approved its decree on justification. It taught that sinners are made just by God’s grace, which no one can earn, and that a person freely cooperates with that grace.

Bishop Jean-Baptiste Pompallier, newly arrived from France, celebrated the first Mass in New Zealand at Totara Point on the Hokianga harbour, in the home of an Irish settler family. He went on to found missions among the Māori.

01-14.t: Death of Blessed Odoric of Pordenone
01-14.x: The Franciscan friar Odoric died at Udine in northern Italy, shortly after returning from a missionary journey of many years. He had travelled through India and the islands of South-East Asia and spent three years in Beijing.

Devasahayam, an official at the court of Travancore in southern India who had become a Christian, was shot after three years of imprisonment and ill-treatment. In 2022 he became the first Indian layman to be canonised.

The Dutch Redemptorist Peter Donders died at Batavia in Suriname. For nearly thirty years he had cared for people with leprosy in the settlement there, and he also travelled into the forest to preach to the indigenous peoples.

01-15.x: The Spanish Dominican Francis Fernández de Capillas was beheaded at Fu’an in Fujian province after months in prison, where he had gone on teaching his fellow prisoners. The Church honours him as the first martyr of China.

Mary MacKillop was born in Melbourne to Scottish parents. She helped to found the Sisters of Saint Joseph of the Sacred Heart, who brought schooling to poor children in the Australian outback. In 2010 she became Australia’s first canonised saint.

At Banneux in Belgium eleven-year-old Mariette Beco saw a lady in white in the garden of her home. In eight appearances that winter the lady called herself the Virgin of the Poor. The Bishop of Liège approved the apparitions in 1949.

01-16.x: Five friars sent by Saint Francis to preach in Morocco, Berard and his companions, were beheaded at Marrakesh. When their bodies were brought to Coimbra in Portugal, a young canon was so moved that he joined the friars. He is known as Saint Anthony of Padua.

Joseph Vaz, a priest from Goa, died at Kandy in Sri Lanka. He had entered the island disguised as a labourer when Catholic priests were banned under Dutch rule, and for twenty-four years he rebuilt the Church there.

01-17.t: Death of Saint Anthony of Egypt
01-17.x: By tradition Anthony died on this day in his hermitage near the Red Sea, aged 105. He had gone into the Egyptian desert as a young man to seek God alone, and the many who followed him made him the father of monks.
Pope Gregory XI entered Rome after a long journey from Avignon, where the popes had lived for nearly seventy years. Saint Catherine of Siena had urged him to return to the city of Saint Peter.

As Prussian troops advanced through western France, children in the village of Pontmain saw the Virgin Mary in the evening sky, with a message calling them to pray and promising that God would soon answer. The advance stopped, and the bishop approved the apparition a year later.

01-18.x: After a break of ten years the Council of Trent met again under Pope Pius IV. In this third and last period it completed its teaching on the Mass, holy orders and marriage, and ordered seminaries to be set up for training priests.

After an inquiry lasting more than three years, Bishop Laurence of Tarbes declared that the Virgin Mary had truly appeared to Bernadette Soubirous at Lourdes. He authorised devotion to Our Lady at the grotto and planned a church on the site.

01-18.t: The first week of prayer for unity
01-18.x: Father Paul Wattson, then an Anglican friar at Graymoor in New York, began an eight-day period of prayer for the unity of Christians. He entered the Catholic Church the next year, and the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity is still kept from 18 to 25 January.

01-19.x: Frederic Baraga, a Slovenian priest who became the first Bishop of Marquette in Michigan, died after nearly forty years among the Ojibwe and Ottawa peoples. He travelled his vast mission on snowshoes and wrote a grammar and dictionary of the Ojibwe language.

The Dutch Carmelite priest and professor Titus Brandsma was arrested at Nijmegen. He had been visiting the editors of Catholic newspapers to urge them not to print Nazi propaganda. He died at Dachau that July and was canonised in 2022.

01-20.x: Pope Fabian died a martyr in Rome at the start of the persecution of the emperor Decius. He had led the Roman Church for fourteen years and divided the city into seven districts, each under a deacon. He was buried in the catacomb of Callistus.

01-20.t: Our Lady appears to Alphonse Ratisbonne
01-20.x: Alphonse Ratisbonne, a young Jewish banker hostile to the Church, saw the Virgin Mary in the Roman church of Sant’Andrea delle Fratte while wearing a Miraculous Medal he had accepted as a dare. He was baptised eleven days later and became a priest.

Cyprian Michael Iwene Tansi died in Leicester. A tireless parish priest among the Igbo people of Nigeria, he had come to England to become a Trappist monk at Mount Saint Bernard Abbey. Pope John Paul II beatified him in Nigeria in 1998.

01-21.x: By tradition the young Roman girl Agnes was put to death on this day, in about 304, because she would not give up her faith or her promise of virginity. She was twelve or thirteen, and her name is in the Roman Canon of the Mass.

The Benedictine monk Alban Roe was hanged, drawn and quartered at Tyburn in London for being a priest, together with the aged priest Thomas Reynolds. Roe had spent many years in prison, where his cheerfulness won over fellow prisoners.

01-21.t: Saint Irenaeus named Doctor of the Church
01-21.x: Pope Francis declared Saint Irenaeus of Lyon a Doctor of the Church with the title Doctor of Unity. Born in Asia Minor and bishop in Gaul in the second century, Irenaeus defended the faith handed down from the apostles.

01-22.x: A company of 150 Swiss soldiers marched into Rome and was blessed by Pope Julius II, who had asked for them to guard his person. The Pontifical Swiss Guard has served the popes ever since.

The Roman priest Vincent Pallotti died in the city where he had spent his life hearing confessions and serving the poor and the sick. He taught that every baptised person, lay or ordained, is called to be an apostle, and founded a society to put this into practice.

Laura Vicuña, a Chilean girl at a Salesian school in the Argentine Andes, died aged twelve. She had offered her life to God for her mother, who was living with a violent man, and her mother returned to the sacraments afterwards.

01-23.t: Death of Saint Ildephonsus of Toledo
01-23.x: Ildephonsus, monk and Archbishop of Toledo, died after ten years as bishop of the chief see of Visigothic Spain. He is remembered above all for his book defending the perpetual virginity of Mary, which shaped Spanish devotion to her.

Barbara Koob was born in Hesse in Germany and grew up in Utica, New York. As Mother Marianne, a Franciscan sister, she went to Hawaii in 1883 to nurse people with leprosy and spent thirty years with them on Molokai.

01-24.x: The Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci reached Beijing with gifts for the emperor, among them two chiming clocks. Allowed to stay, he won respect for the Gospel among Chinese scholars through his learning and his regard for their culture.

01-24.t: Day of prayer for peace at Assisi
01-24.x: Four months after the attacks of 11 September, Pope John Paul II travelled by train to Assisi with leaders of many churches and religions. Together they prayed for peace and declared that violence can never be justified in God’s name.

01-25.t: Jesuits found the mission of São Paulo
01-25.x: On the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul, Jesuit missionaries including the young José de Anchieta celebrated Mass at a new mission school on the plateau of Piratininga. The city of São Paulo in Brazil grew up around it.

Less than three months after his election, Pope John XXIII told a group of cardinals at the basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls that he would call an ecumenical council. The Second Vatican Council opened in October 1962.

01-25.t: The new Code of Canon Law
01-25.x: Pope John Paul II promulgated the revised Code of Canon Law for the Latin Church, twenty-four years to the day after John XXIII had called for it. It replaced the code of 1917 and applied the teaching of the Second Vatican Council.

01-26.x: Paula, a wealthy Roman widow, died at Bethlehem. She had followed Saint Jerome to the Holy Land, founded monasteries beside the cave of the Nativity, and supported and encouraged his work of translating the Bible into Latin.

01-26.t: Death of Saint José Gabriel Brochero
01-26.x: The “gaucho priest” José Gabriel Brochero died in the mountains of Córdoba in Argentina, blind and suffering from leprosy caught from his parishioners. He had ridden his mule across a vast parish, building roads, schools and a retreat house.

The Sicilian Franciscan Gabriele Allegra died in Hong Kong. Arriving in China as a young priest, he gave more than thirty years to translating the whole Bible into Chinese from the original languages, with a team of Chinese friars. It was published in 1968.

01-27.t: Return of Saint John Chrysostom’s relics
01-27.x: The body of John Chrysostom, who had died in exile thirty years before, was brought back to Constantinople and laid in the Church of the Holy Apostles. The emperor Theodosius II asked pardon for the wrong his parents had done the saint.

In the bull Unigenitus Pope Clement VI announced a jubilee for 1350 and set out the Church’s teaching on indulgences. He described the merits of Christ and the saints as a treasury which the Church can share with the faithful.

Angela Merici died at Brescia in northern Italy. Five years earlier she had founded the Company of Saint Ursula, a group of women who taught girls while living in their own homes. From it grew the Ursulines, the first teaching order of women.

01-28.t: Gregory VII absolves Henry IV at Canossa
01-28.x: After the excommunicated King Henry IV of Germany had stood for three days as a penitent outside the castle of Canossa, Pope Gregory VII lifted the sentence. The scene became a lasting sign of the Church’s freedom from royal control.

01-28.t: Relics of Saint Thomas Aquinas reach Toulouse
01-28.x: By order of Pope Urban V the body of Thomas Aquinas was carried to the Dominican church in Toulouse, where the Order of Preachers had begun. The Church keeps his memorial on the anniversary of this day.

Joseph Freinademetz, a Divine Word missionary from the South Tyrol, died of typhus in Shandong after nearly thirty years in China. He adopted Chinese dress and customs and wished to remain Chinese even in heaven. He was canonised in 2003.

01-29.x: Pope Gelasius II, once a monk of Monte Cassino, died at the abbey of Cluny in France after a reign of a year. He had been driven from Rome by the emperor Henry V and by a hostile Roman family, and spent most of his short reign in exile.

01-30.x: Pope Honorius III approved the rule of life that Saint Albert, Patriarch of Jerusalem, had written for the hermits living on Mount Carmel. It became the foundation of the Carmelite Order, which soon afterwards spread to Europe.

Brother Mutien-Marie, a De La Salle Brother, died at Malonne in Belgium, where he had taught music and drawing for more than fifty years. Thought at first unfit to teach, he became known for his patience and constant prayer. He was canonised in 1989.

Columba Marmion, a Dublin priest who became abbot of Maredsous in Belgium, died there during an influenza epidemic. His books, above all Christ, the Life of the Soul, have guided generations of priests, religious and lay people. He was beatified in 2000.

01-31.x: Sylvester was consecrated Bishop of Rome a year after Constantine gave the Church its freedom. During his twenty-one years as pope the first great basilicas of Rome were built and the Council of Nicaea, to which he sent legates, defined the divinity of Christ.

01-31.t: Birth of Saint Louis de Montfort
01-31.x: Louis-Marie Grignion was born at Montfort in Brittany. He spent his priesthood preaching missions in the villages of western France, and his book True Devotion to Mary, found long after his death, has shaped Marian devotion ever since.

John Bosco died in Turin, worn out by his work for poor and abandoned boys. He had given them schools, workshops and a home, guided by reason, religion and kindness, and founded the Salesians to carry on the work.

02-01.t: Death of Saint Brigid of Kildare
02-01.x: By tradition Brigid died on this day in about 525 at the monastery she had founded at Kildare. Stories of her generosity to the poor spread across Ireland and beyond, and she is honoured with Patrick and Columba as a patron of Ireland.

The Roman deacon Adrian was elected pope and went on to reign for nearly twenty-four years. He was a friend and ally of Charlemagne, and he sent legates to the Second Council of Nicaea, which upheld the veneration of holy images.

The Jesuit Henry Morse was hanged, drawn and quartered at Tyburn in London for being a priest. He had earlier nursed the victims of the plague of 1636 at the risk of his life. He was canonised among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.

02-02.x: The French missionary priest Théophane Vénard was beheaded at Hanoi, aged thirty-one, after two months in a bamboo cage. The serene letters he wrote from his cage to his family later moved Saint Thérèse of Lisieux deeply.

Pope Paul VI published his apostolic exhortation on devotion to the Blessed Virgin Mary. It explained Mary’s place in the renewed liturgy and commended the Angelus and the Rosary as prayers rooted in the Gospel.

Benedict Daswa, a headmaster and catechist in the north of South Africa, was beaten to death by men of his own village. He had refused, as a Christian, to pay towards a diviner who would name a witch. He was beatified in 2015.

02-03.x: Ansgar, Archbishop of Hamburg and Bremen, died at Bremen. A monk from northern France, he had carried the Gospel to Denmark and Sweden and built the first churches there. He is known as the Apostle of the North.

Johannes Gutenberg is recorded as having died on this day at Mainz. About thirteen years earlier he had completed the first large book printed in Europe with movable type, an edition of the Latin Vulgate Bible.

02-04.t: Florence lists the books of Scripture
02-04.x: The Council of Florence issued the bull Cantate Domino, a decree of union with the Coptic Church of Egypt. It set out the Church’s faith and listed the books of the Old and New Testaments, the same canon later defined at Trent.

02-04.t: Martyrdom of Saint John de Britto
02-04.x: The Portuguese Jesuit John de Britto was beheaded at Oriyur in southern India. He had lived for years as an Indian holy man in the Madurai mission, and was condemned after a prince he had baptised put away his many wives.

In Abu Dhabi Pope Francis and Ahmad al-Tayyeb, Grand Imam of Al-Azhar, signed a joint declaration calling believers to live as brothers and to reject violence in God’s name. It was the first visit of a pope to the Arabian Peninsula.

02-05.x: By tradition Agatha was put to death on this day at Catania in Sicily, in about 251, during the persecution of Decius. She had refused the advances of a Roman official and held to her faith under torture. Her name is in the Roman Canon.

Twenty-six Christians were crucified on a hill at Nagasaki: six Franciscan missionaries, three Japanese Jesuits including Paul Miki, and seventeen Japanese laymen, three of them boys. Paul Miki preached from his cross and forgave his executioners.

02-06.t: The first diocese in the Philippines
02-06.x: Pope Gregory XIII established the diocese of Manila, the first in the Philippines. Its first bishop, the Dominican Domingo de Salazar, arrived two years later and defended the rights of the Filipino people.

Cardinal Achille Ratti of Milan was elected pope and gave his first blessing from the outer balcony of Saint Peter’s, which no pope had done since 1870. He promoted the missions, settled the Roman Question and spoke out against Nazism and communism.

The Mexican priest Mateo Correa Magallanes was shot near Durango. He had heard the confessions of prisoners awaiting execution, and when the general demanded to know what they had said, he chose death rather than break the seal of confession.

02-07.x: Thomas More was born, most probably on this day, in Milk Street in the City of London, the son of a lawyer. He became a scholar, a devoted father and Lord Chancellor of England, and died in 1535 rather than deny the authority of the pope.

Pope Pius IX died after a reign of more than thirty-one years, the longest of any pope since Saint Peter. He defined the Immaculate Conception in 1854 and called the First Vatican Council. He was beatified in 2000.

02-08.x: Jerome Emiliani, a former Venetian soldier, died at Somasca near Bergamo of a disease caught while nursing the sick. He had gathered orphans into homes and founded a congregation to care for them. He is the patron of orphans and abandoned children.

Josephine Bakhita died at Schio in northern Italy, where she had served for decades as a Canossian sister. Kidnapped in Sudan as a child and sold several times, she found freedom in Italy and forgave those who had enslaved her.

After a show trial in Budapest the communist government of Hungary sentenced Cardinal József Mindszenty, the country’s primate, to life imprisonment. He had been tortured into a confession. His witness became a sign of the Church’s suffering under communism.

02-09.t: Death of Blessed Anne Catherine Emmerich
02-09.x: Anne Catherine Emmerich, an Augustinian nun, died at Dülmen in Westphalia. Bedridden for years and bearing the wounds of Christ, she was known for her visions of his Passion and for her patience in suffering. She was beatified in 2004.

02-09.t: Death of Saint Miguel Febres Cordero
02-09.x: Brother Miguel, a De La Salle Brother from Cuenca in Ecuador, died near Barcelona. A gifted teacher who wrote textbooks used across his country, he loved best to prepare children for their first Holy Communion. He was canonised in 1984.

02-10.t: Martyrdom of Saint José Sánchez del Río
02-10.x: José Sánchez del Río, aged fourteen, was killed at Sahuayo in Mexico during the persecution of the Church. Captured while helping the Cristero fighters, he was tortured to make him renounce his faith and died professing Christ the King.

Pope Pius XI died on the eve of the tenth anniversary of the Lateran Treaty. In seventeen years he had issued encyclicals on Christian marriage and social justice, condemned Nazism and atheistic communism, and consecrated the first Chinese bishops of modern times.

Cardinal Aloysius Stepinac, Archbishop of Zagreb, died under house arrest at Krašić, his home parish. Condemned by a communist court in 1946, he had refused to separate the Church in Croatia from Rome. He was beatified as a martyr in 1998.

02-11.x: Bernadette Soubirous, aged fourteen, was gathering firewood by the river at Lourdes when she saw a lady in white in the grotto of Massabielle. It was the first of eighteen apparitions, and Lourdes became a place of prayer and healing for the world.

The Holy See and Italy signed the Lateran Treaty, ending the dispute that had lasted since Rome was taken from the popes in 1870. It created the Vatican City State and so guaranteed the pope’s independence from any government.

Speaking in Latin to a gathering of cardinals, Pope Benedict XVI announced that he no longer had the strength to carry out his office and would step down at the end of the month. No pope had resigned for almost six hundred years.

02-12.x: According to the record of their trial, forty-nine Christians from Abitinae in North Africa were brought before the proconsul at Carthage for meeting on Sunday against the emperor’s orders. They answered that they could not live without the Lord’s Supper, and died in prison.
Pope Pius XI opened Vatican Radio, built for him by Guglielmo Marconi, and spoke in Latin to listeners around the world. For the first time a pope’s own voice could reach Catholics in every country.
Pope Francis and Patriarch Kirill of Moscow met at Havana airport in Cuba. It was the first meeting between a pope and a patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church, and they signed a joint declaration.

02-13.t: Death of Blessed Jordan of Saxony
02-13.x: Jordan of Saxony, who succeeded Saint Dominic as head of the Order of Preachers, drowned in a shipwreck off the coast of Syria on his way back from the Holy Land. His preaching at the universities had drawn great numbers of students into the order.

02-13.t: Death of Sister Lúcia of Fátima
02-13.x: Sister Lúcia dos Santos, the eldest of the three children who saw Our Lady at Fátima in 1917, died at the Carmelite convent of Coimbra in Portugal, aged ninety-seven. She had outlived her cousins Francisco and Jacinta by more than eighty years.

02-14.x: Cyril, who with his brother Methodius brought the Gospel to the Slavic peoples, died in Rome shortly after becoming a monk. The brothers had devised an alphabet for the Slavs and translated the Scriptures and the liturgy into their language.

02-14.t: Paul VI approves the revised calendar
02-14.x: With the letter Mysterii Paschalis Pope Paul VI approved the reformed calendar of the Roman Rite called for by the Second Vatican Council. It gave Sunday and the seasons of the Lord first place, and came into use on 1 January 1970.

02-15.x: Pope Paschal II took under his protection the hospital of Saint John in Jerusalem, where Blessed Gerard and his brothers cared for poor and sick pilgrims. From this community grew the Order of Malta, which still serves the sick.

02-15.t: Death of Saint Claude La Colombière
02-15.x: The Jesuit Claude La Colombière died at Paray-le-Monial in France. As confessor to Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque he had recognised her visions of the Sacred Heart as genuine and helped to make the devotion known. He was canonised in 1992.

02-15.t: The abbey of Monte Cassino is destroyed
02-15.x: Allied bombers reduced the abbey of Monte Cassino to rubble during the battle for the road to Rome. Founded by Saint Benedict about the year 529, it was rebuilt on the same plan after the war and consecrated by Pope Paul VI in 1964.

02-16.x: The priest Pamphilus was beheaded with his companions at Caesarea in Palestine after two years in prison. A scholar who had built up a famous library and copied the Scriptures with care, he was the teacher of the historian Eusebius.

Joseph Allamano died in Turin, where he had been rector of the shrine of Our Lady of Consolation for forty-six years. He founded the Consolata Missionaries, priests, brothers and sisters, for the missions in Africa. He was canonised in 2024.

02-17.x: Alexis Falconieri, the last survivor of the seven Florentine merchants who founded the Servite Order, died on Monte Senario at a very great age. Out of humility he had never become a priest. The Church keeps the feast of the Seven Founders on this day.

Father Siméon Lourdel and Brother Amans, of the White Fathers, landed on the shore of Lake Victoria near Entebbe, the first Catholic missionaries in Uganda. Within a few years many of their converts gave their lives for Christ as the Uganda Martyrs.

The Gestapo arrested Father Maximilian Kolbe at Niepokalanów, the friary and publishing house he had founded near Warsaw. After three months in a Warsaw prison he was sent to Auschwitz, where he died that August.

02-18.x: The Dominican friar John of Fiesole, known as Fra Angelico, died in Rome. He painted as an act of prayer, and his frescoes still fill the cells of his friary of San Marco in Florence. He is the patron of artists.

At her third appearance at Lourdes the lady spoke to Bernadette for the first time, asking her to come to the grotto for fifteen days. She told the girl, “I do not promise to make you happy in this world, but in the other.”

02-18.t: Lorenzo Ruiz is beatified in Manila
02-18.x: Pope John Paul II beatified Lorenzo Ruiz and fifteen companions, martyred at Nagasaki in the 1630s, before a vast crowd in Manila. It was the first beatification ceremony held outside Rome. Lorenzo later became the first Filipino saint.

02-19.t: Death of Saint Conrad of Piacenza
02-19.x: Conrad, a nobleman of Piacenza, died as a hermit near Noto in Sicily. Years before, a fire he had lit while hunting destroyed fields and woods. He gave up his wealth to pay for the damage, and he and his wife both entered religious life.

02-19.t: Martyrdom of Saint Lucy Yi Zhenmei
02-19.x: Lucy Yi Zhenmei, a Chinese catechist who had consecrated her life to God and taught the faith to women and children, was beheaded in Guizhou province. A missionary priest and three laymen had been executed the day before. All were canonised in 2000.

02-20.x: Pope Martin V died in Rome. His election at the Council of Constance in 1417 had ended the Great Western Schism, during which two and then three men had claimed to be pope. He brought the papacy back to a ruined Rome and began its restoration.

Cardinal Gioacchino Pecci was elected pope at the age of sixty-seven and reigned for twenty-five years. As Leo XIII he wrote Rerum Novarum on the rights of workers, encouraged the study of Saint Thomas Aquinas and wrote often on the Rosary.

Jacinta Marto, the youngest of the three children of Fátima, died alone in a Lisbon hospital, aged nine, after a long illness borne for the conversion of sinners. She and her brother Francisco were canonised in 2017.

02-21.x: Pope Alexander III declared Thomas Becket a saint, little more than two years after the Archbishop of Canterbury was murdered in his cathedral by knights of King Henry II. His shrine became one of the great places of pilgrimage in Europe.

The Jesuit priest and poet Robert Southwell was hanged at Tyburn in London. He had ministered in secret to English Catholics for six years, and then endured three years of prison and repeated torture without betraying anyone.

02-21.t: Birth of Saint John Henry Newman
02-21.x: John Henry Newman was born in London. A leading Anglican clergyman at Oxford, he was received into the Catholic Church in 1845, founded the Oratory in Birmingham and was made a cardinal. He was canonised in 2019.

02-22.t: Death of Saint Margaret of Cortona
02-22.x: Margaret died at Cortona in Tuscany. After nine years as a nobleman’s mistress she had turned to God on finding him murdered, and spent the rest of her life in penance, prayer and nursing the sick poor as a Franciscan tertiary.

02-22.t: The first Holy Year is proclaimed
02-22.x: Pope Boniface VIII proclaimed the first Jubilee, offering a full indulgence to those who confessed their sins and visited the basilicas of Saint Peter and Saint Paul in Rome. Pilgrims came in vast numbers, and Holy Years have been kept ever since.

02-22.t: Saint Faustina sees the merciful Jesus
02-22.x: In her convent cell at Płock in Poland, Sister Faustina Kowalska saw Jesus clothed in white, with red and pale rays streaming from his heart. He asked her to have the image painted with the words “Jesus, I trust in you.”

02-23.x: By tradition Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna, was put to death in the arena on this day in about 155. A disciple of the apostle John, he refused to curse Christ, whom he said he had served for eighty-six years.

Giuseppina Vannini died in Rome. Orphaned as a child and sent home from her first novitiate because of poor health, she founded the Daughters of Saint Camillus with Blessed Luigi Tezza to nurse the sick. She was canonised in 2019.

02-24.x: The emperor Diocletian’s edict against the Christians was posted at Nicomedia. It ordered churches to be pulled down and the Scriptures burned. The persecution that followed was the fiercest the early Church endured, and lasted in places for ten years.

By tradition it was on the feast of Saint Matthias in 1208 that Francis of Assisi heard at Mass the Gospel in which Christ sends out his apostles without money, bag or sandals. He took the words as his own rule and began to preach.

Pope Gregory XIII issued the bull Inter gravissimas, correcting the calendar so that Easter would again be kept at the time fixed by the Council of Nicaea. Ten days were dropped that October, and the Gregorian calendar is now used worldwide.

02-25.x: At the ninth apparition the lady told Bernadette to drink at the spring and wash in it. Bernadette scraped at the muddy ground of the grotto, and water began to flow. The spring has never ceased, and pilgrims still bathe in its water.

Father Toribio Romo, aged twenty-seven, was shot by soldiers in his bed near Tequila in Mexico, where he had been ministering in secret during the persecution. He was canonised in 2000 and is much loved by Mexican migrants.

02-25.t: Martyrdom of Saints Versiglia and Caravario
02-25.x: The Salesian bishop Luigi Versiglia and the young priest Callisto Caravario were shot by river pirates in southern China. They had been travelling by boat on a pastoral visit and died protecting three young women catechists in their party.

02-26.x: Paula Montal died at Olesa de Montserrat in Catalonia. Having worked as a lacemaker from the age of ten, she opened schools for girls and founded the Sisters of the Pious Schools to teach them. She was canonised in 2001.

02-26.t: John Paul II prays at Mount Sinai
02-26.x: During the Great Jubilee Pope John Paul II went as a pilgrim to the monastery of Saint Catherine at the foot of Mount Sinai in Egypt. There he spoke of the Ten Commandments as the law of freedom written on the human heart.

02-27.x: The emperor Theodosius issued an edict at Thessalonica calling all his peoples to hold the faith of Nicaea, as taught by Pope Damasus and Peter of Alexandria. It marked the end of imperial support for Arianism.

Anne Line, a widow and convert who kept a house in London where priests could shelter, was hanged at Tyburn for harbouring a priest. At the scaffold she said she only wished she had received a thousand more.

Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows, a Passionist student, died of tuberculosis at Isola del Gran Sasso in central Italy, aged twenty-three. He had done nothing remarkable except to live his rule with joy and great love of the sorrowful Mother. He is a patron of young people.

02-28.t: The Fourth Council of Constantinople closes
02-28.x: The council held in Hagia Sophia under Pope Adrian II’s legates ended its work. It restored Ignatius as Patriarch of Constantinople in place of Photius and upheld the veneration of sacred images. The Catholic Church counts it as the eighth ecumenical council.

02-28.t: Pius XI calls for local clergy
02-28.x: In the encyclical Rerum Ecclesiae Pope Pius XI urged missionaries to train priests and bishops from among the peoples they served. That October he himself consecrated six Chinese bishops in Saint Peter’s.

02-28.t: Benedict XVI leaves the papal office
02-28.x: At eight o’clock in the evening the resignation of Pope Benedict XVI took effect and the See of Rome fell vacant. He had left the Vatican by helicopter for Castel Gandolfo, saying he was now simply a pilgrim on the last stage of his journey.

02-29.t: Death of Saint Oswald of Worcester
02-29.x: Oswald, Archbishop of York and Bishop of Worcester, died at Worcester just after washing the feet of twelve poor men, as he did every day in Lent. With Saints Dunstan and Ethelwold he had restored monastic life in England.

The French missionary priest Auguste Chapdelaine died in prison at Xilin in the Chinese province of Guangxi after being beaten and locked in a cage. Two of his Chinese converts, Laurence Bai Xiaoman and Agnes Cao Guiying, gave their lives in the same days.

03-01.t: Death of Saint David of Wales
03-01.x: By tradition David, monk and bishop, died on this day in about 589 at the monastery he had founded in the far west of Wales. He is said to have told his monks to be joyful, keep the faith and do the little things.

Pope Sixtus V signed the bull Aeternus ille, introducing the first official printed edition of the Latin Vulgate Bible, as the Council of Trent had requested. Its many faults were corrected in the edition issued under Clement VIII two years later.

Catherine Latapie, whose hand had been crippled by a fall, came before dawn to the grotto at Lourdes and plunged it into the new spring. Her fingers were at once restored. It was the first of the cures later recognised by the Church as miraculous.

03-02.x: Chad, first Bishop of Lichfield, died of the plague after less than three years among the people of Mercia. Saint Bede describes a humble man who preferred to travel his great diocese on foot, as the apostles had done.

03-02.t: Death of Saint Agnes of Bohemia
03-02.x: Agnes, daughter of the King of Bohemia, died in the convent of Poor Clares she had founded in Prague. She had refused royal marriages to follow the poverty of Saint Francis, and Saint Clare wrote her four letters that still survive.

Cardinal Eugenio Pacelli was elected pope on his sixty-third birthday, after only three ballots. He led the Church through the Second World War and in 1950 defined the dogma of the Assumption of Mary.

03-03.x: At its seventh session the Council of Trent affirmed that there are seven sacraments, all instituted by Christ, and that they truly give the grace they signify. It went on to set out the Church’s teaching on baptism and confirmation.

Blessed Liberat Weiss, a Franciscan from Bavaria, and his companions Samuel Marzorati and Michele Pio Fasoli were stoned to death at Gondar in Ethiopia. They had been sent to work for the unity of the Ethiopian Church with Rome.

Katharine Drexel died near Philadelphia aged ninety-six. Heiress to a banking fortune, she spent it and her life on schools and missions for Native American and African American people, and founded the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament.

03-04.x: Prince Casimir, son of the King of Poland, died of a lung disease at Grodno, aged twenty-five. He was known at court for his prayer, his chastity and his gifts to the poor. He is the patron saint of Lithuania.

Pope Pius IX re-established dioceses and bishops in the Netherlands, with an archbishop at Utrecht. Since the Reformation the country’s Catholics had been treated as mission territory, without bishops of their own, for nearly three centuries.

Less than five months after his election Pope John Paul II published Redemptor Hominis. It presented Jesus Christ, the Redeemer of man, as the centre of history, and the dignity of every human person as the path the Church must follow.

03-05.t: Death of Saint John Joseph of the Cross
03-05.x: John Joseph of the Cross, a Franciscan friar born on the island of Ischia, died in Naples. He lived in great poverty and silence yet was sought out by all kinds of people for his counsel. He was canonised in 1839.

Pope Francis landed in Baghdad, the first pope ever to visit Iraq. Over four days he prayed with the country’s battered Christian communities, visited Ur, the homeland of Abraham, and met the Shia leader Grand Ayatollah al-Sistani.

03-06.t: Death of Saint Chrodegang of Metz
03-06.x: Chrodegang, Bishop of Metz, died after more than twenty years as a leader of reform in the Frankish Church. He wrote a rule under which the clergy of his cathedral lived in community, and brought Roman chant to his diocese.

Colette of Corbie died at Ghent. Once a recluse walled into a cell, she had been called to restore the Poor Clares to the strict poverty of Saint Clare, and founded or reformed many convents in France and Flanders.

Tommaso Parentucelli, a scholar of modest birth, was elected pope and took the name Nicholas V. He gathered the manuscripts that became the Vatican Library, kept the Jubilee of 1450 and planned the rebuilding of Saint Peter’s.

03-07.t: Martyrdom of Saints Perpetua and Felicity
03-07.x: Perpetua, a young mother of noble family, and the slave Felicity, who had given birth in prison, died with their companions in the arena at Carthage. Perpetua’s own prison diary is among the earliest writings by a Christian woman.

Thomas Aquinas died at the Cistercian abbey of Fossanova, south of Rome, while travelling to the Second Council of Lyon. He was not yet fifty. Three months earlier he had stopped writing, leaving his Summa Theologiae unfinished.

03-07.t: A pope celebrates Mass in Italian
03-07.x: On the first Sunday of Lent Pope Paul VI celebrated Mass largely in Italian at the Roman parish of All Saints. It was the day the first changes to the liturgy asked for by the Second Vatican Council came into use.

03-08.t: Death of Saint John of God
03-08.x: John of God died at Granada in Spain, worn out by his labours. A former soldier and bookseller, he had been converted by a sermon and opened a hospital for the sick poor. His helpers became the Brothers Hospitallers.

03-09.t: Death of Saint Frances of Rome
03-09.x: Frances died in Rome. A wife for forty years and the mother of three children, she nursed the poor through plague and war and founded a community of women oblates, which she joined after her husband’s death.

03-09.t: Death of Saint Catherine of Bologna
03-09.x: Catherine de’ Vigri, abbess of the Poor Clares at Bologna, died there. A painter and musician brought up at the court of Ferrara, she wrote a treatise on the spiritual life. She is a patron of artists.
Dominic Savio, a pupil of Saint John Bosco in Turin, died at home aged fourteen. Don Bosco had taught him that holiness lay in doing his ordinary duties well and cheerfully. He was canonised in 1954.

03-10.x: The Jesuit John Ogilvie was hanged at Glasgow Cross. Brought up a Calvinist, he had become a Catholic abroad and returned to Scotland as a priest. Under torture he refused to name those he had served. He was canonised in 1976.

Marie-Eugénie of Jesus died in Paris. Raised with little religion, she had been converted by Lenten sermons at Notre-Dame, and at twenty-one she founded the Religious of the Assumption to educate girls. She was canonised in 2007.

The Dominican Marie-Joseph Lagrange died in the south of France. In 1890 he had founded the École Biblique in Jerusalem, where the Bible is studied in the land where it was written. His work opened the way for modern Catholic biblical scholarship.

03-11.x: On the first Sunday of Lent the empress Theodora and the patriarch Methodius led a procession into Hagia Sophia to restore the icons, ending more than a century of conflict over sacred images. Byzantine Christians still keep the day as the Triumph of Orthodoxy.

03-11.t: Martyrdom of Saint Eulogius of Córdoba
03-11.x: The priest Eulogius was beheaded at Córdoba, then the capital of Muslim Spain, for sheltering a young woman who had become a Christian. He had encouraged the Christians of the city and recorded the deaths of its martyrs.

03-12.t: Death of Saint Gregory the Great
03-12.x: Pope Gregory I died in Rome after fourteen years as pope. A monk called to govern a city ravaged by plague and war, he fed its poor, sent missionaries to England and called himself the servant of the servants of God.

Pope Gregory XV canonised Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila, Philip Neri and Isidore the Farmer in a single ceremony at Saint Peter’s. Four of them had died within the previous seventy years.

During the Great Jubilee Pope John Paul II celebrated a Mass in Saint Peter’s at which he asked God’s forgiveness for the sins committed by members of the Church over the centuries, among them sins against unity and against the Jewish people.

03-13.x: Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio, Archbishop of Buenos Aires, was elected pope. He was the first pope from the Americas, the first Jesuit and the first to take the name Francis. Before giving his blessing he asked the crowd to pray for him.

03-14.x: After a conclave of more than three months, held in a monastery in Venice because Rome was in turmoil, the Benedictine cardinal Barnaba Chiaramonti was elected. His predecessor had died a prisoner of the French, and he too would be held captive by Napoleon.

Elizabeth Ann Seton, a widow with five children, was received into the Catholic Church at Saint Peter’s Church in New York. Her decision cost her the support of many friends and relations. She had first been drawn to the faith in Italy.

Pope Pius XI signed the encyclical Mit brennender Sorge, written in German and smuggled into Germany to be read from every Catholic pulpit on Palm Sunday. It condemned the regime’s attacks on the Church and its exaltation of race and state.

03-15.t: Death of Saint Louise de Marillac
03-15.x: Louise de Marillac died in Paris. A widow, she had worked with Saint Vincent de Paul to found the Daughters of Charity, sisters who went out to serve the poor in their homes, in hospitals and in the streets.

03-15.t: Death of Saint Clement Mary Hofbauer
03-15.x: Clement Hofbauer, a Moravian baker who became a Redemptorist priest, died in Vienna. He had carried his congregation north of the Alps, working for twenty years in Warsaw and then reviving Catholic life in Vienna.

Daniel Comboni was born at Limone on Lake Garda in Italy. He gave his life to the mission in central Africa, with the conviction that Africa should be saved through Africans, and died as bishop in Khartoum in 1881.

03-16.t: Death of Saint Heribert of Cologne
03-16.x: Heribert, Archbishop of Cologne and once chancellor to the emperor Otto III, died in his city. He was loved for his care of the poor in time of famine, and was buried in the abbey he had founded at Deutz across the Rhine.

The council opened by Pope Julius II five years earlier ended under Leo X. It had healed a threatened schism and passed some measures of reform, but they went largely unheeded. Seven months later Martin Luther published his theses.

03-16.t: Martyrdom of Saint Jean de Brébeuf
03-16.x: The French Jesuit Jean de Brébeuf was tortured to death by Iroquois warriors who had overrun the Huron mission in what is now Ontario. He had lived among the Hurons for many years. His companion Gabriel Lalemant died the next morning.

03-17.x: By tradition Patrick, the apostle of Ireland, died on this day in about 461. Taken to Ireland as a slave in his youth, he escaped, and later returned as a bishop to preach the Gospel to the people who had held him captive.

03-17.t: Death of Saint Gertrude of Nivelles
03-17.x: Gertrude, abbess of the monastery her mother had founded at Nivelles in what is now Belgium, died aged thirty-three. She was known for her knowledge of Scripture and her welcome to pilgrims and Irish missionary monks.

A group of villagers came to the newly built church at Ōura in Nagasaki and told the French priest Bernard Petitjean that they shared his faith. Their families had kept it in secret, without priests, through two centuries of persecution.

03-18.t: Death of Saint Cyril of Jerusalem
03-18.x: By tradition Cyril, Bishop of Jerusalem, died on this day in 386. Exiled three times in the struggles over Arianism, he is remembered for the instructions he gave to those preparing for baptism. He is a Doctor of the Church.

03-18.t: Death of Saint Edward the Martyr
03-18.x: Edward, the young King of England, was murdered at Corfe in Dorset when he came to visit his stepmother and half-brother. Miracles were soon reported at his tomb, and he was venerated as a saint and martyr.

03-19.t: Birth of Saint José de Anchieta
03-19.x: José de Anchieta was born on Tenerife in the Canary Islands. He sailed for Brazil as a Jesuit at nineteen and spent forty-four years there, learning the Tupi language, writing its first grammar and defending the indigenous peoples.

03-19.t: First stone of the Sagrada Família
03-19.x: On the feast of Saint Joseph the foundation stone of the church of the Holy Family was laid in Barcelona. Antoni Gaudí took charge the following year and worked on it until his death. Pope Benedict XVI consecrated it in 2010.

Marcel Callo, a young printer from Rennes and a leader of the Young Christian Workers, died in the Mauthausen concentration camp, aged twenty-three. Sent to Germany as a forced labourer, he had been arrested for his apostolate among his fellow workers.

03-20.x: Cuthbert, monk and Bishop of Lindisfarne, died in his hermitage on the island of Inner Farne off the coast of Northumbria. A shepherd in his youth, he had travelled the hills on foot to preach to remote villages. His shrine is in Durham Cathedral.

John of Nepomuk, vicar general of the Archbishop of Prague, was tortured and thrown from the Charles Bridge into the river Vltava on the orders of King Wenceslaus IV. He is said to have refused to reveal the queen’s confession.

03-21.x: By tradition Benedict died on this day in about 547 at Monte Cassino, standing in the chapel with his arms raised in prayer and held up by his monks. His Rule became the pattern of monastic life in the West.

On the feast of Saint Benedict, Abbot Robert of Molesme and about twenty monks settled in the marshy woods of Cîteaux in Burgundy to follow the Rule more strictly. Their new monastery gave its name to the Cistercian Order.

03-21.t: Death of Saint Nicholas of Flüe
03-21.x: Nicholas of Flüe, a farmer, soldier and father of ten, died on his seventieth birthday after twenty years as a hermit near his home in Switzerland. His counsel had saved the Swiss cantons from civil war. He is the country’s patron saint.

03-22.x: At the Council of Vienne Pope Clement V dissolved the Order of the Temple, under heavy pressure from King Philip IV of France. He did so by an act of authority, without finding the order guilty of the charges brought against it.

03-22.t: Death of Blessed Clemens August von Galen
03-22.x: Clemens August von Galen, Bishop of Münster, died a few days after returning from Rome as a cardinal. His sermons of 1941 had publicly denounced the Nazi killing of the sick and disabled. He was beatified in 2005.

03-23.t: Death of Saint Turibius of Mogrovejo
03-23.x: Turibius, Archbishop of Lima, died at Saña in northern Peru while visiting his vast diocese, which he crossed three times, mostly on foot. He learned the local languages, defended the indigenous peoples and founded a seminary.

Rafqa, a Lebanese Maronite nun, died at the monastery of Saint Joseph at Jrabta. She had asked to share in the sufferings of Christ, and bore blindness and paralysis for nearly thirty years with constant prayer. She was canonised in 2001.

03-24.t: Death of Saint Catherine of Sweden
03-24.x: Catherine, daughter of Saint Bridget, died at Vadstena in Sweden. She had shared her mother’s years in Rome, brought her body home, and governed the first community of the Bridgettine Order.

03-24.t: Saint Ignatius keeps vigil at Montserrat
03-24.x: On the eve of the Annunciation Ignatius of Loyola, a wounded soldier lately turned to God, spent the night in prayer before the image of Our Lady at Montserrat. He left his sword and dagger there and gave his fine clothes to a beggar.

Archbishop Óscar Romero of San Salvador was shot dead while celebrating Mass in a hospital chapel. He had spoken out week by week for the poor and against the killings in his country. He was canonised in 2018.

03-25.x: On the feast of the Annunciation Pope Eugene IV consecrated the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore in Florence, as Brunelleschi’s great dome was nearing completion. The building had been begun a hundred and forty years before.

Margaret Clitherow, a butcher’s wife in York, was pressed to death for hiding priests in her house. She refused to plead so that her children would not be made to give evidence against her. She was canonised in 1970.

03-25.t: The Lady of Lourdes gives her name
03-25.x: On the feast of the Annunciation Bernadette asked the lady of the grotto who she was. She answered in the local dialect, “I am the Immaculate Conception.” Bernadette did not understand the words, and ran to repeat them to her parish priest.

03-26.x: Ludger, first Bishop of Münster, died at Billerbeck after preaching and celebrating Mass that morning. A Frisian trained at York under Alcuin, he had carried the Gospel to the Frisians and Saxons and founded the abbey of Werden.

On Easter Sunday Pope Paul VI signed his encyclical on the development of peoples. It called on rich nations to help poor ones, and taught that true development must serve the whole person and that it is the new name for peace.

03-26.t: John Paul II at the Western Wall
03-26.x: At the end of his Jubilee pilgrimage to the Holy Land Pope John Paul II prayed at the Western Wall in Jerusalem. Following Jewish custom, he placed in it a written prayer asking God’s forgiveness for the suffering caused to the Jewish people.

03-27.x: Pope Gregory XI died in Rome, little more than a year after bringing the papacy back from Avignon. The disputed election that followed led to the Great Western Schism, which divided the Church for nearly forty years.

03-27.t: The monks of Tibhirine are seized
03-27.x: In the early hours armed men took seven Trappist monks from their monastery at Tibhirine in Algeria. They had chosen to stay with their Muslim neighbours through the civil war. They were killed two months later and beatified in 2018.

03-27.t: Pope Francis blesses a world in pandemic
03-27.x: As the coronavirus pandemic spread, Pope Francis prayed alone in a rain-swept and empty Saint Peter’s Square and gave the blessing Urbi et Orbi with the Blessed Sacrament. Millions followed by television and radio.

03-28.x: Stephen Harding, an English monk and the third abbot of Cîteaux, died there. He had received the young Bernard of Clairvaux as a novice and written the Charter of Charity, which bound the Cistercian monasteries into one order.

03-28.t: Birth of Saint Teresa of Ávila
03-28.x: Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada was born at Ávila in Castile. She reformed the Carmelite Order, founded seventeen convents and wrote some of the greatest books on prayer. In 1970 she became the first woman named a Doctor of the Church.

03-29.t: The first Jesuits land in Brazil
03-29.x: Six Jesuits led by Father Manuel da Nóbrega landed at Bahia with the first governor of Brazil. It was the first Jesuit mission in the Americas, and they soon opened schools and began to learn the local languages.

Miguel Juan Pellicer, a young man of Calanda in Aragon whose leg had been amputated more than two years earlier, was found that night with the leg restored. After hearing many witnesses the Archbishop of Zaragoza declared it a miracle, attributed to Our Lady of the Pillar.

03-29.t: The Knights of Columbus are chartered
03-29.x: The Knights of Columbus, founded by Father Michael McGivney in his parish at New Haven in Connecticut, received their charter. He had begun the society to support the widows and orphans of Catholic working men. He was beatified in 2020.

03-30.x: Leonard Murialdo died in Turin, where for more than thirty years he had directed a college for poor and orphaned working boys. A friend of Don Bosco, he founded the Congregation of Saint Joseph and championed the rights of workers.

Sister Maria Restituta Kafka, a Franciscan nursing sister, was beheaded in Vienna. She had hung crucifixes in a new hospital wing and refused to take them down, and was denounced to the Gestapo over verses mocking Hitler. She was beatified in 1998.

03-31.x: On Easter Sunday Bernard of Clairvaux, at the request of Pope Eugene III, preached the Second Crusade to a great crowd on the hillside at Vézelay in Burgundy. King Louis VII of France and many others took the cross.

On Easter Sunday the chaplain of Magellan’s expedition, Father Pedro de Valderrama, celebrated the first recorded Mass in the Philippines, on the island of Limasawa. The Philippines is today home to more Catholics than any other country in Asia.

Prospero Lambertini was born in Bologna. Elected pope in 1740, he was among the most learned men of his age, respected by Protestants and unbelievers alike, and he set out the rules long followed in the canonisation of saints.

04-01.t: Catherine of Siena receives the stigmata
04-01.x: On the fourth Sunday of Lent in 1375, praying before a crucifix in the church of Santa Cristina in Pisa, Catherine of Siena received the wounds of Christ. At her own request the marks stayed hidden from others for as long as she lived.

04-01.t: Blessed Karl of Austria dies in exile
04-01.x: Karl, the last emperor of Austria and king of Hungary, died of pneumonia on Madeira aged thirty-four. He had sought peace during the First World War and bore exile and poverty with faith. John Paul II beatified him in 2004.

On Easter Sunday 1934 Pius XI canonised John Bosco, the Turin priest who gave his life to poor and abandoned boys and founded the Salesians. The Pope had met him as a young priest and spoke of him from memory.

04-02.t: Francis of Paola dies in France
04-02.x: Francis of Paola, the Calabrian hermit who founded the Order of Minims, died on Good Friday 1507 at Plessis-lès-Tours, aged ninety-one. He had been sent to France years earlier to prepare the dying King Louis XI for death.

04-02.t: Pedro Calungsod is martyred on Guam
04-02.x: Pedro Calungsod, a young Filipino catechist, and the Jesuit priest Diego Luis de San Vitores were killed at Tumon on Guam after baptising a child. Calungsod could have fled but stayed with the priest. He was canonised in 2012.

John Paul II died in the Vatican on the evening of 2 April 2005, the vigil of Divine Mercy Sunday, after more than twenty-six years as pope. Vast crowds were praying in Saint Peter’s Square below his window.

04-03.t: Richard of Chichester dies at Dover
04-03.x: Richard of Wyche, bishop of Chichester, died at Dover on 3 April 1253 while preaching a crusade. Kept out of his see for two years by Henry III, he had lived on the charity of his priests and travelled his diocese on foot.

04-03.t: Paul VI promulgates the revised Roman Missal
04-03.x: On Holy Thursday 1969 Paul VI signed the apostolic constitution Missale Romanum, promulgating the Roman Missal revised after the Second Vatican Council. It brought in new Eucharistic Prayers and a much fuller cycle of Scripture readings at Mass.

04-04.x: Ambrose, bishop of Milan, died on Holy Saturday, 4 April 397. A Roman governor chosen as bishop before he was even baptised, he defended the Church’s freedom before emperors and taught the faith to Augustine. He is a Doctor of the Church.

Isidore, archbishop of Seville for more than thirty years, died on 4 April 636. His Etymologies gathered the learning of the ancient world for the centuries that followed, and he presided over councils that shaped the Church in Spain. He is a Doctor of the Church.

Francisco Marto, one of the three shepherd children of Fatima, died at home in Aljustrel of influenza, aged ten, the day after making his first Holy Communion. He and his sister Jacinta were canonised in 2017.

04-05.x: Juliana of Liège died at Fosses on 5 April 1258. An Augustinian nun, she had worked for years, against much opposition, for a feast in honour of the Blessed Sacrament. Six years after her death Urban IV extended Corpus Christi to the whole Church.

Vincent Ferrer, a Dominican from Valencia, died at Vannes in Brittany on 5 April 1419. For twenty years he had travelled across western Europe preaching repentance, and he worked to end the schism that divided the Church between rival popes.

04-06.t: Methodius, apostle of the Slavs, dies
04-06.x: Methodius, archbishop in Moravia, died on 6 April 885. With his brother Cyril he had brought the Gospel to the Slavs, translating the Scriptures and the liturgy into their language. John Paul II named the brothers co-patrons of Europe in 1980.

The Dominican preacher Peter of Verona was ambushed and killed on the road from Como to Milan by men hired by those whose heresy he opposed. Innocent IV canonised him within a year. One of his killers later became a Dominican lay brother.

Pier Giorgio Frassati was born in Turin on 6 April 1901. A keen mountaineer and student, he quietly spent himself for the poor of the city and died at twenty-four of polio. Leo XIV canonised him in 2025.

04-07.x: On his thirty-fifth birthday Francis Xavier sailed from Lisbon for India, sent by Ignatius of Loyola at the request of the king of Portugal. The voyage took thirteen months. He never saw Europe again, and died off the coast of China in 1552.

04-07.t: John Baptist de la Salle dies
04-07.x: John Baptist de la Salle died at Rouen on Good Friday 1719. A canon of Reims, he gave up his wealth to found the Brothers of the Christian Schools and to teach the children of the poor. He is patron of teachers.

04-07.t: The candle at the Lourdes grotto
04-07.x: During the seventeenth apparition at Lourdes, Bernadette Soubirous knelt in ecstasy while the flame of the candle she held played on her hand for many minutes. Doctor Pierre Dozous, who was watching closely, found no burn on her skin.

04-08.t: Urban VI is elected in a tumult
04-08.x: With a Roman crowd demanding an Italian pope, the cardinals elected Bartolomeo Prignano, who took the name Urban VI. Within months most of them declared the election forced and chose another. The Western Schism that followed divided the Church for nearly forty years.

04-08.t: Trent defines the canon of Scripture
04-08.x: At its fourth session the Council of Trent solemnly listed the books of the Old and New Testaments received by the Church as sacred and canonical, including those the Reformers had set aside, and declared the Latin Vulgate the authentic text for public use.

04-08.t: Baltimore becomes the first American archdiocese
04-08.x: Pius VII made Baltimore an archdiocese and created the dioceses of New York, Philadelphia, Boston and Bardstown. Until then the whole of the United States had been a single diocese under John Carroll, its first bishop.

04-09.t: Thérèse enters the Carmel of Lisieux
04-09.x: Thérèse Martin entered the Carmel of Lisieux at the age of fifteen, having asked Pope Leo XIII in person for leave to enter so young. She lived there hidden for nine years, and her “little way” of trust has since taught millions.

04-10.x: Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, died on 10 April 1028. Under him the cathedral school of Chartres became one of the foremost in Europe, and he began rebuilding the cathedral after the fire of 1020. He had a deep devotion to the Mother of God.

Gregory XIII died in Rome aged eighty-three. He is remembered above all for the reformed calendar of 1582 that bears his name, and he founded or endowed many colleges for training priests, among them the Roman College that became the Gregorian University.

04-10.t: Magdalene of Canossa dies in Verona
04-10.x: Magdalene of Canossa died in Verona on 10 April 1835. Born into one of the great noble families of northern Italy, she left her palace to serve poor girls and the sick, and founded the Canossian Daughters of Charity. She was canonised in 1988.

04-11.x: Stanislaus, bishop of Kraków, was killed on the orders of King Bolesław II, by tradition by the king’s own hand during Mass, after he rebuked the king’s cruelty and excommunicated him. He is the principal patron of Poland.

Gemma Galgani died at Lucca on Holy Saturday 1903, aged twenty-five, of tuberculosis. Orphaned and often ill, she lived in close union with the suffering Christ and bore the marks of his wounds. She was canonised in 1940.

04-11.t: John XXIII signs Pacem in Terris
04-11.x: John XXIII signed Pacem in Terris on Holy Thursday 1963, less than two months before his death. It was the first encyclical addressed to all people of good will, and it grounded peace on truth, justice, charity and freedom.

04-12.t: King Edwin is baptised at York
04-12.x: On Easter Day 627 King Edwin of Northumbria was baptised at York by the missionary bishop Paulinus, in a wooden church built for the occasion and dedicated to Saint Peter. Many of his nobles and people followed him. York Minster traces its beginning to that church.

Soldiers of the Fourth Crusade, turned aside from their purpose, broke into Constantinople on 12 April 1204 and plundered the Christian city and its churches for three days. Innocent III condemned the sack, which deepened the division between East and West for centuries.

Giuseppe Moscati, physician and professor of medicine in Naples, died suddenly between patients on 12 April 1927, aged forty-six. He treated the poor without charge and saw in every sick person the suffering Christ. He was canonised in 1987.

04-13.t: Papal elections are entrusted to the cardinals
04-13.x: Nicholas II, at a synod in the Lateran, issued the decree In nomine Domini, which gave the election of the pope to the cardinals. It was meant to free the papacy from the control of Roman noble families and of emperors.

04-13.t: Catholic emancipation in Britain and Ireland
04-13.x: The Roman Catholic Relief Act received royal assent in London, allowing Catholics in Britain and Ireland to sit in Parliament and hold most public offices. It followed years of peaceful campaigning led by the Irish lawyer Daniel O’Connell.

04-13.t: John Paul II visits Rome’s Great Synagogue
04-13.x: John Paul II visited the Great Synagogue of Rome, the first pope known to have entered a synagogue since the early Church. He embraced the chief rabbi, Elio Toaff, and called the Jewish people the elder brothers of Christians.

04-14.x: By tradition Duke Mieszko I of the Polans was baptised on Holy Saturday, 14 April 966. The year is recorded in early annals, while the day is a later reckoning. His baptism brought his people into Latin Christendom and is counted as the beginning of Christian Poland.

Lydwine of Schiedam in Holland died on 14 April 1433. Crippled by a fall on the ice at fifteen, she spent nearly forty years bedridden in great pain, which she offered in union with Christ. She is a patron of the chronically ill.

Two weeks after the first Mass in the Philippines, Rajah Humabon of Cebu, his wife and many of their people were baptised by the chaplain of Magellan’s expedition. The queen was given a small statue of the Child Jesus, the Santo Niño still venerated in Cebu.

04-15.x: Damien De Veuster, a Belgian priest of the Sacred Hearts, died of leprosy at Kalawao on Molokai, aged forty-nine. For sixteen years he had been priest, nurse, builder and gravedigger to the outcasts sent there. He was canonised in 2009.

04-15.t: Pius X orders catechism in every parish
04-15.x: Pius X issued the encyclical Acerbo Nimis, tracing much of the weakness of faith in his day to ignorance of Christian doctrine. He required every parish to give regular catechism lessons to children and to adults.

Fire broke out under the roof of Notre-Dame in Paris on the Monday of Holy Week, destroying the medieval timber frame and the spire. The Crown of Thorns and the Blessed Sacrament were carried to safety. The restored cathedral reopened in December 2024.

04-16.t: Benedict Joseph Labre dies in Rome
04-16.x: Benedict Joseph Labre collapsed on the steps of a Roman church and died that evening, on the Wednesday of Holy Week, aged thirty-five. Turned away by several monasteries, he had lived as a homeless pilgrim, praying in the shrines of Europe.

Bernadette Soubirous died in the convent of Saint-Gildard at Nevers, aged thirty-five, after years of painful illness. She had left Lourdes to live hidden as a Sister of Charity. She was canonised in 1933.

04-16.t: The future Benedict XVI is born
04-16.x: Joseph Ratzinger was born at Marktl am Inn in Bavaria on Holy Saturday and baptised the same morning with the newly blessed Easter water. Theologian, cardinal and from 2005 Pope Benedict XVI, he died in 2022.

04-17.t: Vincent de Paul founds the Vincentians
04-17.x: With the backing of the Gondi family, Vincent de Paul founded the Congregation of the Mission in Paris, a company of priests to preach to the neglected country poor and to train the clergy. Its members are known as Vincentians or Lazarists.

Kateri Tekakwitha, a Mohawk and Algonquin woman baptised four years earlier, died at the mission of Kahnawake near Montreal, aged twenty-four. She had kept her faith through much hostility in her own village. In 2012 she was canonised, the first indigenous woman of North America to be declared a saint.

On Holy Thursday 2003 John Paul II signed his last encyclical, Ecclesia de Eucharistia. It taught that the Church draws her life from the Eucharist, and urged greater reverence for the Mass and for adoration of the Blessed Sacrament.

04-18.t: First stone of the new Saint Peter’s
04-18.x: Julius II laid the foundation stone of the new Saint Peter’s Basilica in Rome, to replace the church built by Constantine over the Apostle’s tomb. Bramante drew the first plan. The building took one hundred and twenty years to complete.

04-18.t: Blessed Marie of the Incarnation dies
04-18.x: Barbe Acarie died in the Carmel of Pontoise. A Parisian wife and mother of six, she brought the reformed Carmelites of Teresa of Ávila to France, and after her husband’s death entered Carmel herself as a lay sister. She was beatified in 1791.

04-19.x: Alphege, archbishop of Canterbury, was killed by drunken Danish raiders at Greenwich after seven months as their prisoner. He had forbidden his people to pay the huge ransom demanded for him, knowing how poor they were.

Leo IX died in Rome, having asked to be carried into Saint Peter’s. An Alsatian bishop chosen pope in 1049, he travelled widely holding synods against simony and clerical marriage, and began the reform that renewed the medieval Church.

On the second day of the conclave the cardinals elected Joseph Ratzinger, aged seventy-eight, who took the name Benedict XVI. From the balcony of Saint Peter’s he called himself a simple and humble labourer in the vineyard of the Lord.

04-20.x: Agnes of Montepulciano died on 20 April 1317. A Dominican prioress in her Tuscan home town, known for her prayer and for miracles, she was later greatly revered by Catherine of Siena, who made a pilgrimage to her tomb.

Leo XIII issued the encyclical Humanum Genus, the fullest of the papal condemnations of Freemasonry. He held that its principles made human reason the only guide and left no place for revealed religion.

04-21.x: Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, died on the Wednesday of Holy Week, 1109. A monk of Bec born at Aosta in the Alps, he was twice exiled for defending the Church’s freedom, and he described his work as faith seeking understanding. He is a Doctor of the Church.

04-21.t: Conrad of Parzham dies at Altötting
04-21.x: Conrad of Parzham, a Capuchin lay brother, died at Altötting in Bavaria. For forty-one years he was porter at the friary beside the Marian shrine, receiving pilgrims and the poor with unfailing patience. He was canonised in 1934.

Pope Francis died in the Vatican on Easter Monday 2025, aged eighty-eight, the day after giving his last Easter blessing to the city and the world. An Argentine Jesuit, he was the first pope from the Americas.

04-22.x: During the funeral of Alexander II the people and clergy of Rome acclaimed the archdeacon Hildebrand as pope. As Gregory VII he fought to free the Church from the control of lay rulers, a struggle that shaped medieval Europe.

The Council of Constance held its last session. It had ended the Western Schism by removing three rival claimants and, in November 1417, electing Martin V, so restoring a single pope accepted by the whole Church.

04-22.t: The first Jesuits make their vows
04-22.x: On the Friday of Easter week Ignatius of Loyola, newly elected superior general, and his companions in Rome made their solemn vows at the basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls. The Society of Jesus had been approved seven months earlier.

04-23.x: By tradition George, a soldier, was put to death for his faith at Lydda in Palestine on 23 April 303, in the persecution under Diocletian. Little else is known of him for certain, but he has been honoured since the fourth century.

Adalbert, bishop of Prague, was killed by pagan Prussians near the Baltic coast while preaching the Gospel to them. Duke Bolesław of Poland ransomed his body, and it was enshrined at Gniezno. He is a patron of Bohemia and of Poland.

04-23.t: The Society of Saint Vincent de Paul begins
04-23.x: Frédéric Ozanam, a law student at the Sorbonne, and a few friends held the first meeting of their Conference of Charity in Paris on his twentieth birthday. Visiting the poor in their homes, it grew into the worldwide Society of Saint Vincent de Paul.

04-24.x: At the Easter Vigil in Milan, in the night of 24 to 25 April 387, Bishop Ambrose baptised Augustine, then thirty-two, with his son Adeodatus and his friend Alypius. His mother Monica had prayed for this for many years.

Fidelis of Sigmaringen, a lawyer who became a Capuchin friar, was killed by armed Calvinist peasants at Seewis in the Swiss Grisons after preaching there. He is honoured as the first martyr of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith.

04-24.t: Vatican I teaches on faith and reason
04-24.x: The First Vatican Council approved the constitution Dei Filius. It taught that God can be known with certainty from created things by the light of human reason, and that faith and reason, both coming from God, can never truly contradict each other.

04-25.t: Louis IX of France is born
04-25.x: Louis IX of France was born at Poissy on 25 April 1214. King at twelve, he was known for his justice, his care for the poor and his devotion. He is said to have held the place of his baptism dearer than that of his crowning.

Peter of Saint Joseph de Betancur died in Antigua Guatemala. A Canary Islander who failed his studies for the priesthood, he became a Franciscan tertiary, opened a hospital and school for the poor and founded the Bethlehemites. He was canonised in Guatemala City in 2002.

By the constitution Scripturarum Thesaurus John Paul II promulgated the Nova Vulgata, a revision of the Latin Bible asked for by the Second Vatican Council and begun under Paul VI. It is the Church’s official Latin text for the liturgy.

04-26.x: The Sainte-Chapelle in Paris was consecrated. Louis IX had built it within his palace to house the Crown of Thorns and other relics of the Passion, which he had acquired from the Latin emperor of Constantinople.

On the Sunday after Easter the Franciscan Henrique de Coimbra celebrated the first Mass in Brazil, on an islet off the coast of Bahia, four days after the fleet of Pedro Álvares Cabral first sighted land.

04-26.t: Our Lady of Perpetual Help is enthroned
04-26.x: The ancient icon of Our Lady of Perpetual Help was carried in procession to the Redemptorist church of Sant’Alfonso in Rome and placed above the high altar. Pius IX had entrusted it to the Redemptorists so that they might make her known.

04-27.x: On Divine Mercy Sunday Pope Francis canonised John XXIII and John Paul II in Saint Peter’s Square, with Benedict XVI concelebrating. It was the first time two popes were declared saints in a single ceremony.
