04-28.x: Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort died at Saint-Laurent-sur-Sèvre, aged forty-three, worn out by preaching missions across western France. His True Devotion to Mary, lost for over a century after his death, has shaped Marian devotion ever since.

04-28.t: Peter Chanel is martyred on Futuna
04-28.x: Peter Chanel, a French Marist priest, was clubbed to death on the Pacific island of Futuna on the orders of a chief whose son had asked for baptism. Within a few years the whole island was Christian. He is patron of Oceania.

Gianna Beretta Molla, an Italian paediatrician, died a week after the birth of her fourth child. Found to have a tumour early in the pregnancy, she had insisted that the child’s life be saved before her own. She was canonised in 2004.

04-29.t: Catherine of Siena dies in Rome
04-29.x: Catherine of Siena died in Rome aged thirty-three. A Dominican tertiary with no formal schooling, she counselled popes and urged Gregory XI to return from Avignon. She is a Doctor of the Church and a patron of Italy and of Europe.
Joan of Arc, seventeen years old, rode into the besieged city of Orléans with supplies. Nine days later the English siege was broken, the first step towards the crowning of Charles VII at Reims.

04-30.x: An edict of the dying emperor Galerius, posted at Nicomedia, ended the great persecution begun under Diocletian. It allowed Christians to exist again and to rebuild their meeting places, and asked them to pray for the emperors.

04-30.t: Marie of the Incarnation dies in Quebec
04-30.x: Marie of the Incarnation died in Quebec. A widow from Tours who became an Ursuline, she sailed to New France in 1639, founded a school for French and native girls and compiled dictionaries of the Algonquin and Iroquois languages. She was canonised in 2014.

John Paul II canonised Faustina Kowalska, the Polish nun to whom Christ entrusted the message of his mercy, and announced that the second Sunday of Easter would be kept throughout the Church as Divine Mercy Sunday.

05-01.x: Pius V, a Dominican friar, died in Rome on 1 May 1572. He put the decrees of the Council of Trent into effect, issuing the Roman Catechism, Breviary and Missal, and he asked all Christendom to pray the Rosary before the battle of Lepanto.

05-01.t: The feast of Saint Joseph the Worker
05-01.x: Addressing Italian workers gathered in Saint Peter’s Square, Pius XII announced a new feast of Saint Joseph the Worker, to be kept each year on 1 May, giving a Christian meaning to the day of labour.
Benedict XVI beatified his predecessor John Paul II on Divine Mercy Sunday, before more than a million pilgrims in Rome, six years after his death. He was canonised in 2014.

05-02.x: Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria for forty-five years, died on 2 May 373. Exiled five times for refusing to compromise the faith of Nicaea that the Son is truly God, he lived to see it prevail. He is a Doctor of the Church.

Antoninus, the Dominican archbishop of Florence, died on 2 May 1459. He had founded the convent of San Marco, and as archbishop was loved for his simple life and care for the poor. His writings on moral questions were used for centuries.

John Paul II beatified Padre Pio of Pietrelcina, the Capuchin friar of San Giovanni Rotondo who bore the stigmata for fifty years and spent long hours each day hearing confessions. He was canonised three years later.

05-03.t: The king of Kongo is baptised
05-03.x: Nzinga a Nkuwu, king of Kongo in central Africa, was baptised by Portuguese priests and took the name João. His son Afonso, who reigned for more than thirty years, made the kingdom Christian and sent his own son to be ordained a bishop.

Julius II opened the Fifth Lateran Council in Rome. Meeting until March 1517, it called for reform of the clergy and the curia, but its decrees were little applied. Seven months after it closed, Luther published his theses.

Carlo Acutis was born in London to Italian parents on 3 May 1991. Raised in Milan, he went to Mass daily, built a website cataloguing Eucharistic miracles and died of leukaemia at fifteen. Leo XIV canonised him in 2025.

05-04.t: The Carthusian martyrs die at Tyburn
05-04.x: Three Carthusian priors, John Houghton, Robert Lawrence and Augustine Webster, with the Bridgettine Richard Reynolds and the priest John Haile, were executed at Tyburn for refusing to accept Henry VIII as head of the Church in England. They were the first martyrs of the English Reformation.

05-05.t: The Second Council of Constantinople opens
05-05.x: The Second Council of Constantinople, the fifth ecumenical council, opened under the emperor Justinian. It condemned writings known as the Three Chapters in an effort to reconcile those who rejected the Council of Chalcedon, whose teaching on Christ it reaffirmed.

05-05.t: “Queen of Peace” is added to the litany
05-05.x: In the third year of the First World War Benedict XV wrote to his Secretary of State ordering that the invocation “Queen of Peace, pray for us” be added to the Litany of Loreto. Eight days later Our Lady appeared at Fatima.

05-06.t: The Swiss Guard falls defending the pope
05-06.x: Mutinous troops of the emperor Charles V stormed and sacked Rome. Of the 189 Swiss Guards, 147 died near Saint Peter’s covering the escape of Clement VII to Castel Sant’Angelo. New guards are still sworn in on this day.

Francis Xavier landed at Goa after thirteen months at sea. He began by tending the sick in the hospitals and teaching children the catechism in the streets, then set out along the coasts of India and on to Malacca, the Moluccas and Japan.

05-06.t: The Korean martyrs are canonised in Seoul
05-06.x: In Seoul John Paul II canonised 103 martyrs of Korea, among them Andrew Kim Taegon, the first Korean priest, and the lay catechist Paul Chong Hasang. The Church in Korea had been begun by lay people, before any missionary arrived.

05-07.x: John of Beverley died on 7 May 721 at the monastery he had founded in Yorkshire. Bishop of Hexham and then of York, he ordained Bede, who records his holiness and his care for the sick and the poor.

05-07.t: The Second Council of Lyons opens
05-07.x: Gregory X opened the Second Council of Lyons, which achieved a short-lived reunion with the Greek Church and laid down the rules of the conclave. Thomas Aquinas died on his way to it, and Bonaventure died while it was sitting.

05-07.t: Pius X founds the Pontifical Biblical Institute
05-07.x: By the apostolic letter Vinea Electa Pius X founded the Pontifical Biblical Institute in Rome and entrusted it to the Jesuits, as a centre for advanced study of the Scriptures and of the languages of the biblical world.

05-08.t: The siege of Orléans is lifted
05-08.x: The English abandoned the siege of Orléans, nine days after Joan of Arc entered the city and a day after she was wounded by an arrow in the assault on the fortress of Les Tourelles. The city has kept the anniversary ever since.

John Vianney was born at Dardilly near Lyons on 8 May 1786 and baptised the same day. He grew up while the Revolution was closing churches, and made his first Communion in secret. He became the parish priest of Ars and patron of parish priests.

On the second day of the conclave the cardinals elected Robert Francis Prevost, an Augustinian friar born in Chicago who had served for many years in Peru. He took the name Leo XIV and became the first pope from the United States.

05-09.t: The relics of Saint Nicholas reach Bari
05-09.x: Sailors from Bari brought the relics of Nicholas of Myra into their harbour, having taken them from his tomb in Asia Minor, by then under Turkish rule. The basilica built to hold them made Bari one of the great pilgrim shrines of East and West.

05-09.t: Blessed Theresa Gerhardinger dies in Munich
05-09.x: Mary Theresa of Jesus Gerhardinger died in Munich. A Bavarian teacher, she founded the School Sisters of Notre Dame to educate girls, especially the poor, sending her sisters in twos and threes to villages. She was beatified in 1985.

05-09.t: Leo XIII’s encyclical on the Holy Spirit
05-09.x: Leo XIII issued the encyclical Divinum Illud Munus on the Holy Spirit, and directed that a novena of prayer to the Holy Spirit be made each year before Pentecost in every parish church.

05-10.x: John of Ávila died at Montilla on 10 May 1569. For some forty years he preached across Andalusia, and he was the friend and adviser of Teresa of Ávila, Ignatius of Loyola and John of God. Benedict XVI declared him a Doctor of the Church in 2012.

Father Damien De Veuster, aged thirty-three, landed at the leprosy settlement on the Kalaupapa peninsula of Molokai, having volunteered to serve there. He was meant to stay only a few months. He remained until his death sixteen years later.

05-11.x: Constantine dedicated his new capital, Constantinople, on the site of Byzantium. Founded as a Christian city, it became the seat of a patriarch and the centre of Eastern Christianity for more than eleven hundred years.

The Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci died in Beijing, where he had won the respect of Chinese scholars by his learning and by presenting the faith in terms they understood. The emperor granted land for his burial, a rare honour for a foreigner.

05-11.t: Francis de Geronimo dies in Naples
05-11.x: The Jesuit Francis de Geronimo died in Naples, where for forty years he had preached in the streets, prisons and galleys and reconciled great numbers of people to God. He was canonised in 1839.

05-12.x: Sylvester II died in Rome. As Gerbert of Aurillac he had been the most learned man of his age, a teacher of mathematics and astronomy, and he was the first French pope. He is said to have sent Stephen of Hungary his crown.

Leopold Mandić was born at Herceg Novi on the Adriatic coast. A small and frail Capuchin, he spent more than thirty years in a tiny room in Padua hearing confessions for many hours a day. He was canonised in 1983.
In Rome Leo XIII made John Henry Newman a cardinal. In his speech of thanks Newman said he had for decades resisted the idea that religion is only a matter of opinion. He was canonised in 2019.

05-13.x: Boniface IV consecrated the Pantheon in Rome, a temple given to him by the emperor Phocas, as the church of Saint Mary and the Martyrs. It was the first pagan temple in the city to become a church.

05-13.t: Our Lady first appears at Fatima
05-13.x: Three children, Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, saw a lady brighter than the sun above a holm oak at the Cova da Iria near Fatima in Portugal. She asked them to pray the Rosary daily for peace and to return each month.

John Paul II was shot and gravely wounded in Saint Peter’s Square by Mehmet Ali Ağca. He attributed his survival to Our Lady of Fatima, later visited his attacker in prison and forgave him, and had the bullet set in the crown of her statue.

05-14.x: Michael Garicoïts, a Basque priest, died at Bétharram near Lourdes on Ascension Day 1863. He had founded the Priests of the Sacred Heart of Bétharram to preach parish missions and run schools. He was canonised in 1947.

Maria Domenica Mazzarello died at Nizza Monferrato, aged forty-four. A village seamstress from Mornese, she founded with John Bosco the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians, the Salesian Sisters, to educate girls. She was canonised in 1951.

Eighty years after Rerum Novarum, Paul VI issued the apostolic letter Octogesima Adveniens. It applied Catholic social teaching to new problems such as the growth of cities, the place of women and care for the environment.

05-15.t: The first authorised Mass in Australia
05-15.x: Father James Dixon, an Irish priest transported as a convict, celebrated the first Mass permitted by the government of New South Wales, in Sydney. Catholics in the colony, most of them Irish prisoners, had been without public worship for fifteen years.

Leo XIII issued Rerum Novarum on the condition of workers. It defended just wages, the right to form unions and the right to property, and rejected both socialism and unbridled capitalism. It founded the Church’s modern social teaching.

05-15.t: Charles de Foucauld and Devasahayam are canonised
05-15.x: Pope Francis canonised ten saints, among them Charles de Foucauld, the hermit of the Sahara, the Dutch Carmelite Titus Brandsma, killed at Dachau, and Devasahayam, an eighteenth-century convert from Hinduism and the first Indian layman to be declared a saint.

05-16.t: Thomas More resigns as Lord Chancellor
05-16.x: Thomas More resigned as Lord Chancellor of England the day after the English clergy submitted to Henry VIII. He withdrew to private life and silence, but three years later was beheaded for refusing to acknowledge the king as head of the Church.

The Jesuit Andrew Bobola was seized by Cossacks at Janów in what is now Belarus and tortured to death for refusing to give up the Catholic faith. He had spent years preaching in the villages of the region. He was canonised in 1938.

Benedict XV canonised Joan of Arc in Saint Peter’s, nearly five hundred years after she was burned at Rouen. A Church court had already declared her innocent in 1456. She is a secondary patron of France.

05-17.x: Paschal Baylon, a Franciscan lay brother and former shepherd, died at Villarreal in Spain on Pentecost Sunday 1592. He spent long hours before the Blessed Sacrament, and Leo XIII named him patron of Eucharistic congresses and associations.

Paul de Maisonneuve, Jeanne Mance and some forty settlers reached the island of Montreal on 17 May 1642 to found Ville-Marie, a colony intended as a mission to the native peoples. The Jesuit Barthélemy Vimont said the first Mass there once they had landed.

Pius XI canonised Thérèse of the Child Jesus only twenty-eight years after her death at twenty-four in the Carmel of Lisieux. He called her the star of his pontificate, and later named her patron of the missions.

05-18.t: Pope John I dies in prison
05-18.x: Pope John I died in prison at Ravenna. The Arian king Theodoric had sent him to Constantinople to plead for the Arians there, and on his return, suspecting him of plotting with the emperor, had him confined. He is honoured as a martyr.

Felix of Cantalice died in Rome on 18 May 1587. For forty years this Capuchin lay brother begged food for his friary through the streets, thanking everyone with the words Deo gratias. He was a friend of Philip Neri and the first Capuchin saint.

Karol Wojtyła was born at Wadowice in southern Poland. He lost his mother at eight and his brother and father before he was twenty-one, worked in a quarry under German occupation and studied for the priesthood in secret. In 1978 he became Pope John Paul II.

05-19.x: Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, died on 19 May 988, two days after preaching on Ascension Day. Abbot of Glastonbury before he was a bishop, he restored monastic life in England after the Viking wars and advised several kings.

Celestine V died in confinement in the castle of Fumone. An aged hermit when elected in 1294, he resigned after five months, knowing himself unfit to govern. His successor Boniface VIII had him held for fear he would be used to cause a schism.

05-19.t: John Fisher and Thomas More are canonised
05-19.x: Pius XI canonised John Fisher, bishop of Rochester, and Thomas More, four hundred years after they were beheaded for refusing to deny the authority of the pope. Both had been among the most learned men in England.

05-20.x: The First Council of Nicaea, the first ecumenical council, is traditionally said to have opened on 20 May 325, though the ancient sources do not agree on the day. Some three hundred bishops met and confessed that the Son is of one substance with the Father.

Bernardine of Siena died at L’Aquila on the eve of the Ascension, 1444. A Franciscan, he was the most famous preacher in Italy in his day and spread devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus, shown by the letters IHS.

05-20.t: Ignatius of Loyola is wounded at Pamplona
05-20.x: A French cannonball shattered the leg of Íñigo de Loyola as he defended the fortress of Pamplona. During the long months of recovery he read the lives of Christ and the saints and resolved to serve God alone. He went on to found the Society of Jesus.

05-21.x: Eugène de Mazenod, bishop of Marseilles, died on 21 May 1861. He had founded the Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate to preach to the poor of Provence, and lived to send them to Canada, Ceylon and southern Africa. He was canonised in 1995.

Pius XI canonised Peter Canisius and declared him a Doctor of the Church on the same day. The Dutch Jesuit had spent his life restoring Catholic faith in the German lands, and his catechisms went through hundreds of editions.

05-21.t: The monks of Tibhirine are killed
05-21.x: Seven French Trappist monks of Tibhirine in Algeria, kidnapped in March by an armed Islamist group, were reported by their captors to have been killed on this day. They had chosen to stay among their Muslim neighbours during the civil war. They were beatified in 2018.

05-22.x: The emperor Constantine died near Nicomedia on Pentecost Sunday, having been baptised shortly before. He had ended the persecution of Christians, restored their property, built great churches in Rome and the Holy Land and summoned the Council of Nicaea.

Rita of Cascia died in the Augustinian convent at Cascia in Umbria, the date traditionally given being 22 May 1457. A wife and mother widowed by a vendetta, she became a nun and bore on her forehead a wound like that of a thorn.

05-23.x: John Baptist de Rossi died in Rome on 23 May 1764. Though epileptic, he spent forty years as a priest among the poor of the city, in its hospitals and prisons, and in a hospice for homeless women. He was canonised in 1881.

Óscar Romero, archbishop of San Salvador, was beatified in his own city before a vast crowd. He had been shot at the altar in 1980 after speaking out for the poor and against violence. He was canonised in 2018.

05-24.x: Pius VII re-entered Rome after nearly five years as a prisoner of Napoleon. In thanksgiving he established the feast of Mary Help of Christians on this day, the title under which he had prayed to her during his captivity.

05-24.t: De la Salle and Rita are canonised
05-24.x: Leo XIII canonised John Baptist de la Salle, founder of the Brothers of the Christian Schools, and Rita of Cascia, the Augustinian nun of Umbria invoked in desperate cases, more than four centuries after her death.

On Pentecost Sunday Pope Francis signed the encyclical Laudato Si’, on care for our common home. It taught that concern for the natural world, justice for the poor and peace of heart cannot be separated.

05-25.t: The Venerable Bede dies at Jarrow
05-25.x: Bede died at Jarrow on the evening of 25 May 735, as the feast of the Ascension was beginning. A monk from boyhood, he wrote the history of the English Church, and according to his pupil Cuthbert he was dictating an English translation of Saint John’s Gospel to the end.

Gregory VII died at Salerno, driven from Rome by the emperor Henry IV. His last words are reported as: “I have loved justice and hated iniquity, therefore I die in exile.” The reform he fought for outlived him.

05-25.t: Cristóbal Magallanes is shot in Mexico
05-25.x: Cristóbal Magallanes, a parish priest of Jalisco, was shot without trial at Colotlán during the persecution of the Church in Mexico, together with the young priest Agustín Caloca. He is named first among twenty-five Mexican martyrs canonised in 2000.

05-26.x: Augustine, first archbishop of Canterbury, died on 26 May in about 604. A Roman monk sent by Gregory the Great, he had landed in Kent in 597, baptised King Ethelbert and established the Church among the English.

Philip Neri died in Rome in the early hours of 26 May 1595, having heard confessions and received visitors all through the feast of Corpus Christi. Founder of the Oratory, he had renewed the faith of the city by friendship, cheerfulness and prayer.

Mariana de Jesús de Paredes died in Quito aged twenty-six. She lived as a recluse in her family’s house, and during the earthquakes and epidemic of 1645 publicly offered her life for the city. She was canonised in 1950.

05-27.x: Margaret Pole, Countess of Salisbury, aged sixty-seven, was beheaded in the Tower of London without trial. Mother of Cardinal Reginald Pole, who had opposed Henry VIII, she died protesting her innocence. She was beatified in 1886.

05-27.t: The first Code of Canon Law
05-27.x: On Pentecost Sunday Benedict XV promulgated the first Code of Canon Law, gathering the scattered laws of the Latin Church into a single ordered book. The work had been begun by Pius X in 1904, and the Code came into force at Pentecost 1918.

05-28.x: Germanus, bishop of Paris, died on 28 May 576. A former abbot known for his generosity to the poor and to prisoners, he was buried in the abbey he had helped to found, which became Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

05-28.t: The Shroud of Turin is first photographed
05-28.x: The lawyer Secondo Pia took the first successful photographs of the Shroud of Turin. On developing the glass plate that night he saw that the negative showed the figure as a lifelike positive image, which began the modern study of the cloth.

Cardinal Stefan Wyszyński, primate of Poland for thirty-two years, died in Warsaw on Ascension Day. Held in confinement by the communist government from 1953 to 1956, he had guided the Church through decades of pressure. He was beatified in 2021.

05-29.x: Constantinople fell to the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II after a siege of fifty-three days. The last emperor, Constantine XI, died defending the walls, and the great church of Hagia Sophia was turned into a mosque.

Pius XII canonised Pius X, the pope who had encouraged frequent Communion and opened the Eucharist to young children. The son of a village postman, he was the first pope to be canonised since Pius V in 1712.

05-29.t: John Paul II prays at Canterbury
05-29.x: John Paul II and the Archbishop of Canterbury, Robert Runcie, prayed side by side in Canterbury Cathedral and renewed their baptismal promises together. It was the first visit of a reigning pope to Britain.

05-30.x: At Spoleto on Pentecost Sunday Gregory IX canonised Anthony of Padua, less than a year after the Franciscan preacher’s death. It remains one of the quickest canonisations in the history of the Church.

Ferdinand III, king of Castile and León, died at Seville on 30 May 1252. He had recovered Córdoba and Seville from Moorish rule, begun the cathedral of Burgos and was known for his justice. He was canonised in 1671.

05-30.t: Joan of Arc is burned at Rouen
05-30.x: Joan of Arc, aged about nineteen, was burned at the stake in the market place of Rouen after a trial conducted by her enemies. She died calling on the name of Jesus. The verdict was annulled in 1456.

05-31.x: Labourers digging for pozzolana on the Via Salaria in Rome broke into a forgotten catacomb with painted walls. The discovery reawakened interest in the burial places of the first Christians of Rome, most of which had been lost for centuries.

Pius XI canonised John Vianney, the Curé of Ars, who for forty years drew penitents from all over France to his village confessional. Four years later the same pope named him patron of parish priests.

05-31.t: John Paul II’s letter on Sunday
05-31.x: On Pentecost Sunday John Paul II issued the apostolic letter Dies Domini on keeping Sunday holy. It presented Sunday as the day of the risen Lord, of the Eucharist and of rest, and urged Catholics to rediscover it.

06-01.x: Gregory XVI, a Camaldolese monk before he was pope, died in Rome. He strongly promoted the foreign missions, creating dozens of new dioceses and vicariates overseas, and in 1839 he condemned the slave trade.

06-01.t: Hannibal Di Francia dies at Messina
06-01.x: Hannibal Mary Di Francia died at Messina. A priest who gave his life to the orphans and poor of the worst slum in the city, he founded the Rogationists and the Daughters of Divine Zeal to pray and work for vocations. He was canonised in 2004.

06-02.t: Paul III defends the peoples of America
06-02.x: In the bull Sublimis Deus Paul III declared that the native peoples of the Americas are truly human and capable of receiving the faith, and that they must not be deprived of their liberty or their property, even if they are not Christians.

06-02.t: The future Pius X is born
06-02.x: Giuseppe Sarto was born at Riese in the Veneto, the second of ten children of the village postman. Parish priest, bishop of Mantua and patriarch of Venice, he was elected pope in 1903 as Pius X.

06-02.t: John Paul II returns to Poland
06-02.x: John Paul II began his first visit to Poland as pope. At Mass in Victory Square in Warsaw, on the eve of Pentecost, he prayed that the Holy Spirit would come down and renew the face of the land.

06-03.t: Junípero Serra founds the Carmel mission
06-03.x: On Pentecost Sunday Junípero Serra founded the mission of San Carlos Borromeo at Monterey, the second of the California missions. Moved to Carmel the following year, it became his headquarters, and he is buried there.

06-03.t: The Uganda martyrs are burned at Namugongo
06-03.x: Charles Lwanga and a group of young Catholic and Anglican converts, most of them royal pages, were burned alive at Namugongo on the orders of Mwanga, king of Buganda, for refusing to give up their faith. Twenty-two Catholic martyrs of Uganda were canonised in 1964.

John XXIII died in the Vatican on the Monday after Pentecost, aged eighty-one. Elected in 1958 and expected to be a caretaker, he had called the Second Vatican Council and opened it less than eight months before his death.

06-04.x: Francis Caracciolo died at Agnone on 4 June 1608, aged forty-four. A Neapolitan nobleman healed of a skin disease in his youth, he helped to found the Clerics Regular Minor, who keep continual adoration of the Blessed Sacrament.

06-05.x: Boniface, the English monk who became the apostle of Germany, was killed with some fifty companions by pagan raiders at Dokkum in Frisia as he waited to confirm new converts. He is buried at Fulda, the abbey founded at his direction.
John Bosco was ordained priest in Turin. That December he began gathering the homeless boys of the city for catechism and games, the beginning of his Oratory and, in time, of the Salesian family.

06-06.x: Norbert, archbishop of Magdeburg, died on 6 June 1134. A worldly cleric converted after a brush with death, he founded the canons of Prémontré, who joined the life of the cloister to preaching and parish work.

06-06.t: The Order of the Visitation is founded
06-06.x: On Trinity Sunday Francis de Sales and Jane Frances de Chantal founded the Order of the Visitation at Annecy, for women drawn to a life of prayer whose age or health barred them from the stricter orders.

Marcellin Champagnat died at the Hermitage near Saint-Chamond in France. Moved by meeting a dying boy who had never been taught about God, he founded the Marist Brothers to teach country children. He was canonised in 1999.

06-07.t: Blessed Anne of Saint Bartholomew dies
06-07.x: Anne of Saint Bartholomew died at Antwerp. A shepherdess who became a Carmelite lay sister, she was the nurse and secretary of Teresa of Ávila, who died in her arms, and later founded Carmels in France and Flanders. She was beatified in 1917.

06-07.t: The Vatican City State is born
06-07.x: The Lateran Treaty between the Holy See and Italy was ratified, and the Vatican City State came into being. It ended the dispute that had followed the loss of the Papal States in 1870 and secured the independence of the pope.

06-07.t: John Paul II prays at Auschwitz
06-07.x: John Paul II celebrated Mass at Auschwitz-Birkenau during his first return to Poland. He prayed in the cell where Maximilian Kolbe died, and paused before the memorial stones, especially those inscribed in Hebrew, Russian and Polish.

06-08.x: Viking raiders sacked the monastery of Lindisfarne off the Northumbrian coast, killing monks and plundering the church of Saint Cuthbert. The attack shocked Christian Europe and is taken to mark the beginning of the Viking age.

06-08.t: The martyrs of Japan are canonised
06-08.x: Pius IX canonised the twenty-six martyrs of Japan, crucified at Nagasaki in 1597, among them the Jesuit Paul Miki and three boys. Bishops came to Rome from all over the world for the ceremony.

06-08.t: Jacques Berthieu is martyred in Madagascar
06-08.x: The French Jesuit Jacques Berthieu was killed at Ambiatibe in Madagascar by rebels who had offered to spare him if he gave up his faith. He had stayed with his people as they fled. He was canonised in 2012.

06-09.x: Ephrem the Syrian, deacon of Edessa, died on 9 June 373, the date recorded in the Chronicle of Edessa, after caring for the victims of a famine. His hymns taught the faith in poetry of great beauty. He is a Doctor of the Church.

Columba died before the altar of his monastery on Iona, soon after midnight on 9 June 597. An Irish abbot, he had settled there thirty-four years earlier, and from Iona the faith spread through Scotland and northern England.

06-09.t: José de Anchieta dies in Brazil
06-09.x: José de Anchieta, a Jesuit from the Canary Islands, died at Reritiba in Brazil after forty-four years as a missionary. He wrote the first grammar of the Tupi language and helped to found São Paulo. He was canonised in 2014.

06-10.x: Antoni Gaudí died in Barcelona three days after being struck by a tram on his way to evening prayer. He had given his last years wholly to building the church of the Sagrada Família. Pope Francis declared him Venerable in 2025.

06-11.t: The choir of Saint-Denis is consecrated
06-11.x: The new choir of the abbey church of Saint-Denis near Paris was consecrated in the presence of King Louis VII. Abbot Suger had filled it with coloured light, and it is regarded as the first work of Gothic architecture.

06-11.t: The world is consecrated to the Sacred Heart
06-11.x: At the direction of Leo XIII the whole human race was consecrated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus, in churches throughout the world. He had announced it in the encyclical Annum Sacrum, and is said to have called it the greatest act of his pontificate.

Ignatius Maloyan, Armenian Catholic archbishop of Mardin, was shot during the deportation of his people after refusing to renounce his faith. He was one of a great number of Christians killed in 1915. Leo XIV canonised him in 2025.

06-12.x: Leo III died in Rome after a reign of twenty years. On Christmas Day 800 he had crowned Charlemagne emperor in Saint Peter’s, binding the papacy and the rulers of the West together for centuries.

Gaspar Bertoni died in Verona. A priest who spent much of his life bedridden, he founded the Stigmatines to serve bishops as preachers and teachers, and guided many people from his sickroom. He was canonised in 1989.
Pius XII canonised Dominic Savio, a pupil of John Bosco who died in 1857 a few weeks before his fifteenth birthday. His life showed that holiness is possible in the ordinary days of a schoolboy.

06-13.x: The emperor Licinius published at Nicomedia the policy he had agreed with Constantine at Milan, granting Christians and all others freedom to follow the religion they chose and ordering confiscated church property to be returned.
Anthony of Padua died at Arcella outside Padua, aged about thirty-five. A Portuguese Augustinian canon who joined the Franciscans, he was the finest preacher of his day. He is a Doctor of the Church.

06-13.t: Our Lady appears again at Fatima
06-13.x: Our Lady appeared a second time to the three children at Fatima, as about fifty people looked on. She told Lúcia that Francisco and Jacinta would soon be taken to heaven, and she showed them her Immaculate Heart.

06-14.x: Methodius, patriarch of Constantinople, died on 14 June 847. Imprisoned for years for defending the veneration of icons, he restored them to the churches in 843, an event the Eastern Churches still celebrate as the Triumph of Orthodoxy.

06-15.t: Magna Carta promises the Church’s freedom
06-15.x: King John of England sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede. Archbishop Stephen Langton of Canterbury had guided the barons in drawing it up, and its first clause promised that the English Church should be free.
Leo X issued the bull Exsurge Domine, condemning forty-one propositions drawn from the writings of Martin Luther and giving him sixty days to recant. Luther burned the bull publicly that December.

06-16.x: Lutgardis died at the Cistercian abbey of Aywières in Brabant after eleven years of blindness. Her life of prayer centred on the wounded heart of Christ, and she is counted among the earliest witnesses to that devotion.

06-16.t: Christ asks for a feast of his Heart
06-16.x: During the octave of Corpus Christi, on a day commonly given as 16 June 1675, Christ showed his heart to Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial and asked for a feast of reparation in its honour.

After a conclave of two days the cardinals elected Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti, who took the name Pius IX. His reign of nearly thirty-two years, the longest on record, saw the definition of the Immaculate Conception and the First Vatican Council.

06-17.x: The Jesuit Jacques Marquette and the explorer Louis Jolliet paddled out of the Wisconsin River into the Mississippi. Marquette, who spoke several native languages, preached to the peoples they met on the journey south.

06-18.x: Gregory Barbarigo, cardinal bishop of Padua, died on 18 June 1697. Modelling himself on Charles Borromeo, he visited every parish, enlarged the seminary and set up a press to print books in Eastern languages. John XXIII canonised him in 1960.

06-19.x: Romuald died alone in his cell at Val di Castro on 19 June 1027. A nobleman of Ravenna turned monk, he founded hermitages across Italy, among them Camaldoli, joining the solitary life to the Rule of Benedict.

Juliana Falconieri died in Florence on 19 June 1341. She founded the Servite sisters known as the Mantellate, who nursed the sick. Too ill to receive Communion at the end, she is said to have asked that the Host be laid on her breast.

06-19.t: The martyrs of Vietnam are canonised
06-19.x: John Paul II canonised 117 martyrs of Vietnam, killed between 1745 and 1862. They included bishops, priests and lay people, Vietnamese, Spanish and French, among them the priest Andrew Dung-Lac.

06-20.x: Adalbert, first archbishop of Magdeburg, died on 20 June 981. Earlier he had been sent as a missionary bishop to Kiev at the request of Princess Olga, and from Magdeburg he directed missions among the Slavs east of the Elbe.

06-20.t: Leo XIII’s encyclical on human freedom
06-20.x: Leo XIII issued the encyclical Libertas on the nature of human freedom. He taught that true liberty is the power to choose the good in accordance with reason and the law of God, and is not a licence to do anything at all.

06-21.x: Aloysius Gonzaga, a Jesuit student aged twenty-three, died in Rome of a fever caught while nursing the victims of an epidemic. Heir to a princely house, he had given up his inheritance to enter the Society. He is patron of young people.

06-21.t: John Rigby is martyred at Southwark
06-21.x: John Rigby, a Lancashire layman, was hanged, drawn and quartered at Southwark for having been reconciled to the Catholic Church. Offered his life if he would attend the established church, he refused. He was canonised in 1970.

The cardinals elected Giovanni Battista Montini, archbishop of Milan, who took the name Paul VI. He at once announced that the Second Vatican Council would continue, and he brought it to its close in 1965.

06-22.x: The Council of Ephesus, the third ecumenical council, opened under Cyril of Alexandria. It condemned the teaching of Nestorius and upheld the title Theotokos, Mother of God, for the Virgin Mary, because her Son is one divine person.
John Fisher, bishop of Rochester, was beheaded on Tower Hill, alone among the English bishops in refusing to accept Henry VIII as head of the Church. The pope had made him a cardinal a month earlier.

By the bull Inscrutabili Divinae Gregory XV formally constituted the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, which he had set up that January to direct the missions of the Church throughout the world.

06-23.x: Etheldreda, an East Anglian princess and former queen of Northumbria, died as abbess of the double monastery she had founded at Ely. Bede records that her body was found incorrupt sixteen years later.

06-23.t: Thomas Garnet is martyred at Tyburn
06-23.x: Thomas Garnet, a Jesuit priest, was hanged at Tyburn after refusing the oath of allegiance devised under James I, which denied the authority of the pope. He was the first martyr among former pupils of the English college at Saint-Omer.
Joseph Cafasso died in Turin aged forty-nine. A teacher of priests and the confessor of John Bosco, he was best known for accompanying condemned prisoners to the scaffold. He is patron of prisoners.

06-24.t: Ignatius and Xavier are ordained priests
06-24.x: Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier and several of their companions were ordained priests in Venice, where they had been serving in the hospitals while waiting for a ship to the Holy Land.

Pius XII canonised Maria Goretti in Saint Peter’s Square, before a crowd too large for the basilica. Her mother Assunta was present. Maria had died in 1902, aged eleven, forgiving the young man who stabbed her.

06-24.t: Paul VI’s encyclical on priestly celibacy
06-24.x: Paul VI issued the encyclical Sacerdotalis Caelibatus, reaffirming the celibacy of priests in the Latin Church as a sign of undivided love for Christ and for his people.

06-25.x: According to tradition it was on 25 June 1115 that Bernard, aged twenty-five, and twelve monks sent from Cîteaux founded the abbey of Clairvaux in Champagne. In his lifetime it sent out dozens of daughter houses across Europe.

06-25.t: John Neumann is ordained in New York
06-25.x: John Neumann, newly arrived from Bohemia, was ordained priest in New York by Bishop John Dubois and sent to the scattered German settlers near Buffalo. He later became a Redemptorist and bishop of Philadelphia. He was canonised in 1977.

06-25.t: The Catechism of the Catholic Church is approved
06-25.x: John Paul II approved the text of the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the first catechism for the whole Church since the Council of Trent. He promulgated it that October, thirty years after the opening of the Second Vatican Council.

06-26.x: The emperor Julian, who had abandoned Christianity and tried to restore the pagan cults, died of a spear wound in battle against the Persians after a reign of under two years. The attempt to revive paganism died with him.
Josemaría Escrivá died suddenly in Rome. A Spanish priest, he had founded Opus Dei in 1928 to teach that ordinary work and family life are a path to holiness. He was canonised in 2002.

06-26.t: The third secret of Fatima is published
06-26.x: The Holy See published the third part of the secret entrusted to the children of Fatima in 1917, a vision of a bishop in white struck down among martyrs, with a commentary by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger.

06-27.x: Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria, died on 27 June 444. He defended against Nestorius the truth that Christ is one person, God and man, and so that Mary is rightly called Mother of God. He is a Doctor of the Church.

06-27.t: Ukrainian martyrs are beatified at Lviv
06-27.x: At Lviv, during his visit to Ukraine, John Paul II beatified twenty-eight Ukrainian Greek Catholics, nearly all of them martyrs who died under Soviet rule, among them several bishops.

06-28.x: Pope Paul I died in Rome on 28 June 767. Brother and successor of Stephen II, he upheld the veneration of images against the iconoclast emperors and gave shelter in Rome to Greek monks driven out by them.

06-28.t: The First Council of Lyons opens
06-28.x: Innocent IV, who had fled from Italy, opened the First Council of Lyons. It deposed the emperor Frederick II, and considered the defence of Christendom against the Mongols and the plight of the Holy Land.
Westminster Cathedral in London, the mother church of Catholics in England and Wales, was consecrated. It had been in use since 1903, but could not be consecrated until its building debts were paid.

06-29.t: José Gregorio Hernández dies in Caracas
06-29.x: José Gregorio Hernández, a physician and professor in Caracas, was struck by a car and killed while on his way to fetch medicine for a poor patient. Known as the doctor of the poor, he was canonised in 2025, one of the first two saints of Venezuela.

In the middle of the Second World War Pius XII issued the encyclical Mystici Corporis Christi, teaching that the Church is the Mystical Body of Christ, in which all the members depend on one another and on him.
Joseph Ratzinger and his elder brother Georg were ordained priests together in the cathedral of Freising by Cardinal Michael von Faulhaber. Fifty-four years later Joseph became Pope Benedict XVI.

06-30.x: Otto, bishop of Bamberg, died on 30 June 1139. At the invitation of the duke of Poland he made two missionary journeys to Pomerania on the Baltic, baptising thousands and founding churches. He is called the apostle of Pomerania.

Paul VI was crowned in Saint Peter’s Square, the last pope to receive the tiara. The following year he laid it on the altar of Saint Peter’s as a gift for the poor, and none of his successors has worn one.

06-30.t: Paul VI’s Credo of the People of God
06-30.x: Closing the Year of Faith, Paul VI proclaimed the Credo of the People of God in Saint Peter’s Square, a solemn profession of faith that restated the Nicene Creed for a time of confusion after the Council.

07-01.t: Saint Oliver Plunkett martyred at Tyburn
07-01.x: Oliver Plunkett, Archbishop of Armagh, was hanged, drawn and quartered at Tyburn on a false charge of treason, the date being reckoned by the calendar then used in England. He was the last Catholic martyr to die there and was canonised in 1975.

The first number of L’Osservatore Romano appeared in Rome. Founded to defend the Pope and the Church in the troubled years of Italian unification, it became the daily newspaper of the Holy See and is still published today.

The Holy Office, with the approval of Pius XII, issued a decree declaring that Catholics who knowingly professed, defended or spread the materialist and anti-Christian teaching of communism incurred excommunication. It shaped Catholic life throughout the Cold War.

07-02.x: Bernardino Realino, a lawyer who became a Jesuit, died at Lecce in southern Italy after some forty years as the city’s confessor and preacher. So loved was he that the magistrates came to his deathbed to ask him to be Lecce’s patron in heaven.

07-02.t: John Paul II issues Ecclesia Dei
07-02.x: Two days after Archbishop Lefebvre consecrated four bishops without papal mandate, John Paul II issued the letter Ecclesia Dei. It lamented the break and made provision for Catholics attached to the older Latin liturgy who wished to remain in full communion with Rome.

07-03.t: Council of Orange teaches on grace
07-03.x: Bishops of southern Gaul met at Orange under Saint Caesarius of Arles and taught that even the first beginning of faith is a gift of God’s grace. Their canons, later confirmed by Rome, settled the long dispute about grace in the West.

By the bull Religionis zelus, Pope Clement VII approved a small group of Franciscans who wished to live the Rule of Saint Francis in strict poverty and prayer. They became the Capuchins, among the great preachers and missionaries of the following centuries.

The Holy Office, with the approval of Saint Pius X, issued the decree Lamentabili, which condemned sixty-five propositions drawn from Modernist writers on Scripture, revelation and dogma. It prepared the way for the encyclical Pascendi two months later.

07-04.t: Death of Saint Ulrich of Augsburg
07-04.x: Ulrich, Bishop of Augsburg for fifty years, died after a life spent caring for his people and defending his city against the Magyars. In 993 Pope John XV declared him a saint, the first canonisation known to have been made by a pope.

07-04.t: Death of Saint Elizabeth of Portugal
07-04.x: Elizabeth, widowed Queen of Portugal, died at Estremoz after travelling in the summer heat to make peace between her son and the King of Castile. Known for her charity to the poor, she had spent her last years beside the Poor Clares at Coimbra.

07-04.t: Gregory XII resigns to end the schism
07-04.x: At the Council of Constance, the envoys of Pope Gregory XII formally convoked the council in his name and then announced his resignation. His act opened the way to ending the Great Western Schism, which had divided the Church for nearly forty years.

Pier Giorgio Frassati died in Turin of polio at the age of twenty-four, probably caught from the sick he visited. A student, mountaineer and friend of the poor, he was canonised together with Carlo Acutis in September 2025.

07-05.t: The hermit Celestine V elected pope
07-05.x: After a vacancy of more than two years, the cardinals at Perugia elected the aged hermit Peter of Morrone, who took the name Celestine V. Overwhelmed by the office, he resigned five months later. He was canonised in 1313.

07-05.t: Death of Saint Anthony Mary Zaccaria
07-05.x: Anthony Mary Zaccaria, a physician who became a priest, died at Cremona aged thirty-six. He had founded the Barnabites to renew the clergy and people of northern Italy, and he spread devotion to the Eucharist and to Christ crucified.

07-06.t: Union with the Greeks at Lyon
07-06.x: At the fourth session of the Second Council of Lyon, the envoys of the Byzantine Emperor Michael VIII professed the faith of the Roman Church and the reunion of East and West was celebrated. The union did not outlast the emperor.

In the cathedral of Florence the decree Laetentur Caeli was read out in Latin and in Greek, proclaiming union between the Latin and Greek Churches. It was soon rejected in the East, but its teaching is still studied wherever Christian unity is sought.

Thomas More, once Lord Chancellor of England, was beheaded on Tower Hill for refusing to accept Henry VIII as head of the Church in England. He is reported to have said that he died the king’s good servant, but God’s first.

Maria Goretti, aged eleven, died in hospital at Nettuno a day after being stabbed while resisting an assault. Before she died she forgave her attacker, Alessandro Serenelli, who later repented in prison. She was canonised in 1950.

07-07.x: Pope Benedict XI, a Dominican, died at Perugia after a reign of little more than eight months, spent trying to heal the wounds left by the quarrel between Boniface VIII and the King of France. He was beatified in 1736.

In the archbishop’s palace at Rouen, judges appointed by Pope Callixtus III declared the trial that had condemned Joan of Arc null and void. She had been burned in that city twenty-five years earlier and was canonised in 1920.

Pius XII canonised Frances Xavier Cabrini, the Italian-born foundress who crossed the Atlantic many times to serve immigrants in the Americas. She was the first citizen of the United States to be declared a saint.

Benedict XVI issued the letter Summorum Pontificum, which allowed priests of the Latin Church to celebrate Mass according to the Roman Missal of 1962 more freely. He wrote that what earlier generations held sacred remained sacred and great.

07-08.x: Blessed Eugene III, the first Cistercian pope and a pupil of Saint Bernard, died at Tivoli. Bernard wrote for him the treatise On Consideration, urging him to remain a man of prayer amid the business of governing the Church.

On his first journey outside Rome, Pope Francis went to the island of Lampedusa. He cast a wreath on the sea for migrants drowned on the crossing from Africa and celebrated Mass, speaking against what he called the globalisation of indifference.

07-09.x: Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury, died at Slindon in Sussex. As a teacher in Paris he is believed to have devised the division of the Bible into the chapters still used today, and he had a hand in Magna Carta.

07-09.t: Saint Pius V publishes the Roman Breviary
07-09.x: With the bull Quod a nobis, Saint Pius V published the revised Roman Breviary called for by the Council of Trent. It gave the Latin Church a common form of the Divine Office that lasted, with revisions, for four centuries.

07-09.t: Martyrs of Gorkum hanged at Brielle
07-09.x: Nineteen priests and religious, most of them Franciscans, were hanged at Brielle in Holland by Calvinist forces after refusing to deny the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist and the authority of the Pope. They were canonised in 1867.

During the Boxer Rebellion two Franciscan bishops, Gregory Grassi and Francis Fogolla, were killed at Taiyuan with friars, seven Franciscan Missionaries of Mary, and Chinese seminarians and lay helpers. They were canonised among the Martyrs of China in 2000.

07-10.t: Saint Canute of Denmark killed at Odense
07-10.x: King Canute IV of Denmark was killed by rebels before the altar of Saint Alban’s church in Odense, together with his brother Benedict and seventeen companions. He was canonised in 1101 and is a patron of Denmark.

At Alcalá de Henares the printing of the Complutensian Polyglot was finished. Sponsored by Cardinal Cisneros, its six volumes set the Hebrew, Greek and Latin texts of Scripture side by side and contained the first Greek New Testament ever printed.

In the night of 9 to 10 July, eight Franciscan friars and three Maronite laymen, the Massabki brothers, were killed in Damascus after refusing to renounce Christ. Pope Francis canonised the eleven martyrs in October 2024.

07-11.t: Death of Saint Olga of Kiev
07-11.x: Olga, princess of Kiev, died after years as regent for her son. Baptised at Constantinople, she was the first ruler of the Rus to become a Christian, and her grandson Vladimir later led his people to baptism.

07-11.t: Clement VII condemns Henry VIII’s marriage
07-11.x: Clement VII declared Henry VIII’s marriage to Anne Boleyn void and pronounced him excommunicated unless he took back Catherine of Aragon. The king refused, and within eighteen months Parliament had separated England from the authority of Rome.

07-11.t: Benedict XIV rules on the Chinese rites
07-11.x: In the bull Ex quo singulari, Benedict XIV confirmed the ban on the Chinese rites honouring Confucius and the ancestors, and bound missionaries by oath to observe it. The decision weighed on the China mission until Pius XII relaxed it in 1939.

07-12.x: John Gualbert died at Passignano near Florence. He is said to have spared his brother’s killer one Good Friday and then become a monk. He founded the Vallombrosan monks and fought the buying and selling of offices in the Church.

07-12.t: Saint John Jones martyred at Southwark
07-12.x: John Jones, a Welsh Franciscan friar, was hanged, drawn and quartered at Southwark for being a priest in England, after torture at the hands of the priest-hunter Richard Topcliffe. He is one of the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.

07-12.t: Civil Constitution of the Clergy passed
07-12.x: The French National Assembly passed the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, which reorganised the Church in France under the state without the consent of the Pope. Priests who refused the oath to it were later exiled, imprisoned or killed in great numbers.

07-13.t: Death of the Emperor Saint Henry II
07-13.x: The Emperor Henry II died near Göttingen. With his wife, Saint Cunegund, he had founded the diocese of Bamberg and supported the reform of monasteries. He was canonised in 1146 and lies buried in Bamberg Cathedral.

Just after midnight, in the church of Notre-Dame at Alençon, the watchmaker Louis Martin married the lacemaker Zélie Guérin. They became the parents of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, and in 2015 were the first married couple to be canonised together.

At the third apparition at Fátima, Our Lady showed the three shepherd children a vision of hell, asked for prayer and penance for sinners, and entrusted to them what became known as the secret of Fátima.

07-14.t: Saint Pius V promulgates the Roman Missal
07-14.x: By the bull Quo primum, Saint Pius V promulgated the Roman Missal revised after the Council of Trent and required its use throughout the Latin Church, except where a rite more than two hundred years old was in use.

Francis Solano, a Spanish Franciscan, died in Lima after some twenty years as a missionary in what are now Argentina, Paraguay and Peru. He learned the languages of the peoples he served and is said to have drawn them with his violin.

07-14.t: Death of Saint Camillus de Lellis
07-14.x: Camillus de Lellis, a former soldier and gambler, died in Rome. After his conversion he founded the Ministers of the Sick, who wore a red cross and vowed to serve the sick even at the risk of their lives. He is a patron of nurses.

07-15.t: Death of Saint Vladimir of Kiev
07-15.x: Vladimir, Grand Prince of Kiev, died at Berestove near his capital. Baptised about 988, he had brought his people to Christianity, built churches and cared for the poor. He is honoured as a saint by Catholics and Orthodox alike.

07-15.t: Crusader Church of the Holy Sepulchre consecrated
07-15.x: Fifty years to the day after the First Crusade took Jerusalem, the rebuilt Church of the Holy Sepulchre was consecrated. The new building gathered Calvary and the tomb of Christ under one roof, and much of it still stands.

Bonaventure, Franciscan Minister General, cardinal and theologian, died at Lyon while the Second Council of Lyon was sitting. Known as the Seraphic Doctor, he joined deep learning to a tender love of Christ. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1588.

07-15.t: Trent orders a seminary in every diocese
07-15.x: At its twenty-third session the Council of Trent set out its teaching on the sacrament of Holy Orders and decreed that every diocese should have a seminary to train its priests, one of the most lasting reforms of the council.

Blessed Ignatius de Azevedo and thirty-nine fellow Jesuits, sailing to the missions of Brazil, were killed off the Canary Islands when Huguenot corsairs captured their ship. Their bodies were thrown into the sea. They were beatified in 1854.

07-16.t: Excommunication laid on the altar of Hagia Sophia
07-16.x: Cardinal Humbert, legate of the late Pope Leo IX, laid a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. The patriarch answered in kind, and the day became the symbol of the schism between East and West.

Less than two years after his death, Francis of Assisi was canonised in his home town by Pope Gregory IX, who had known him well. The next day the pope laid the first stone of the basilica built to receive his body.

07-16.t: Our Lady and the brown scapular
07-16.x: According to Carmelite tradition, Our Lady appeared on this day to Saint Simon Stock, prior general of the order, at Aylesford or Cambridge in England, and gave him the brown scapular as a sign of her protection.

Junípero Serra raised a cross and celebrated Mass on a hill above San Diego Bay, founding the first of the twenty-one Franciscan missions of Alta California. Serra himself founded nine of them. He was canonised in 2015.

On the feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, Bernadette Soubirous saw the Blessed Virgin for the eighteenth and last time. The grotto had been fenced off, so she knelt across the river Gave, and said afterwards that she had never seen Our Lady so beautiful.

07-17.x: Twelve Christians from Scilli in North Africa, seven men and five women, were tried at Carthage and beheaded for refusing to swear by the emperor. The record of their trial is the oldest dated document of the Church in Africa.

At the final session of the First Council of Lyon, Pope Innocent IV pronounced the Emperor Frederick II deposed. The council had also sought help for the Holy Land and for the Christian lands overrun by the Mongols.

07-17.t: Death of Saint Jadwiga of Poland
07-17.x: Jadwiga, Queen of Poland, died at Kraków aged about twenty-five, soon after the death of her newborn daughter. Her marriage to Jogaila of Lithuania had led to the baptism of that nation, and she left her jewels to restore the university of Kraków.

Sixteen Carmelites of Compiègne went to the guillotine in Paris singing hymns, each renewing her vows before the prioress, who died last. Ten days later the Terror ended. Pope Francis declared them saints in 2024.

07-18.x: At Avignon, forty-nine years after his death, Thomas Aquinas was canonised by Pope John XXII. The pope is reported to have said that Thomas had worked as many miracles as he had written articles.

07-18.t: Our Lady appears to Catherine Labouré
07-18.x: Late in the night, in the chapel of the Daughters of Charity in the rue du Bac in Paris, the novice Catherine Labouré saw the Blessed Virgin for the first time and spoke with her. The vision of the Miraculous Medal followed in November.

At its fourth session the First Vatican Council approved the constitution Pastor Aeternus, defining the primacy of the Pope and his infallibility when he solemnly defines a doctrine of faith or morals. A thunderstorm broke over Saint Peter’s as the votes were cast.

07-19.x: Pope Symmachus died after a reign of fifteen years troubled by a rival claimant and by riots in Rome. He upheld the independence of the Roman see, ransomed captives and sent help to African bishops exiled by the Arian Vandals.

07-19.t: Pius XII among the bombed of Rome
07-19.x: After the first Allied bombing of Rome struck the district of San Lorenzo, Pius XII left the Vatican and went among the people in the ruins, praying with them and giving out money. The ancient basilica of Saint Lawrence was badly damaged.

07-20.x: Hormisdas, a deacon of Rome, was elected pope. Five years later his formula of faith, signed by the bishops of the East, ended the Acacian schism that had separated Rome and Constantinople for thirty-five years.

At the village of Zhujiahe in northern China, during the Boxer Rebellion, the French Jesuits Léon-Ignace Mangin and Paul Denn were killed with a great number of Chinese Catholics who had taken refuge in the church. The two priests were canonised in 2000.

Leo XIII died at the age of ninety-three after a reign of twenty-five years. He had renewed the study of Saint Thomas Aquinas, opened the Vatican archives to scholars and, in Rerum Novarum, set out the Church’s teaching on labour and justice.

07-21.t: Paul III founds the Roman Inquisition
07-21.x: By the bull Licet ab initio, Paul III set up a commission of cardinals in Rome to guard the faith against heresy. From it descends, after many reforms, the present Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith.

Under pressure from the Bourbon courts, Clement XIV signed the brief Dominus ac Redemptor suppressing the Society of Jesus. More than twenty thousand Jesuits were dispersed and their schools and missions closed or handed over. Pius VII restored the Society in 1814.

07-22.t: Belgrade saved from the Ottoman siege
07-22.x: The Ottoman army besieging Belgrade was driven off by the forces of John Hunyadi and a crusade of peasants preached by the Franciscan Saint John of Capistrano. Pope Callixtus III had ordered church bells to be rung at midday for the defenders.

07-22.t: Death of Saint Lawrence of Brindisi
07-22.x: Lawrence of Brindisi, Capuchin preacher, master of the biblical languages and papal envoy, died at Lisbon on his sixtieth birthday while on a mission to the King of Spain. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1959.

07-22.t: Birth of Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque
07-22.x: Margaret Mary Alacoque was born at Verosvres in Burgundy. As a Visitation nun at Paray-le-Monial she received the visions of the Sacred Heart of Jesus from which the feast and the First Friday devotion spread through the Church.

07-22.t: Saints Philip Evans and John Lloyd martyred
07-22.x: The Jesuit Philip Evans and the secular priest John Lloyd were executed at Cardiff for being priests, in the panic stirred up by the invented Popish Plot. Both Welshmen, they were canonised among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales in 1970.

07-23.x: Pope Clement V named the Franciscan John of Montecorvino Archbishop of Khanbaliq, the Beijing of today. Working almost alone since about 1294, he had built churches, baptised thousands and translated the New Testament and the Psalms for his people.

07-23.t: Death of Saint Bridget of Sweden
07-23.x: Bridget of Sweden died in Rome soon after returning from a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. A widow and mother of eight, she founded the Bridgettine order and urged the popes to return from Avignon. She is a patron of Europe.

Twelve young priests and seminarians, some ordained only the day before, climbed to the shrine of Our Lady of Fourvière in Lyon and pledged to found a Society of Mary. From that promise grew the Marist priests, brothers and sisters.

07-24.t: Death of Saint Kinga of Poland
07-24.x: Kinga, a Hungarian princess who became Duchess of Kraków, died in the Poor Clare convent she had founded at Stary Sącz. As duchess she had given her dowry to help rebuild the land after the Mongol raids. John Paul II canonised her in 1999.

07-24.t: Saint John Boste martyred at Durham
07-24.x: John Boste, a priest who had ministered in secret across the north of England for more than ten years, was hanged, drawn and quartered at Durham. He is said to have recited the Angelus as he climbed the ladder. He was canonised in 1970.

Three Discalced Carmelite nuns of Guadalajara, Sisters María Pilar, Teresa and María Ángeles, were shot in the street in the first days of the Spanish Civil War. In 1987 they became the first martyrs of that persecution to be beatified.

07-25.x: On the death of his father at York, Constantine was proclaimed emperor by the army. Six years later he took Rome, and in 313 he and Licinius granted Christians freedom of worship, bringing the age of persecution to an end.

07-25.t: Henry IV of France becomes a Catholic
07-25.x: Henry IV of France, raised a Protestant, made his abjuration before the Archbishop of Bourges at the abbey of Saint-Denis and was received into the Catholic Church. His conversion brought the French Wars of Religion towards their end.

Paul VI signed the encyclical Humanae Vitae on married love and the transmission of life. It reaffirmed that the unitive and procreative meanings of marriage belong together, and so that contraception is not morally permissible.

07-26.t: Blessed Andrew of Phú Yên martyred
07-26.x: Andrew of Phú Yên, a catechist of about nineteen trained by the Jesuit Alexandre de Rhodes, was put to death in central Vietnam for refusing to give up his faith. He is honoured as the first martyr of Vietnam and was beatified in 2000.

07-26.t: Saint Titus Brandsma killed at Dachau
07-26.x: Titus Brandsma, a Dutch Carmelite priest, professor and journalist, was killed by lethal injection in Dachau. He had been arrested for urging Catholic newspapers to refuse Nazi propaganda. He gave his rosary to the nurse who killed him. He was canonised in 2022.

07-26.t: Father Jacques Hamel killed at Mass
07-26.x: Father Jacques Hamel, aged eighty-five, was killed by two Islamist attackers while celebrating morning Mass at Saint-Étienne-du-Rouvray in Normandy. The cause for his beatification as a martyr was opened in the diocese of Rouen soon afterwards.

07-27.t: Death of Pope Saint Celestine I
07-27.x: Pope Celestine I died, by the reckoning now generally accepted. He had condemned the teaching of Nestorius, sent legates to the Council of Ephesus in 431, and sent Palladius as the first bishop to the Christians of Ireland.

07-28.t: Saint Pedro Poveda martyred in Madrid
07-28.x: Pedro Poveda, a priest who had worked among the cave dwellers of Guadix and founded the Teresian Association for lay teachers, was shot in Madrid in the first days of the Spanish Civil War. He was canonised in 2003.

07-28.t: Death of Saint Alphonsa of India
07-28.x: Sister Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception, a Franciscan Clarist of the Syro-Malabar Church, died at Bharananganam in Kerala after years of illness borne quietly. In 2008 she became the first woman born in India to be canonised.

07-28.t: Blessed Stanley Rother killed in Guatemala
07-28.x: Father Stanley Rother, a priest of Oklahoma who had served the Tz’utujil people of Santiago Atitlán in Guatemala for thirteen years, was shot dead in his rectory. In 2017 he became the first martyr born in the United States to be beatified.

07-29.x: King Olaf Haraldsson fell at the battle of Stiklestad while trying to regain his throne. Miracles were soon reported at his grave, and devotion to him did much to root the Christian faith in Norway, whose patron he remains.

Blessed Urban II died in Rome two weeks after the First Crusade, which he had preached, took Jerusalem, and before the news could reach him. A former monk of Cluny, he had carried forward the reforms of Saint Gregory VII.

Louis Martin, father of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, died at La Musse near Évreux after years of illness. All five of his surviving daughters entered religious life. He was canonised together with his wife Zélie in 2015.

07-30.x: Three priests, Thomas Abel, Edward Powell and Richard Fetherston, were executed at Smithfield in London for defending Queen Catherine’s marriage and refusing the royal supremacy. They were dragged there on hurdles beside three Protestants who were burned for heresy.

Leopold Mandić, a Capuchin friar born on the coast of Montenegro, died in Padua. Small and frail, he spent long hours each day in the confessional for more than thirty years, and offered his life for the reunion of Eastern Christians with Rome.

07-31.t: Death of Saint Ignatius of Loyola
07-31.x: Ignatius of Loyola died in Rome. A Basque soldier converted while recovering from a wound, he wrote the Spiritual Exercises and founded the Society of Jesus, which at his death numbered about a thousand members across Europe, Asia and the Americas.

07-31.t: Death of Saint Justin de Jacobis
07-31.x: Justin de Jacobis, an Italian Vincentian and first Vicar Apostolic of Abyssinia, died of fever in what is now Eritrea. He lived as the people did, trained a native clergy, and suffered prison and exile for his flock.

Solanus Casey, a Capuchin friar, died in Detroit. Ordained without faculties to preach or hear confessions, he served for decades as a doorkeeper, and thousands came to him for counsel and prayer. He was beatified in 2017.

Paul VI landed at Entebbe in Uganda, the first reigning pope to visit Africa. That day he told the bishops of the continent that they could and must have an African Christianity. He went on to honour the Uganda Martyrs.

07-31.t: Juan Diego canonised in Mexico City
07-31.x: In the Basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City, John Paul II canonised Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin, to whom Our Lady appeared in 1531. He was the first indigenous saint of the Americas.

08-01.x: Peter Faber, the first priest among the companions of Ignatius of Loyola, died in Rome, worn out by his journeys across Europe and about to set out for the Council of Trent. Gentle in his dealings with Protestants, he was canonised in 2013.

08-01.t: Marie of the Incarnation lands at Quebec
08-01.x: Marie of the Incarnation landed at Quebec with two other Ursulines and three hospital sisters from Dieppe. She opened the first school for girls in New France and learned several native languages. She was canonised in 2014.

Alphonsus Liguori died at Pagani near Naples aged ninety. A lawyer who became a priest, he founded the Redemptorists to preach to the neglected poor, and his moral theology won him the title of Doctor of the Church.

Benedict XV sent a note to the heads of the nations at war proposing a peace without victors, with disarmament, arbitration, freedom of the seas and the return of occupied lands. The governments set it aside, and the war went on for fifteen more months.

08-01.t: Bishop Pierre Claverie killed in Oran
08-01.x: Pierre Claverie, Dominican Bishop of Oran in Algeria, was killed by a bomb at the door of his house together with his young Muslim driver, Mohamed Bouchikhi. He was beatified at Oran in 2018 with eighteen other martyrs of Algeria.

08-02.x: According to Franciscan tradition, the little chapel of the Portiuncula near Assisi was consecrated on this day, and Saint Francis announced the indulgence he had obtained from Pope Honorius III for all who would visit it, known as the Pardon of Assisi.

08-02.t: Paul VI at the shrine of Namugongo
08-02.x: At Namugongo in Uganda, Paul VI consecrated the altar of the shrine rising on the spot where Saint Charles Lwanga and his companions were burned in 1886. He had canonised the Uganda Martyrs five years earlier, during the Second Vatican Council.

08-03.x: Stefan Wyszyński was born at Zuzela in Poland. As Primate he led the Church through three decades of communist rule, including three years of internment, and he encouraged the future John Paul II. He was beatified in 2021.

08-03.t: Bishop von Galen condemns Nazi euthanasia
08-03.x: From the pulpit of Saint Lambert’s in Münster, Bishop Clemens August von Galen denounced the Nazi killing of the mentally ill and the disabled as plain murder. Copies of the sermon spread across Germany. He was beatified in 2005.

08-04.t: Death of the Curé of Ars
08-04.x: John Vianney died at Ars near Lyon after forty-one years as its parish priest. He had turned a neglected village to God and spent up to sixteen hours a day in the confessional. He is the patron of parish priests.

In the encyclical Aeterni Patris, Leo XIII called for Christian philosophy to be restored in Catholic schools according to the mind of Saint Thomas Aquinas. It began a revival of Thomist thought that marked Catholic learning for a century.

Cardinal Giuseppe Sarto, Patriarch of Venice and the son of a village postman, was elected pope and took the name Pius X. He chose as his motto to restore all things in Christ, and opened Holy Communion to young children.

Enrique Angelelli, Bishop of La Rioja in Argentina and a defender of the rural poor, died in what the military regime presented as a road accident. A court later found that he had been murdered. He was beatified as a martyr in 2019.

08-05.x: Oswald, King of Northumbria, was killed in battle at Maserfield against the pagan Penda of Mercia, in 642 by Bede’s reckoning. He had brought Saint Aidan from Iona to preach to his people and often acted as his interpreter.

At Mornese in Piedmont, Mary Mazzarello and her first companions made their vows before Saint John Bosco, founding the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians. The Salesian Sisters became one of the largest congregations of women in the Church.

08-06.x: Under the Emperor Valerian’s edict, Pope Sixtus II was seized while teaching his people in a cemetery on the Appian Way and beheaded on the spot with deacons of the Roman Church. Saint Cyprian recorded the news in a letter.

Dominic died at Bologna, lying on ashes in a borrowed habit. A Castilian priest, he had founded the Order of Preachers to teach the faith by study, poverty and preaching, and in five years had sent his friars across Europe.

Paul VI died at Castel Gandolfo on the feast of the Transfiguration. He had brought the Second Vatican Council to its close, carried out its reforms, and was the first pope in modern times to travel to every inhabited continent.

08-06.t: John Paul II signs Veritatis Splendor
08-06.x: John Paul II signed the encyclical Veritatis Splendor on the foundations of the Church’s moral teaching. It held that freedom depends on truth and that some acts are always wrong, whatever the intention or the circumstances.

08-07.x: Cajetan of Thiene died in Naples. A priest of noble family, he founded the Theatines with Gian Pietro Carafa to reform the clergy by example, served the incurably sick, and set up a loan bank to protect the poor from usurers.

A few months after his return from captivity under Napoleon, Pius VII celebrated Mass at the Gesù in Rome and had the bull Sollicitudo omnium ecclesiarum read out, restoring the Society of Jesus throughout the world after forty-one years of suppression.

08-08.x: Mary MacKillop died in Sydney. With Father Julian Tenison Woods she had founded the Sisters of Saint Joseph to teach poor children in the Australian bush, and she bore an unjust excommunication with patience. She is Australia’s first canonised saint.

08-08.t: Children admitted to early First Communion
08-08.x: By the decree Quam singulari, approved by Saint Pius X, children were to be admitted to confession and Holy Communion once they reached the age of reason, at about seven. Until then many had been made to wait until twelve or older.

08-09.x: Pope Innocent IV approved the Rule of Saint Clare with the bull Solet annuere. It was the first rule for religious written by a woman. The bull was brought to Clare on her deathbed, and she died on 11 August.

Marianne Cope, a Franciscan sister from Syracuse in New York, died at Kalaupapa on the Hawaiian island of Molokai. She had cared for people with leprosy there for thirty years and nursed Saint Damien in his last illness. She was canonised in 2012.

Edith Stein, a Jewish philosopher who became a Carmelite as Sister Teresa Benedicta of the Cross, was killed with her sister Rosa in the gas chambers of Auschwitz, most probably on this day. She was canonised in 1998 and is a patron of Europe.

Franz Jägerstätter, an Austrian farmer, husband and father of three daughters, was beheaded at Brandenburg for refusing to serve in Hitler’s army, which he judged he could not do as a Christian. He was beatified in 2007.

The atomic bomb dropped on Nagasaki exploded above Urakami, the heart of Japanese Catholicism. It destroyed the cathedral and killed some eight thousand of the parish’s twelve thousand faithful, descendants of Christians who had kept the faith in secret for centuries.

08-10.x: Lawrence, deacon of Rome, was put to death four days after Pope Sixtus II in the persecution of Valerian. Tradition holds that he presented the poor as the treasures of the Church and was roasted on a gridiron.

According to the order’s tradition, Peter Nolasco founded the Order of Our Lady of Mercy in the cathedral of Barcelona, in the presence of King James I of Aragon. Its friars pledged themselves to ransom Christian captives, even at the cost of their own freedom.

Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli, a farmer’s son from Sotto il Monte near Bergamo, was ordained a priest in the church of Santa Maria in Monte Santo in Rome. Fifty-four years later he was elected pope as John XXIII and called the Second Vatican Council.

08-11.t: Death of Saint Clare of Assisi
08-11.x: Clare died at San Damiano outside Assisi, where she had lived for more than forty years in poverty and prayer with her sisters. The first woman to follow Saint Francis, she was canonised only two years later.

With the bull Transiturus, Pope Urban IV extended the feast of Corpus Christi to the whole Latin Church. By tradition Saint Thomas Aquinas composed the hymns and prayers for its Mass and Office, among them the Pange lingua.

At Orvieto, Pope Boniface VIII canonised Louis IX of France, twenty-seven years after the king’s death on crusade at Tunis. Louis was remembered for his justice, his care of the poor and the Sainte-Chapelle he built for the Crown of Thorns.

08-11.t: Death of Saint John Henry Newman
08-11.x: John Henry Newman died at the Birmingham Oratory aged eighty-nine. A leader of the Oxford Movement, he became a Catholic in 1845, founded the Oratory in England and was made a cardinal in 1879. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 2025.

08-12.x: Blessed Innocent XI died after nearly thirteen years as pope. Austere and upright, he resisted the claims of Louis XIV over the Church in France and helped to form the alliance that relieved Vienna in 1683. He was beatified in 1956.

Karl Leisner died of tuberculosis at Planegg near Munich, a few months after his liberation from Dachau. Imprisoned as a deacon, he had been secretly ordained in the camp by a French bishop who was a fellow prisoner, and celebrated Mass only once.

Pius XII issued the encyclical Humani Generis, warning against opinions that threatened to undermine Catholic doctrine. It also left scholars free to study the evolution of the human body, while holding that every soul is created directly by God.

08-13.t: Death of Saint Maximus the Confessor
08-13.x: Maximus the Confessor died in exile in Lazica, on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, aged about eighty. For teaching that Christ has a human will as well as a divine will, his tongue and right hand had been cut off.

John Berchmans, a Flemish Jesuit student, died in Rome at twenty-two, holding his crucifix, his rosary and his rule. He sought holiness in doing ordinary duties well and is a patron of altar servers. He was canonised in 1888.

08-14.x: At Mainz, Johann Fust and Peter Schöffer finished printing a Latin Psalter, the first printed book to carry its date and the names of its printers. Made for use in choir, it was also the first to be printed in more than one colour.

On a hill outside Otranto in southern Italy, Ottoman troops beheaded some eight hundred men of the captured city who had refused to renounce Christ. A tailor, Antonio Primaldo, spoke for them all. Pope Francis canonised them in 2013.

Michael McGivney, a parish priest in Connecticut and the son of Irish immigrants, died of pneumonia at thirty-eight. He had founded the Knights of Columbus to support Catholic working men and their widows and orphans. He was beatified in 2020.

08-14.t: Saint Maximilian Kolbe killed at Auschwitz
08-14.x: Maximilian Kolbe, a Polish Conventual Franciscan, was killed by injection in the starvation bunker at Auschwitz, having offered to take the place of a condemned man with a family. John Paul II canonised him as a martyr of charity in 1982.

08-15.t: Death of Saint Stephen of Hungary
08-15.x: Stephen, first King of Hungary, died on the feast of the Assumption, having entrusted his kingdom to Our Lady. He had founded dioceses and monasteries and brought the Magyar people into the Church. He was canonised in 1083.

08-15.t: First Mass in the Sistine Chapel
08-15.x: Pope Sixtus IV celebrated the first Mass in the newly built chapel of the Vatican Palace and dedicated it to the Assumption of Our Lady. The Sistine Chapel, later painted by Michelangelo, is where the cardinals meet to elect the pope.

08-15.t: Ignatius and companions vow at Montmartre
08-15.x: In a chapel on Montmartre in Paris, Ignatius of Loyola and six companions, among them Francis Xavier and Peter Faber, vowed poverty, chastity and a pilgrimage to Jerusalem or else service of the Pope. From their vow grew the Society of Jesus.

Francis Xavier came ashore at Kagoshima with two Jesuit companions and the Japanese convert Anjirō, bringing the Gospel to Japan for the first time. Within a few decades the Church there counted hundreds of thousands of faithful.

08-15.t: First bishop of the United States consecrated
08-15.x: In the chapel of Lulworth Castle in Dorset, John Carroll was consecrated first Bishop of Baltimore, and so the first Catholic bishop of the United States. His diocese then covered the whole of the new nation.

08-16.x: John Bosco was born to a peasant family at Becchi in Piedmont and lost his father at two. As a priest in Turin he gave his life to poor and abandoned boys and founded the Salesians to continue the work.
