08-17.t: Death of Saint Clare of Montefalco
08-17.x: Clare of Montefalco, an Augustinian abbess in Umbria, died after a life of penance and contemplation of the Passion of Christ. People of every rank had sought her counsel at the convent grille. She was canonised by Leo XIII in 1881.

After a conclave of six months, Cardinal Prospero Lambertini of Bologna was elected pope as Benedict XIV. Learned, witty and moderate, he set out the rules for canonisation that long remained in force and was respected even by critics of the Church.

08-18.x: Alberto Hurtado, a Chilean Jesuit, died of cancer in Santiago aged fifty-one. He founded the Hogar de Cristo to shelter the homeless, defended the rights of workers and drew many young people to the faith. He was canonised in 2005.

08-19.t: Death of Saint Louis of Toulouse
08-19.x: Louis of Anjou, who had given up the crown of Naples to become a Franciscan, died at Brignoles in Provence aged twenty-three, only months after being made Bishop of Toulouse. He was canonised in 1317.

John Eudes died at Caen in Normandy. A tireless preacher of parish missions, he founded seminaries and the Congregation of Jesus and Mary, and composed the first Mass and Office in honour of the Hearts of Jesus and Mary.

Because the three children of Fátima had been held by the local administrator on 13 August, Our Lady appeared to them six days later at Valinhos, near their village. She asked them to go on praying the Rosary and to make sacrifices for sinners.

08-20.t: Stephen of Hungary raised to the altars
08-20.x: With the approval of Pope Gregory VII, the relics of King Stephen of Hungary were solemnly raised at Székesfehérvár in the presence of King Ladislaus, which at that time amounted to canonisation. The day is still kept as Hungary’s national feast.

08-20.t: Death of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux
08-20.x: Bernard died at Clairvaux, the abbey he had founded thirty-eight years earlier and from which he sent out some sixty-eight daughter houses. Counsellor of popes and kings, he is remembered above all for his writings on the love of God.

Pius VII died in Rome aged eighty-one after a reign of twenty-three years. A Benedictine monk, he had signed a concordat with Napoleon, endured five years as his prisoner, and returned to rebuild the Church after the Revolution.

Pius X died in the Vatican within weeks of the outbreak of the First World War, which he had dreaded and grieved over. He had encouraged frequent Communion, reformed Church music and begun the first Code of Canon Law.

08-21.t: Birth of Saint Francis de Sales
08-21.x: Francis de Sales was born at the château of Sales in Savoy. As Bishop of Geneva he won back many to the Church by patience and kindness, and his Introduction to the Devout Life taught lay people that holiness was for them too.

On a wet evening at Knock in County Mayo, fifteen people of all ages saw Our Lady, Saint Joseph and Saint John the Evangelist beside an altar with a lamb and a cross at the gable of the parish church. No words were spoken.

Victoire Rasoamanarivo, a noblewoman of Madagascar, died at Antananarivo. When the missionaries were expelled in 1883 she held the Catholic community together, leading prayer in the churches until the priests could return. She was beatified in 1989.

08-22.x: Philip Benizi died at Todi. Trained as a physician, he entered the Servites as a lay brother, became their prior general and saved the young order from suppression. He is said to have hidden in the hills when there was talk of electing him pope.

08-22.t: Saints John Kemble and John Wall martyred
08-22.x: Two priests were executed on the same day in the aftermath of the invented Popish Plot: John Kemble, aged eighty, at Hereford after fifty-four years of ministry, and the Franciscan John Wall at Worcester. Both were canonised in 1970.

08-22.t: Paul VI arrives in Latin America
08-22.x: Paul VI landed at Bogotá in Colombia for the International Eucharistic Congress, the first pope to visit Latin America. On arrival he knelt and kissed the ground. Two days later he opened the general conference of Latin American bishops.

08-23.x: The Tower of David, the last stronghold in Jerusalem, surrendered to the Khwarezmian horsemen who had stormed and sacked the city that summer. Jerusalem did not come under Christian rule again until 1917.

08-23.t: A baptismal vigil at World Youth Day in Paris
08-23.x: At the Longchamp racecourse John Paul II kept vigil with hundreds of thousands of young people and baptised ten of them, drawn from every continent. At Mass the next morning he announced that Saint Thérèse of Lisieux would be declared a Doctor of the Church.

08-24.t: Sack of Rome by the Goths
08-24.x: Alaric’s Goths entered Rome and plundered it for three days, sparing those who took refuge in the great basilicas. The shock moved Saint Augustine to begin The City of God, on the earthly city and the city that endures.

Heinrich Cremer, vicar of Saint Stephen’s in Mainz, noted that he had finished rubricating and binding a copy of the Bible printed by Johann Gutenberg. His note, in the copy now in Paris, is the earliest dated witness to the first printed Bible.

08-24.t: Teresa of Ávila founds Saint Joseph’s
08-24.x: In Ávila, Teresa of Jesus opened the small convent of Saint Joseph with four novices, the first house of her reform of Carmel. From it grew the Discalced Carmelites, given to poverty, enclosure and prayer for the Church.

08-24.t: Death of Saint Rose of Lima
08-24.x: Rose of Lima, a Dominican tertiary who lived in prayer and penance in a hut in her parents’ garden and cared for the sick poor, died aged thirty-one. In 1671 she became the first person born in the Americas to be canonised.

08-25.t: Death of Saint Louis IX of France
08-25.x: King Louis IX of France died of sickness in the crusader camp before Tunis, lying on a bed of ashes. A just ruler, husband and father of eleven, he fed the poor at his own table and built the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris.

Joseph Calasanz died in Rome aged ninety. A Spanish priest, he opened in 1597 what is counted the first free public school in Europe and founded the Piarists to teach poor children. He bore the suppression of his order with patience.

Helena Kowalska was born at Głogowiec in Poland, the third of ten children of a poor farming family. As Sister Faustina she recorded in her diary the message of Divine Mercy, and in 2000 she became the first saint canonised in the new millennium.

08-26.x: Mariam Baouardy, a Melkite Catholic from Galilee who became the Carmelite Sister Mary of Jesus Crucified, died at the Carmel she had helped to found in Bethlehem. Unlettered and deeply prayerful, she was canonised in 2015.

Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu, the future Mother Teresa of Calcutta, was born to an Albanian family in Skopje and baptised the next day. At eighteen she left home to join the Loreto Sisters and was sent to India.

08-26.t: Poland renews its vows at Jasna Góra
08-26.x: With Cardinal Wyszyński still interned by the communist government, about a million pilgrims gathered at Jasna Góra in Częstochowa and made the vows of the Polish nation to Our Lady, which he had written in captivity. His empty chair stood by the altar.

On the first day of voting in the conclave, Cardinal Albino Luciani, Patriarch of Venice, was elected pope. He was the first to take a double name, honouring his two predecessors. He died thirty-three days later and was beatified in 2022.

08-27.t: Saint David Lewis martyred at Usk
08-27.x: David Lewis, a Jesuit who had served the Catholics of South Wales for thirty years and was known as the father of the poor, was executed at Usk. He was the last of the Welsh martyrs and was canonised in 1970.

Dominic Barberi, an Italian Passionist who had longed since his youth to work in England, died at Reading after eight years of mission there. In October 1845 he had received John Henry Newman into the Church. He was beatified in 1963.

08-28.t: Council of Carthage lists the Scriptures
08-28.x: A council of African bishops meeting at Carthage listed the books that might be read in church as divine Scripture. Its list of the Old and New Testaments agrees with the canon the Catholic Church holds today.

Augustine died at Hippo in North Africa, where he had been bishop for thirty-four years, while the Vandals besieged the city. He had the penitential psalms hung on the wall by his bed. His writings have shaped Christian thought ever since.

Junípero Serra died at Mission San Carlos in Carmel, California, aged seventy. A Franciscan professor from Majorca, he had spent thirty-five years as a missionary in Mexico and California. Pope Francis canonised him in 2015.

08-29.t: Pius VI dies a prisoner in France
08-29.x: Pius VI died a prisoner of the French Directory at Valence, aged eighty-one, having been carried over the Alps in his last illness. Many thought the papacy would end with him, yet a successor was elected in Venice within seven months.

Edmund Rice died at Waterford in Ireland. A prosperous merchant and widower, he gave his fortune to educate poor boys and founded the Christian Brothers and the Presentation Brothers. He was beatified in 1996.

Jeanne Jugan died at Saint-Pern in Brittany, unknown to the young sisters around her as their foundress. She had begun the Little Sisters of the Poor by giving her own bed to a blind old woman. She was canonised in 2009.

Sister Euphrasia Eluvathingal, a Carmelite of the Syro-Malabar Church, died at Ollur in Kerala. She spent nearly all her religious life in one convent, where people knew her as the praying mother. She was canonised in 2014.

08-30.t: Saint Margaret Ward hanged at Tyburn
08-30.x: Margaret Ward was hanged at Tyburn for helping a priest to escape from prison with a rope. She refused to say where he was hidden. John Roche, the boatman who had helped her, died with her, as did a priest and three other laymen.

Blessed Alfredo Ildefonso Schuster, Benedictine monk and Cardinal Archbishop of Milan for twenty-five years, died at Venegono. A scholar of the liturgy, he guided his diocese through fascism and war. He was beatified in 1996.

08-31.t: Death of Saint Aidan of Lindisfarne
08-31.x: Aidan, monk of Iona and first Bishop of Lindisfarne, died leaning against the wall of the church at Bamburgh. Travelling on foot, he had won the people of Northumbria to Christ by his gentleness and his care for the poor.

09-01.t: Death of Adrian IV, the English pope
09-01.x: Adrian IV, born Nicholas Breakspear near St Albans and the only Englishman to be pope, died at Anagni. Before his election he had reorganised the Church in Norway and Sweden as papal legate.

09-01.t: Gregory X elected after nearly three years
09-01.x: After nearly three years, the longest papal election in the Church’s history, the cardinals at Viterbo elected Teobaldo Visconti, then on crusade in the Holy Land. As Gregory X he called the Second Council of Lyon and laid down rules for the conclave.

09-01.t: Leo XIII establishes the hierarchy in India
09-01.x: By the letter Humanae salutis auctor, Leo XIII set up a regular hierarchy of archdioceses and dioceses in India and Ceylon in place of the vicariates apostolic, a sign that the Church there had taken firm root.

09-02.t: Death of Saint Emeric of Hungary
09-02.x: Emeric, only surviving son and heir of Saint Stephen of Hungary, was killed by a wild boar while hunting. His father had written for him a book of counsels on Christian kingship. Father and son were both canonised in 1083.

In Paris, mobs broke into the prisons and killed hundreds of inmates. At the Carmelite house in the rue de Vaugirard, three bishops and more than a hundred priests who had refused the oath to the Civil Constitution were put to death. In 1926, 191 victims were beatified.

09-03.x: Gregory, a monk and former prefect of Rome, was consecrated pope while plague raged in the city. He reformed worship and the care of the poor, sent Augustine to convert the English, and called himself servant of the servants of God.

A month into the First World War, Cardinal Giacomo della Chiesa, Archbishop of Bologna, was elected pope as Benedict XV. He kept the Holy See impartial, pleaded for peace, and organised relief for prisoners and the hungry on every side.

Shortly before the last session of the Second Vatican Council, Paul VI issued the encyclical Mysterium Fidei. It reaffirmed the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist, the term transubstantiation, and the worship given to the Blessed Sacrament outside Mass.

09-03.t: Pius IX and John XXIII beatified
09-03.x: John Paul II beatified two popes together in Saint Peter’s Square: Pius IX, who called the First Vatican Council, and John XXIII, who called the Second. With them were beatified Tommaso Reggio, William Chaminade and Columba Marmion.

09-04.x: Pope Francis canonised Mother Teresa of Calcutta in Saint Peter’s Square on the eve of the nineteenth anniversary of her death, during the Jubilee of Mercy. She had founded the Missionaries of Charity to serve the poorest of the poor.
Pope Francis beatified John Paul I, pope for thirty-three days in 1978, in a rain-soaked Saint Peter’s Square. He was remembered for his smile, his humility and his plain way of teaching the faith.

09-05.x: Mother Teresa died in Calcutta aged eighty-seven. From one woman tending the dying in the streets, her Missionaries of Charity had grown to some four thousand sisters in more than a hundred countries. India gave her a state funeral.

09-06.x: After two days of battle at the river Frigidus, on the eastern edge of Italy, the Christian Emperor Theodosius defeated the usurper Eugenius, whose supporters had restored pagan worship in Rome. It was the last armed stand of the old religion in the empire.

09-07.x: Agents of King Philip IV of France and the Colonna family stormed the papal palace at Anagni and held Boniface VIII prisoner until the townspeople freed him. He died a month later, and the papacy soon passed under French influence at Avignon.

At Košice, in present-day Slovakia, Calvinist soldiers tortured three priests who would not renounce the Catholic faith: the Croatian canon Mark Križin and the Jesuits Stephen Pongrácz and Melchior Grodziecki. Two died that day and Pongrácz the next. John Paul II canonised them in 1995.

09-07.t: Legion of Mary founded in Dublin
09-07.x: At Myra House in Francis Street, Dublin, Frank Duff and a small group of lay people, most of them young women, met around a statue of Our Lady and began the work that became the Legion of Mary, now found across the world.

09-07.t: Carlo Acutis and Pier Giorgio Frassati canonised
09-07.x: In Saint Peter’s Square, Pope Leo XIV canonised Carlo Acutis, who died of leukaemia in 2006 aged fifteen, and Pier Giorgio Frassati, who died in 1925 aged twenty-four. Acutis is the first saint of the generation raised with the internet.

09-08.t: First Mass at Saint Augustine, Florida
09-08.x: Pedro Menéndez de Avilés landed in Florida and founded Saint Augustine. Father Francisco López de Mendoza Grajales celebrated Mass on the shore, the beginning of the oldest parish in what is now the United States.

Peter Claver died at Cartagena in Colombia. For nearly forty years the Spanish Jesuit met the slave ships as they docked, bringing food, medicine and the faith to the captives. He called himself the slave of the Africans for ever.

Frédéric Ozanam died at Marseille aged forty. A professor at the Sorbonne, husband and father, he had founded the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul as a student of twenty, so that faith might be shown in service of the poor.

Saint Pius X issued the encyclical Pascendi Dominici Gregis against Modernism, which he described as the synthesis of all heresies. It rejected the view that dogma is only the changing expression of religious feeling.

09-09.x: Jacques-Désiré Laval, a French doctor who became a Spiritan priest, died at Port Louis in Mauritius. For twenty-three years he had lived among the newly freed slaves, teaching and baptising many thousands. His was the first beatification of John Paul II, in 1979.

09-10.x: Nine Franciscan friars led by Blessed Agnellus of Pisa landed at Dover, sent by Saint Francis himself. Within months they had houses at Canterbury, London and Oxford, and the order spread quickly through England.

09-10.t: Death of Saint Nicholas of Tolentino
09-10.x: Nicholas of Tolentino, an Augustinian friar, died in the town where he had spent thirty years preaching, hearing confessions and visiting the sick and the dying. He is especially invoked for the souls in purgatory. He was canonised in 1446.

On a hill at Nagasaki fifty-five Christians were put to death, some burned and some beheaded: Jesuit, Dominican and Franciscan missionaries, and Japanese and Korean lay people, among them women and small children. Blessed Charles Spinola was one of them.

09-10.t: Mother Teresa’s call within a call
09-10.x: On a train to Darjeeling for her annual retreat, Sister Teresa of the Loreto Sisters heard what she called a call within a call: to leave the convent and serve Christ in the poorest of the poor. Her sisters keep it as Inspiration Day.

09-10.t: Pope Francis celebrates Mass in East Timor
09-10.x: Pope Francis celebrated Mass at Tasitolu near Dili in East Timor before a crowd reckoned at some six hundred thousand, close to half the people of the country. Almost all East Timorese are Catholic.

09-11.x: By a charter dated this day, in 910 by the usual reckoning, Duke William of Aquitaine founded the abbey of Cluny in Burgundy and placed it under the protection of the Apostles Peter and Paul, free of any lord or bishop. Cluny became the heart of monastic reform in Europe.

John Gabriel Perboyre, a French Vincentian missionary, was strangled on a cross at Wuchang after a year of imprisonment and torture, having been betrayed by a catechumen. In 1996 he became the first saint of China to be canonised.

09-12.t: Vienna relieved from the Ottoman siege
09-12.x: A relief army led by King John III Sobieski of Poland broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna. In thanksgiving, Blessed Innocent XI extended the feast of the Holy Name of Mary to the whole Church.
In Warsaw, Cardinal Stefan Wyszyński, Primate of Poland from 1948 to 1981, was beatified together with Mother Elżbieta Róża Czacka, the blind foundress of a community serving blind people at Laski.

09-13.t: Basilica of the Holy Sepulchre dedicated
09-13.x: The basilica built by the Emperor Constantine over Calvary and the tomb of Christ in Jerusalem was dedicated in the presence of many bishops. The feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, kept on the following day, grew from this celebration.

09-13.t: Leo XIII rules on Anglican orders
09-13.x: In the letter Apostolicae Curae, Leo XIII gave judgement on a question long discussed and declared ordinations carried out according to the Anglican rite to be invalid, on the grounds of defect of form and of intention.

Before a crowd of many thousands at the Cova da Iria, Our Lady appeared to the three children of Fátima for the fifth time. She asked them to keep praying the Rosary for the end of the war and promised a miracle in October.

In Vilnius, Sister Faustina Kowalska recorded a vision of an angel sent to chastise the world, and found herself pleading for mercy in words she heard within. The next day she was taught to pray them on rosary beads as the Chaplet of Divine Mercy.

09-14.x: Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, was beheaded before a crowd of his people after refusing to sacrifice to the gods. On hearing the sentence he answered with thanks to God. His letters and his treatise on the unity of the Church are still read.

John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople, died at Comana in Pontus, forced to march into ever more distant exile for rebuking the vices of the court. His last words are recorded as glory to God for all things.

About the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross, while praying on Mount La Verna, Francis of Assisi saw a crucified seraph and received in his hands, feet and side the wounds of Christ. Brother Leo was with him on the mountain.

At the tomb of Saint Peter in Rome, Cajetan of Thiene, Gian Pietro Carafa and two companions made their solemn vows, founding the Theatines, the first of the orders of clerks regular that helped to renew the clergy in the sixteenth century.

Paul VI canonised Elizabeth Ann Seton, a New York widow and convert who founded the Sisters of Charity and opened a free Catholic school at Emmitsburg in Maryland. She was the first person born in the United States to be declared a saint.

09-14.t: John Paul II signs Fides et Ratio
09-14.x: John Paul II signed the encyclical Fides et Ratio, on the relationship between faith and reason. It opens by likening them to two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth.

09-15.t: Death of Saint Catherine of Genoa
09-15.x: Catherine of Genoa died in the hospital where she had nursed the sick and the plague-stricken for more than thirty years. Converted suddenly in 1473 from a worldly and unhappy life, she left a teaching on purgatory as the fire of God’s love.

For the fifteenth centenary of the death of Saint Jerome, Benedict XV issued the encyclical Spiritus Paraclitus. It defended the truth and inspiration of Scripture and urged all the faithful to read the Gospels and the rest of the New Testament every day.

09-15.t: Paul VI establishes the Synod of Bishops
09-15.x: On the second day of the last session of the Second Vatican Council, Paul VI established the Synod of Bishops by the letter Apostolica sollicitudo, so that bishops from across the world could regularly advise the pope.

09-15.t: Father Pino Puglisi killed by the Mafia
09-15.x: Father Pino Puglisi, parish priest of the Brancaccio district of Palermo, was shot by the Mafia outside his home on his fifty-sixth birthday. He had drawn the young away from organised crime. He was beatified as a martyr in 2013.

09-16.t: Pope Saint Martin I dies in exile
09-16.x: Pope Martin I died in exile at Cherson in the Crimea, worn down by hunger and ill-treatment. He had been seized in Rome and condemned at Constantinople for upholding the two wills of Christ. He is the last pope honoured as a martyr.

The Third Council of Constantinople held its final session. It taught that Christ has two wills, divine and human, in harmony, as he has two natures, and so brought the Monothelite controversy to an end.

Andrew Kim Taegon, the first Korean-born priest, was beheaded by the Han River near Seoul at twenty-five, thirteen months after his ordination in Shanghai. He was canonised in Seoul in 1984 with 102 other martyrs of Korea.

09-17.t: Death of Saint Hildegard of Bingen
09-17.x: Hildegard of Bingen died at her monastery on the Rupertsberg by the Rhine, aged eighty-one. Abbess, visionary, composer and writer on medicine and nature, she preached reform to clergy and people. Benedict XVI declared her a Doctor of the Church in 2012.

09-17.t: Trent teaches on the sacrifice of the Mass
09-17.x: At its twenty-second session the Council of Trent taught that the Mass is a true sacrifice, in which the one sacrifice of Christ on the cross is made present and its saving power applied, and that it is offered for the living and the dead.

09-17.t: Saint Pius V commends the Rosary
09-17.x: In the bull Consueverunt Romani Pontifices, Saint Pius V, himself a Dominican, described and commended the Rosary as the praying of a hundred and fifty Hail Marys, with an Our Father for each ten, while meditating on the life of Christ.

Robert Bellarmine, Jesuit and cardinal, died in Rome. His Controversies answered the Protestant reformers point by point with learning and courtesy, and his catechisms were used for three centuries. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1931.

09-18.t: Death of Saint Joseph of Cupertino
09-18.x: Joseph of Cupertino, a Conventual Franciscan, died at Osimo. Slow at his studies and often rapt in ecstasy, he was reported by many witnesses to rise from the ground at prayer, and his superiors kept him away from the crowds. He is a patron of students.

09-19.t: Death of Saint Theodore of Canterbury
09-19.x: Theodore of Tarsus, a Greek monk sent from Rome at the age of sixty-six to be Archbishop of Canterbury, died after twenty-one years in office. He organised the English Church into dioceses and founded a famous school at Canterbury.

09-19.t: Our Lady appears at La Salette
09-19.x: High in the French Alps near La Salette, two young cowherds, Mélanie Calvat and Maximin Giraud, saw a woman in light, seated and weeping, who called for conversion, prayer and respect for Sunday. The Bishop of Grenoble approved the apparition in 1851.
At Cofton Park in Birmingham, Benedict XVI beatified John Henry Newman during his visit to Britain, setting aside his custom of leaving beatifications to others. Newman was canonised in 2019.

09-20.x: Cardinals who had declared the election of Urban VI invalid met at Fondi and elected Robert of Geneva, who took the name Clement VII and settled at Avignon. So began the Great Western Schism, which divided Catholic Europe for thirty-nine years.

09-20.t: Rome taken and the Papal States ended
09-20.x: Italian troops breached the walls of Rome near the Porta Pia, and Pius IX ordered his small army to cease resistance. The Papal States, which had lasted more than a thousand years, came to an end, and the First Vatican Council was suspended.

While praying before a crucifix in the choir of the friary at San Giovanni Rotondo, the Capuchin Padre Pio received the wounds of Christ in his hands, feet and side. He bore them for fifty years, until shortly before his death.

09-20.t: Mar Ivanios received into communion with Rome
09-20.x: At Kollam in Kerala, Archbishop Mar Ivanios, Bishop Mar Theophilos and three companions of the Malankara Orthodox tradition were received into full communion with Rome. From this small beginning grew the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church.

09-21.x: Bishop Laurent Imbert and the priests Pierre Maubant and Jacques Chastan, of the Paris Foreign Missions, were beheaded at Saenamteo near Seoul. They had given themselves up to spare their Korean flock further torture. They were canonised in 1984.

On the feast of Saint Matthew, the sixteen-year-old Jorge Mario Bergoglio stopped at his parish church in Buenos Aires to go to confession and came away knowing that God was calling him to be a priest. In 2013 he was elected Pope Francis.

09-22.x: Paul Chong Hasang, a lay leader of the Korean Church, was beheaded outside the walls of Seoul. He had travelled to Beijing many times to beg for priests and had written to the Pope asking for a bishop. He was canonised in 1984.

09-23.t: Death of Saint Adomnán of Iona
09-23.x: Adomnán, ninth abbot of Iona, died on the island. He wrote the Life of Saint Columba, and at the Synod of Birr in 697 he won acceptance for the Law of the Innocents, protecting women, children and clergy in time of war.

By the Concordat of Worms, the Emperor Henry V gave up the claim to invest bishops with ring and staff, and Pope Callixtus II allowed him to be present at their election. The agreement ended the long investiture struggle between papacy and empire.

09-23.t: Death of Saint Pio of Pietrelcina
09-23.x: Padre Pio died at San Giovanni Rotondo, the day after celebrating Mass for the fiftieth anniversary of his stigmata. A Capuchin friar and confessor sought out by multitudes, he founded a great hospital for the suffering. He was canonised in 2002.

At the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception in Washington, Pope Francis canonised Junípero Serra, apostle of California. It was the first canonisation ever celebrated in the United States.

09-24.x: The Second Council of Nicaea opened under the Patriarch Tarasius, with legates of Pope Hadrian I present. It restored the veneration of holy images, teaching that the honour paid to an icon passes to the one it represents.

Gerard, a Venetian monk who became the first Bishop of Csanád and tutor to Saint Emeric, was killed at Buda in a pagan uprising. Tradition says he was thrown from the hill above the Danube that now bears his name.

09-24.t: Death of Blessed Herman of Reichenau
09-24.x: Blessed Herman of Reichenau, called the Cripple, died at his abbey on Lake Constance. Unable to walk and barely able to speak, he became a renowned scholar of music, mathematics and the stars. The Salve Regina has long been attributed to him.

09-24.t: Catherine McAuley opens the House of Mercy
09-24.x: On the feast of Our Lady of Mercy, Catherine McAuley opened the House of Mercy in Baggot Street, Dublin, built with her inheritance to shelter and teach poor women and girls. From it grew the Sisters of Mercy, founded four years later.

09-25.x: The Peace of Augsburg allowed each prince of the Holy Roman Empire to choose between the Catholic faith and the Lutheran confession for his territory. It ended a generation of religious war in Germany and made the division of Western Christendom lasting.

Late at night, Poland’s communist authorities arrested the Primate, Cardinal Stefan Wyszyński, who had refused to let the state control appointments in the Church. He was held for three years, during which he wrote the vows of the nation to Our Lady.

09-25.t: Our Lady appears at San Nicolás
09-25.x: At San Nicolás de los Arroyos in Argentina, Gladys Quiroga de Motta, a mother and grandmother, saw Our Lady while praying the Rosary at home. The Bishop of San Nicolás declared the apparitions worthy of belief in 2016.

09-26.x: Thérèse Couderc died at Lyon. She had founded the Sisters of the Cenacle at La Louvesc to give retreats to women, was set aside as superior, and spent decades in hidden tasks without complaint. She was canonised in 1970.

Giovanni Battista Montini was born at Concesio near Brescia. Elected pope as Paul VI in 1963, he guided the Second Vatican Council to its end and carried through its reforms. He was canonised in 2018.

09-27.t: Paul III approves the Society of Jesus
09-27.x: By the bull Regimini militantis Ecclesiae, Pope Paul III approved the Society of Jesus, at first limited to sixty members. Ignatius of Loyola and his companions placed themselves at the Pope’s disposal for missions anywhere in the world.

09-27.t: Death of Saint Vincent de Paul
09-27.x: Vincent de Paul died in Paris aged about eighty, seated in his chair. He had founded the Congregation of the Mission and, with Saint Louise de Marillac, the Daughters of Charity, and organised relief for the poor, foundlings, galley slaves and provinces ruined by war.

09-27.t: Teresa of Ávila named Doctor of the Church
09-27.x: Paul VI proclaimed Saint Teresa of Ávila a Doctor of the Church, the first woman to be given the title. A week later he conferred it on Saint Catherine of Siena.

09-28.t: Pope Saint Pontian resigns in exile
09-28.x: Exiled to the mines of Sardinia under the Emperor Maximinus, Pope Pontian resigned so that the Church of Rome could choose a successor. It is the first papal resignation on record and the earliest exact date in the history of the popes.

Wenceslaus, Duke of Bohemia, was killed at the church door in Stará Boleslav by followers of his brother Boleslaus, in 935 or, by an older reckoning, 929. Soon honoured as a martyr, he became the patron of the Czech people.

John Paul I died in the night after only thirty-three days as pope, aged sixty-five. In that short time his warmth and simple way of teaching won him the name of the smiling pope. He was beatified in 2022.

09-29.t: Saint Leo the Great consecrated pope
09-29.x: Leo, a deacon of Rome recalled from a mission in Gaul, was consecrated pope. His Tome on the two natures of Christ was acclaimed at the Council of Chalcedon, and in 452 he went out to meet Attila and turned him back from Rome.

09-29.t: Saint Lorenzo Ruiz martyred at Nagasaki
09-29.x: Lorenzo Ruiz, a married clerk from Manila and father of three, died at Nagasaki after days of torture, hung head down over a pit. He had declared that he would give a thousand lives for God. He is the first Filipino saint.

René Goupil, a French surgeon working with the Jesuit mission, was killed with a tomahawk at the Mohawk village of Ossernenon after making the sign of the cross over a child. He was the first of the eight North American Martyrs to die.

09-29.t: Hierarchy restored in England and Wales
09-29.x: By the letter Universalis Ecclesiae, Pius IX restored a hierarchy of diocesan bishops in England and Wales, the first since the Reformation, with Nicholas Wiseman as Archbishop of Westminster and twelve other sees.

09-30.x: Jerome died at Bethlehem, by the traditional reckoning on this day in 420. He had spent more than thirty years there in study and prayer, translating the Scriptures from Hebrew and Greek into the Latin Bible later called the Vulgate.

09-30.t: Death of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux
09-30.x: Thérèse of the Child Jesus died of tuberculosis in the Carmel of Lisieux aged twenty-four. Her Story of a Soul, published a year later, spread her little way of trust and love across the world. She is a Doctor of the Church.

09-30.t: Pius XII issues Divino Afflante Spiritu
09-30.x: On the feast of Saint Jerome, Pius XII issued the encyclical Divino Afflante Spiritu. It encouraged Catholic scholars to study the Bible in its original languages and to attend to the literary forms used by the sacred writers.

09-30.t: Sunday of the Word of God instituted
09-30.x: On the feast of Saint Jerome, Pope Francis issued the letter Aperuit illis, setting aside the Third Sunday in Ordinary Time each year as the Sunday of the Word of God, given to the celebration, study and spreading of Scripture.

10-01.x: Pope John Paul II canonised 120 martyrs of China, killed for the faith between 1648 and 1930. Most were Chinese lay people, among them children and catechists. On the same day he canonised Katharine Drexel and Josephine Bakhita.

10-02.x: After a short siege, the Christian defenders of Jerusalem surrendered the city to Saladin, eighty-eight years after the First Crusade had taken it. The loss shook Christendom, and the Third Crusade set out to recover the Holy City.

Charles Borromeo was born in the castle of Arona on Lake Maggiore. As Archbishop of Milan he put the reforms of the Council of Trent into practice, founding seminaries and caring for the sick during the plague of 1576.

During a retreat in Madrid, the young priest Josemaría Escrivá saw that God was asking him to begin Opus Dei, a way of holiness for lay people in their ordinary work and family life. He was canonised in 2002.

10-03.t: Death of Saint Francis of Assisi
10-03.x: Francis of Assisi died at the Portiuncula on the evening of 3 October, lying on the bare ground at his own request. He was about forty-four and had borne the stigmata for two years. He was canonised in 1228.

Pope Francis signed his encyclical Fratelli tutti at the tomb of Saint Francis in Assisi. Written during the pandemic, it called for fraternity and social friendship among all peoples, taking the parable of the Good Samaritan as its guide.

10-04.t: Death of Saint Teresa of Ávila
10-04.x: Teresa of Jesus died at Alba de Tormes, worn out by her journeys founding reformed Carmelite convents. Because the Gregorian calendar came into force that night, the following day was 15 October, which is why her feast is kept then.

10-04.t: Death of Blessed Francis Xavier Seelos
10-04.x: The Bavarian Redemptorist Francis Xavier Seelos died of yellow fever in New Orleans, caught while visiting the sick. He had spent over twenty years as a missionary and confessor among immigrants in the United States. He was beatified in 2000.

10-04.t: Paul VI addressed the United Nations
10-04.x: Pope Paul VI became the first pope to visit the Americas and to address the United Nations in New York. Speaking in French, he pleaded with the nations, “No more war, war never again,” then returned to the Council in Rome.

10-05.x: The Fourth Council of Constantinople opened in Hagia Sophia with legates of Pope Adrian II present. It confirmed Saint Ignatius as patriarch, condemned Photius and reaffirmed the veneration of holy images. The West counts it the eighth ecumenical council.

Bartolo Longo died at Pompeii. A lawyer who returned to the faith after years astray, he spent his life spreading the Rosary, built the Shrine of Our Lady of the Rosary there, and founded homes for orphans. He was canonised in 2025.

Sister Faustina Kowalska died of tuberculosis in her convent in Kraków, aged thirty-three. Her diary recorded the message of Divine Mercy that she believed Christ had entrusted to her. Pope John Paul II canonised her in 2000.

10-06.x: Bruno of Cologne died at his hermitage of La Torre in Calabria. A renowned teacher at Reims, he had withdrawn in 1084 to the mountains near Grenoble, where he began the Carthusian Order, with its life of silence and solitude.

Matteo Ricci was born at Macerata in Italy. As a Jesuit he entered China in 1583, learned its language and classics, and was welcomed at Beijing in 1601. His respect for Chinese culture opened a way for the Gospel there.

Pope John Paul II canonised Josemaría Escrivá, founder of Opus Dei, before a great crowd in Saint Peter’s Square. Escrivá had taught that daily work and family life can be a path to holiness for everyone.

10-07.x: Pope Mark died after a reign of less than nine months and was buried in the catacomb of Balbina. He is credited with founding the church of San Marco in Rome, which still bears his name.

The fleet of the Holy League defeated the Ottoman navy at Lepanto, off western Greece. Pope Pius V, who had asked Christians to pray the Rosary for victory, established in thanksgiving the feast now kept as Our Lady of the Rosary.

The Holy See approved Mother Teresa’s new congregation, the Missionaries of Charity, in the Archdiocese of Calcutta. It began with a handful of sisters vowed to serve the poorest of the poor without payment, and spread to every continent.

10-08.x: More than five hundred bishops gathered at Chalcedon, across the Bosphorus from Constantinople, for the fourth ecumenical council. Guided by the Tome of Pope Leo the Great, it would teach that Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human.

10-08.t: The new millennium entrusted to Mary
10-08.x: At the Jubilee of Bishops in Saint Peter’s Square, Pope John Paul II and bishops from around the world entrusted the new millennium to the Blessed Virgin Mary, before the statue of Our Lady brought from Fátima.

10-09.x: The Dominican Louis Bertrand died in Valencia. He had spent seven years preaching to the native peoples of what is now Colombia and the Caribbean, and spoke out against the cruelty of the colonists. He is a patron of Colombia.

John Henry Newman, the leading mind of the Oxford Movement, was received into the Catholic Church at Littlemore by the Passionist Blessed Dominic Barberi. He became a priest and cardinal, was canonised in 2019 and named a Doctor of the Church in 2025.
Pope Pius XII died at Castel Gandolfo after a reign of nineteen years. He had led the Church through the Second World War and in 1950 defined the dogma of the Assumption of Our Lady.

10-10.x: Bishop Daniel Comboni died of fever in Khartoum, aged fifty. He had given his life to the mission in central Africa, convinced that Africans themselves would evangelise Africa, and founded the Comboni Missionaries. He was canonised in 2003.

Pope John Paul II canonised the Polish Franciscan Maximilian Kolbe as a martyr of charity. In Auschwitz in 1941 he had offered his life in place of a condemned father, Franciszek Gajowniczek, who was present in Saint Peter’s Square that day.
Carlo Acutis, an Italian teenager who loved the Eucharist and used his skill with computers to catalogue Eucharistic miracles, was beatified in Assisi, where he is buried. He was canonised in 2025.

10-11.x: In its thirteenth session the Council of Trent defined that Christ is truly, really and substantially present in the Eucharist, and that the change of bread and wine into his Body and Blood is fittingly called transubstantiation.

Pope John XXIII opened the Second Vatican Council in Saint Peter’s Basilica, with more than 2,400 bishops present. He asked that the Church’s unchanging teaching be presented in a way suited to the present age.

10-11.t: Catechism of the Catholic Church promulgated
10-11.x: Thirty years to the day after the opening of the Second Vatican Council, Pope John Paul II signed the constitution Fidei depositum, ordering the publication of the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the first universal catechism since that of Trent.

10-12.x: Christopher Columbus made landfall in the Bahamas. The voyage opened the Americas to the preaching of the Gospel, and also to conquest and great injustice against their peoples, which missionaries such as Bartolomé de las Casas would denounce.

The statue of Christ the Redeemer was dedicated on Corcovado mountain above Rio de Janeiro. Thirty metres tall, with arms outstretched over the city, it became a symbol of the faith of the Brazilian people.

Carlo Acutis died of leukaemia in Monza, aged fifteen, having offered his sufferings for the Pope and the Church. He went to Mass daily and called the Eucharist his highway to heaven. He was canonised in 2025.

10-13.x: At its seventh session the Second Council of Nicaea defined that images of Christ, Our Lady and the saints may be venerated, since the honour paid to an image passes to the one it represents. Adoration belongs to God alone.

Cardinal Alessandro Farnese was elected pope and took the name Paul III. He approved the Society of Jesus in 1540, condemned the enslavement of the peoples of the Americas, and in 1545 opened the Council of Trent.

At Fátima in Portugal, tens of thousands who had gathered in the rain for the last of Our Lady’s six apparitions to three shepherd children saw the sun appear to spin and plunge towards the earth. The Church approved the apparitions in 1930.

10-14.t: Paul VI and Óscar Romero canonised
10-14.x: Pope Francis canonised Pope Paul VI, who brought the Second Vatican Council to its close, and Óscar Romero, Archbishop of San Salvador, shot at the altar in 1980 after defending the poor. Five others were canonised with them.

10-15.x: Hedwig, Duchess of Silesia, died at the Cistercian convent of Trzebnica, which she had founded with her husband. A wife and mother of seven, she used her wealth for the poor and the sick. She was canonised in 1267.

By decree of Pope Gregory XIII, ten days were dropped from the calendar in Italy, Spain, Portugal and Poland, so that 4 October was followed by 15 October. The reform kept Easter in its proper season and is now used worldwide.

10-16.x: Gerard Majella, a Redemptorist lay brother, died of tuberculosis at Materdomini in southern Italy, aged twenty-nine. Known for his obedience, his charity and the many miracles reported of him, he is invoked as the patron of expectant mothers.

10-16.t: Election of Pope John Paul II
10-16.x: Cardinal Karol Wojtyła, Archbishop of Kraków, was elected pope and took the name John Paul II. Aged fifty-eight, he was the first Polish pope and the first from outside Italy in 455 years. He reigned for over twenty-six years.

10-16.t: Luminous Mysteries added to the Rosary
10-16.x: In the apostolic letter Rosarium Virginis Mariae, Pope John Paul II proposed five new mysteries of the Rosary, the Mysteries of Light, drawn from Christ’s public ministry, and proclaimed a Year of the Rosary.

10-17.t: Death of Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque
10-17.x: Margaret Mary Alacoque died at the Visitation convent of Paray-le-Monial in France, aged forty-three. Through the revelations she received there, devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus spread through the whole Church.

10-17.t: Birth of Pope John Paul I
10-17.x: Albino Luciani was born into a poor family at Forno di Canale in the Italian Dolomites. Elected pope in August 1978, he died after only thirty-three days, remembered for his humility and his smile. He was beatified in 2022.

Pope Benedict XVI canonised Mary of the Cross MacKillop, founder of the Sisters of Saint Joseph, who brought schooling to poor children across the Australian bush. She became Australia’s first saint. Brother André Bessette of Montreal was canonised the same day.

10-18.x: The French Jesuit Isaac Jogues was killed with a tomahawk at the Mohawk village of Ossernenon, in present-day New York State. He had already been tortured and enslaved there, escaped to France, and freely returned to the mission.

10-18.t: Death of Saint Paul of the Cross
10-18.x: Paul of the Cross died in Rome, aged eighty-one. He had founded the Passionists, who bind themselves to keep alive the memory of Christ’s Passion, and spent decades preaching missions throughout Italy.

During the Second Vatican Council, Pope Paul VI canonised Charles Lwanga and his twenty-one companions, young Catholic men killed between 1885 and 1887 by order of King Mwanga of Buganda. They were the first saints of sub-Saharan Africa in modern times.

10-19.x: Father Jerzy Popiełuszko, chaplain to the Solidarity movement in Warsaw, was abducted and killed by officers of Poland’s communist security police. He had preached that evil must be overcome with good. He was beatified as a martyr in 2010.

10-19.t: Thérèse of Lisieux named a Doctor
10-19.x: On Mission Sunday, a century after her death, Pope John Paul II declared Saint Thérèse of the Child Jesus a Doctor of the Church. She had died at twenty-four, and is the youngest of all the Doctors.
Pope John Paul II beatified Mother Teresa of Calcutta in Saint Peter’s Square, only six years after her death, before some 300,000 people. She was canonised by Pope Francis in 2016.

10-20.x: A month after Italian troops took Rome, Pope Pius IX suspended the First Vatican Council indefinitely. It had defined papal infallibility in July but never met again, and was formally closed only in 1960.

10-20.t: Death of Saint Maria Bertilla Boscardin
10-20.x: Sister Maria Bertilla Boscardin died in Treviso, aged thirty-four. A farm girl thought slow by others, she became a devoted nurse, staying beside her patients through the air raids of the First World War. She was canonised in 1961.

Weeks after the outbreak of the Second World War, Pope Pius XII issued Summi Pontificatus. It mourned the fate of Poland, rejected racism and the worship of the state, and insisted on the unity of the whole human family.

10-21.x: Mother Laura Montoya died in Medellín. A teacher, she had gone to live among the indigenous peoples of the Colombian forests and founded a congregation of missionary sisters to serve them. In 2013 she became Colombia’s first saint.

Pope John Paul II beatified Luigi and Maria Beltrame Quattrocchi, a Roman couple who raised four children. They were the first husband and wife to be beatified together, and three of their children were present.

Pope Benedict XVI canonised Kateri Tekakwitha, a Mohawk and Algonquin woman who died in 1680, as the first Native American saint. With her were canonised six others, among them Pedro Calungsod of the Philippines and Marianne Cope of Molokai.

10-22.x: At its fifth session the Council of Chalcedon agreed its definition of faith: Jesus Christ is one person in two natures, truly God and truly man, without confusion or division. It was solemnly proclaimed three days later before the Emperor Marcian.

10-22.t: John Paul II began his ministry
10-22.x: At the Mass inaugurating his pontificate in Saint Peter’s Square, Pope John Paul II said, “Do not be afraid. Open wide the doors for Christ.” The Church now keeps his feast on this day.

10-23.t: The Second Council of Nicaea closed
10-23.x: By the traditional account, the seventh ecumenical council held a final session on this day in the Magnaura Palace at Constantinople, where the Empress Irene and her son Constantine VI signed its decree restoring the veneration of holy images. Some scholars now doubt the record of this session.

10-23.t: Death of Saint John of Capistrano
10-23.x: The Franciscan preacher John of Capistrano died of plague at Ilok, on the Danube, aged seventy. Three months earlier he had helped to rally the army that relieved the siege of Belgrade.

10-24.x: The cathedral of Our Lady at Chartres, rebuilt after the fire of 1194, was dedicated, by tradition in the presence of King Louis IX of France. Its sculpture and stained glass make it one of the great achievements of Christian art.

10-24.t: Death of Saint Anthony Mary Claret
10-24.x: Anthony Mary Claret died in exile at the Cistercian abbey of Fontfroide in France. A weaver’s son from Catalonia, he founded the Claretian missionaries, served as Archbishop of Santiago de Cuba, and wrote and preached without rest.

10-24.t: Saint Benedict named patron of Europe
10-24.x: Pope Paul VI consecrated the rebuilt abbey church of Monte Cassino, destroyed in the war in 1944, and proclaimed Saint Benedict the principal patron of Europe, calling him a messenger of peace.

10-25.x: Pope Paul VI canonised forty men and women put to death for the Catholic faith in England and Wales between 1535 and 1679. They included priests such as Edmund Campion and lay people such as Margaret Clitherow.

10-26.x: Cedd, a monk of Lindisfarne who became bishop of the East Saxons, died of plague at his monastery of Lastingham in Yorkshire. Earlier that year he had served as interpreter at the Synod of Whitby.

The Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I arrived in Rome to visit Pope Paul VI, and the two prayed together in Saint Peter’s Basilica. It was the first visit of a Patriarch of Constantinople to Rome in many centuries.

10-27.t: World Day of Prayer for Peace
10-27.x: At the invitation of Pope John Paul II, leaders of the Christian churches and of the world’s religions came to Assisi to fast and to pray for peace. He asked that all fighting cease for that day.

10-28.t: The Battle of the Milvian Bridge
10-28.x: Constantine defeated his rival Maxentius outside Rome after, it is said, marking his soldiers’ shields with the sign of Christ. Within months he and Licinius granted Christians freedom of worship, and the age of persecution drew to its end.
In Saint Peter’s Basilica, Pope Pius XI himself consecrated six Chinese priests as bishops, the first of modern times. It was a decisive step towards a Church in China led by its own people.

Cardinal Angelo Roncalli, Patriarch of Venice, was elected pope at the age of seventy-six and took the name John XXIII. Expected to be a caretaker, within three months he announced an ecumenical council.

The Second Vatican Council issued its declaration on the Church’s relation to other religions. It rejected the charge that the Jewish people bear guilt for Christ’s death and condemned antisemitism and every form of discrimination.

10-29.t: First African bishop of modern times
10-29.x: Pope Pius XII consecrated twelve missionary bishops in Saint Peter’s on the feast of Christ the King. Among them was Joseph Kiwanuka of Uganda, the first black African bishop of the Latin Church in modern times.

Chiara Badano was born at Sassello in northern Italy, an only child long prayed for. A lively member of the Focolare Movement, she died of bone cancer at eighteen, accepting her illness with joy. She was beatified in 2010.

10-30.x: With the apostolic letter Vigilantiae studiique, Pope Leo XIII set up the Pontifical Biblical Commission, a body of scholars charged with promoting the study of Scripture and guarding its right interpretation.

10-31.x: On the eve of All Saints, Pope Julius II celebrated Vespers beneath the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, newly finished by Michelangelo after four years of work. Its scenes from Genesis have shaped how Christians picture the Creation.

Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar at Wittenberg, sent his ninety-five theses against the sale of indulgences to the Archbishop of Mainz. The dispute that followed grew into the Protestant Reformation and the lasting division of Western Christians.

10-31.t: World consecrated to the Immaculate Heart
10-31.x: In a radio message to Portugal for the twenty-fifth anniversary of Fátima, Pope Pius XII consecrated the Church and the whole human race to the Immaculate Heart of Mary, in the midst of the Second World War.

At Augsburg, representatives of the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint declaration stating that they share a common understanding of justification by God’s grace through faith in Christ.

11-01.x: The Jesuit Rupert Mayer collapsed and died while preaching at Mass on All Saints’ Day in Munich. He had spoken openly against the Nazis and suffered prison and a concentration camp for it. He was beatified in 1987.

Karol Wojtyła, who had studied in secret during the German occupation of Poland, was ordained a priest by Cardinal Adam Sapieha in the archbishop’s private chapel in Kraków. In 1978 he became Pope John Paul II.

By the constitution Munificentissimus Deus, Pope Pius XII solemnly defined that the Immaculate Mother of God, when the course of her earthly life was finished, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory.

11-02.x: Malachy, Archbishop of Armagh and reformer of the Irish Church, died at Clairvaux on his way to Rome, in the arms of his friend Saint Bernard, who wrote his life. In 1190 he became the first Irish saint canonised by a pope.

11-03.x: Charles Borromeo, Cardinal Archbishop of Milan, died late at night aged forty-six, exhausted by his labours. He had been the leading figure in carrying out the reforms of the Council of Trent. His feast is kept on 4 November.

11-03.t: Death of Saint Martin de Porres
11-03.x: Martin de Porres, a Dominican lay brother, died in Lima. The son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed African woman, he spent his life nursing the sick and feeding the poor of every race. He was canonised in 1962.

11-04.x: Pope John XXIII was crowned at Saint Peter’s in Rome. He chose the feast of Saint Charles Borromeo for the ceremony, out of devotion to the reforming bishop whose work he had studied for many years.

Pope Benedict XVI signed the apostolic constitution Anglicanorum coetibus, allowing groups of Anglicans to enter full communion with the Catholic Church through personal ordinariates while keeping elements of their own liturgy and heritage.

11-05.x: The Council of Constance opened in southern Germany, at a time when three men claimed to be pope. Over the next three years it ended the Great Western Schism and elected Martin V.

11-05.t: Death of Saint Guido Maria Conforti
11-05.x: Guido Maria Conforti, Bishop of Parma, died in his city. Unable through ill health to go to the missions himself, he had founded the Xaverian Missionaries, who went first to China. He was canonised in 2011.

11-06.t: First diocese in the United States
11-06.x: Pope Pius VI established the Diocese of Baltimore, the first in the United States, and named John Carroll, a former Jesuit, as its bishop. Its territory covered the whole of the new nation.

11-07.x: The sixth ecumenical council opened in the imperial palace at Constantinople. It taught that Christ, being truly God and truly man, has two wills, divine and human, in perfect harmony, against those who allowed him only one.

Willibrord, a monk from Northumbria, died at his abbey of Echternach in present-day Luxembourg, aged eighty-one. For nearly fifty years he had preached the Gospel to the Frisians as the first Bishop of Utrecht.

11-08.t: Death of Saint Martin of Tours
11-08.x: Martin, Bishop of Tours, died at Candes while on a pastoral visit. A former soldier who had shared his cloak with a beggar, he became a monk and bishop. His burial at Tours on 11 November is kept as his feast.

11-08.t: Death of Blessed John Duns Scotus
11-08.x: The Scottish Franciscan John Duns Scotus died in Cologne, aged about forty-two. Called the Subtle Doctor, he argued that Our Lady was preserved from original sin, preparing the way for the dogma of the Immaculate Conception.

11-09.x: By tradition, Pope Sylvester I dedicated the basilica built by Constantine at the Lateran on this day. It is the cathedral of the Bishop of Rome and is honoured as the mother and head of all churches.

Pope Clement VIII issued the revised edition of the Latin Vulgate called for by the Council of Trent. Known as the Clementine Vulgate, it remained the Catholic Church’s official Bible text for nearly four centuries.

11-09.t: Death of Saint Elizabeth of the Trinity
11-09.x: Elizabeth of the Trinity died in the Carmel of Dijon, aged twenty-six, after months of painful illness. Her writings on the indwelling of the Holy Trinity in the soul have helped many to pray. She was canonised in 2016.

11-10.t: Death of Pope Saint Leo the Great
11-10.x: Pope Leo I died after a reign of twenty-one years. His teaching on the two natures of Christ was acclaimed at Chalcedon, and in 452 he persuaded Attila the Hun to turn back from Rome.

The Theatine priest Andrew Avellino suffered a stroke as he began Mass in Naples and died that day, aged about eighty-seven. A former church lawyer, he had become a sought-after confessor and a reformer of religious houses.
In the apostolic letter Tertio millennio adveniente, Pope John Paul II set out a plan of prayer and repentance to prepare the Church for the Great Jubilee of the year 2000.

11-11.t: Death of Saint Theodore the Studite
11-11.x: Theodore, abbot of the Stoudios monastery in Constantinople, died in exile. He had suffered imprisonment and flogging for defending the veneration of holy images, and his monastic rule shaped Eastern monasticism for centuries.

Pope Innocent III opened the largest council of the Middle Ages. It used the word transubstantiation of the Eucharist and required every Catholic to confess at least once a year and to receive Holy Communion at Easter.

At the Council of Constance, Cardinal Oddone Colonna was elected pope and took the name Martin, after the saint of the day. His election ended the Great Western Schism, which had divided the Church for nearly forty years.

11-12.t: Death of Saint Didacus of Alcalá
11-12.x: Didacus, or Diego, a Franciscan lay brother, died at Alcalá in Spain. He had served as a missionary in the Canary Islands and nursed the sick in Rome. The city of San Diego in California is named after him.
Josaphat Kuntsevych, Archbishop of Polotsk, was killed by a mob at Vitebsk in present-day Belarus. He had worked without rest for the union of Eastern Christians with Rome. He was canonised in 1867.

11-13.x: Augustine was born at Thagaste in Roman North Africa, now Souk Ahras in Algeria, to a pagan father and the Christian Saint Monica. After a restless youth he was baptised in 387 and became the most influential theologian of the West.

11-13.t: Death of Pope Saint Nicholas I
11-13.x: Pope Nicholas I died after nine years as pope. He upheld the authority of the Roman See over powerful bishops, defended the marriage bond against King Lothair II, and encouraged the mission to the Bulgarians.

Homobonus, a married cloth merchant of Cremona known for honest dealing and generosity to the poor, died during Mass in the church of Saint Giles. Pope Innocent III canonised him just over a year later.

11-14.x: Laurence O’Toole, Archbishop of Dublin, died at Eu in Normandy while seeking King Henry II to plead for peace in Ireland. A former abbot of Glendalough, he had attended the Third Lateran Council. He was canonised in 1225.

The Croatian Franciscan Nicholas Tavelić and three companions, friars of the Custody of the Holy Land, were put to death in Jerusalem after publicly preaching Christ before the Muslim judge. They were canonised in 1970.

11-15.t: Death of Saint Albert the Great
11-15.x: Albert the Great, Dominican friar, bishop and teacher of Thomas Aquinas, died in Cologne. He studied the whole of nature as well as theology, and is the patron saint of scientists and a Doctor of the Church.

Roque González, a Jesuit born in Asunción, was killed at the mission of Caaró, in what is now southern Brazil. He had founded several of the Paraguay reductions, where the Guaraní lived in Christian communities protected from slavers.

11-15.t: The École Biblique opened in Jerusalem
11-15.x: The Dominican Marie-Joseph Lagrange opened a school of biblical studies at the priory of Saint Stephen in Jerusalem. The École Biblique pioneered Catholic study of Scripture in the land of the Bible and later produced the Jerusalem Bible.

11-16.t: Death of Saint Margaret of Scotland
11-16.x: Queen Margaret died in Edinburgh Castle, three days after her husband, King Malcolm III, was killed in battle. An English princess raised in Hungary, she reformed the Scottish Church and fed the poor with her own hands.

11-16.t: Death of Saint Hugh of Lincoln
11-16.x: Hugh of Avalon, a Carthusian monk who became Bishop of Lincoln, died in London. He rebuilt his cathedral, stood up to three kings, cared for lepers and protected the Jews of his diocese from mob violence.

Soldiers of the Salvadoran army entered the Central American University by night and shot six Jesuit priests, their housekeeper and her daughter. The Jesuits had worked for a negotiated end to the civil war.

11-17.t: Death of Saint Hilda of Whitby
11-17.x: Hilda died at Whitby, the double monastery of monks and nuns she had founded and governed. Kings and bishops sought her counsel, five of her monks became bishops, and she hosted the Synod of Whitby in 664.

11-17.t: Death of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary
11-17.x: Elizabeth, a king’s daughter and widow of the Landgrave of Thuringia, died at Marburg aged twenty-four. After her husband’s death she had given up her wealth to nurse the sick in the hospital she built. She was canonised in 1235.

11-17.t: Deaths of Mary I and Cardinal Pole
11-17.x: Queen Mary I of England and Cardinal Reginald Pole, Archbishop of Canterbury, died within hours of each other. With them ended the brief restoration of Catholic England, and under Elizabeth I the country broke again with Rome.

11-18.x: Pope Urban VIII consecrated the new Saint Peter’s Basilica, built over 120 years above the tomb of the Apostle. The work of Bramante, Michelangelo, Maderno and others replaced the church first raised by Constantine.

11-18.t: Death of Saint Rose Philippine Duchesne
11-18.x: Rose Philippine Duchesne, a French religious of the Sacred Heart, died at St Charles, Missouri, aged eighty-three. She opened the first free school west of the Mississippi and at seventy-one went to live among the Potawatomi, who named her the woman who always prays.

11-18.t: Leo XIII on the study of Scripture
11-18.x: Pope Leo XIII issued the encyclical Providentissimus Deus, the first great papal document on biblical studies. It urged Catholics to study Scripture in its original languages and affirmed that the sacred books are inspired and free from error.
The Second Vatican Council issued Dei Verbum, its constitution on divine revelation. It taught that Scripture and Tradition flow from one source, and urged all the faithful to read the Bible often.

11-19.x: After a conclave of fifty days, Cardinal Giulio de’ Medici was elected pope as Clement VII. His troubled reign saw the sack of Rome in 1527 and the break of King Henry VIII of England with the Church.

11-20.x: Edmund, King of East Anglia, was captured by the invading Danes and, by tradition, shot with arrows and beheaded for refusing to renounce Christ. His shrine at Bury St Edmunds became one of the great pilgrimage places of England.

11-20.t: Death of Saint Bernward of Hildesheim
11-20.x: Bernward, Bishop of Hildesheim in Saxony and tutor to the Emperor Otto III, died in the monastery of Saint Michael, which he had founded. The bronze doors and column he commissioned still tell the story of salvation.

11-21.x: The Second Vatican Council issued Lumen gentium, its constitution on the Church, with the decrees on ecumenism and the Eastern Churches. In his closing address Pope Paul VI proclaimed Our Lady Mother of the Church.

11-22.t: Florence decreed union with the Armenians
11-22.x: At the Council of Florence, Pope Eugene IV issued a decree of union with the Armenian Church. It set out the Church’s teaching on the seven sacraments more fully than any council had before.

On the feast of Saint Cecilia, Pope Pius X issued Tra le sollecitudini on sacred music. It restored Gregorian chant to pride of place and called for the active participation of the faithful in the liturgy.
Pope John Paul II issued the apostolic exhortation Familiaris consortio on the Christian family in the modern world. It described the family as a domestic church and a community of life and love.

11-23.x: For two hours on this night the mathematician Blaise Pascal was overwhelmed by an experience of the living God. He wrote it down on a parchment headed “Fire” and kept it sewn into his coat until his death.

The Jesuit Miguel Pro, who had ministered in secret during the persecution of the Church in Mexico, was shot without trial in Mexico City. He died with arms outstretched as a cross, crying “Viva Cristo Rey.” He was beatified in 1988.

11-24.x: Junípero Serra was born at Petra on the island of Majorca. A Franciscan and professor of philosophy, he left for the New World at thirty-five and founded the first nine missions of California. He was canonised in 2015.

The French missionary bishop-elect Pierre Dumoulin-Borie was beheaded at Đồng Hới in Vietnam, and two Vietnamese priests were put to death with him. The Church keeps the feast of the 117 Martyrs of Vietnam on this day.

At the close of the Year of Faith, Pope Francis issued Evangelii gaudium, on the joy of the Gospel. It called every Catholic to be a missionary disciple and the whole Church to go out to those on the margins.

11-25.x: Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli was born at Sotto il Monte near Bergamo, into a large family of tenant farmers, and was baptised the same day. As Pope John XXIII he called the Second Vatican Council. He was canonised in 2014.

11-26.t: Death of Saint Leonard of Port Maurice
11-26.x: The Franciscan Leonard of Port Maurice died in Rome after more than forty years of preaching parish missions across Italy. He spread the devotion of the Stations of the Cross, setting them up in hundreds of places, including the Colosseum.

Katharine Drexel was born in Philadelphia, heiress to a banking fortune. She gave her life and her inheritance to the education of Native American and African American people, founding the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament. She was canonised in 2000.

Father James Alberione died in Rome, shortly after a visit from Pope Paul VI. He had founded the Society of Saint Paul and the Daughters of Saint Paul to spread the Gospel through the press, film and broadcasting.

11-27.t: Urban II preached the First Crusade
11-27.x: At the close of the Council of Clermont in France, Pope Urban II called on the knights of the West to go to the aid of Eastern Christians and to free Jerusalem. The response became the First Crusade.

11-27.t: Our Lady and the Miraculous Medal
11-27.x: In the chapel of the Daughters of Charity in the rue du Bac, Paris, Our Lady appeared to the novice Catherine Labouré and showed her the design of a medal to be struck. It soon became known as the Miraculous Medal.

In Saint Peter’s Basilica, Pope John Paul II gave relics of Saint Gregory Nazianzen and Saint John Chrysostom, long kept in Rome, to the Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew I, as a sign of the desire for unity.

11-28.t: Death of Saint James of the Marches
11-28.x: The Franciscan James of the Marches died in Naples. A companion of John of Capistrano, he preached for decades across Italy and central Europe and promoted the montes pietatis, which lent to the poor at low interest.

At a school in Kibeho, Rwanda, Our Lady appeared to the student Alphonsine Mumureke, calling herself Mother of the Word. The apparitions to three girls, which urged prayer and conversion, were approved by the local bishop in 2001.

11-29.t: The Rule of Saint Francis approved
11-29.x: By the bull Solet annuere, Pope Honorius III gave final approval to the Rule that Francis of Assisi had written for his Friars Minor. It begins by stating that their life is to observe the holy Gospel.

Five children at Beauraing in Belgium saw Our Lady near the railway viaduct beside a convent school. She appeared to them thirty-three times until 3 January 1933, asking for prayer. The Bishop of Namur approved the apparitions in 1949.

Dorothy Day died in New York, aged eighty-three. A convert and journalist, she founded the Catholic Worker movement with Peter Maurin in 1933, opening houses of hospitality for the homeless. The Church has opened her cause for canonisation.

11-30.x: In Rome, Pope Gregory II consecrated the English monk Boniface as a bishop and sent him back to preach to the German peoples. He organised the Church in Germany and died a martyr in Frisia in 754.

On Saint Andrew’s Day, Cardinal Reginald Pole, the Pope’s legate, absolved the kneeling Parliament of England from schism and restored the kingdom to communion with Rome. The reunion lasted until the death of Queen Mary four years later.
Pope Benedict XV issued the apostolic letter Maximum illud. It told missionaries to serve the Gospel and not the interests of their own nations, and called urgently for the training of local clergy.

11-30.t: John Paul II visited the Phanar
11-30.x: On the feast of Saint Andrew, Pope John Paul II attended the Divine Liturgy celebrated by the Ecumenical Patriarch Dimitrios I in Istanbul. Together they announced a commission for theological dialogue between the Catholic and Orthodox Churches.

12-01.x: The Jesuit Edmund Campion, once the most admired scholar in Oxford, was hanged, drawn and quartered at Tyburn with the priests Ralph Sherwin and Alexander Briant. All three were canonised among the Forty Martyrs in 1970.

12-01.t: Death of Saint Charles de Foucauld
12-01.x: Charles de Foucauld, a former army officer who lived as a hermit among the Tuareg of the Sahara, was shot by raiders at Tamanrasset in Algeria. He had sought to be a brother to all. He was canonised in 2022.

Sister Marie-Clémentine Anuarite Nengapeta, a young Congolese religious, was killed at Isiro during the Simba rebellion for refusing a rebel officer’s advances. She forgave him as she died. Pope John Paul II beatified her in Kinshasa in 1985.

12-02.t: Death of Blessed John of Ruysbroeck
12-02.x: The Flemish priest John of Ruysbroeck died at the priory of Groenendaal near Brussels, aged eighty-eight. His writings in his native Dutch on the soul’s union with God rank among the great works of Christian mysticism.

12-02.t: Four churchwomen killed in El Salvador
12-02.x: The Maryknoll sisters Ita Ford and Maura Clarke, the Ursuline Dorothy Kazel and the lay missionary Jean Donovan, all from the United States, were murdered by Salvadoran soldiers. They had been helping refugees of the civil war.

12-03.x: Francis Xavier died of fever on the island of Shangchuan, within sight of the China he longed to enter. In ten years he had preached in India, the Moluccas and Japan. He is a patron of the missions.

On the feast of Saint Francis Xavier, the Jesuit Francis Xavier Gautrelet proposed to his students at Vals in France that they offer their daily prayer and work for the missions. This became the Apostleship of Prayer, now the Pope’s Worldwide Prayer Network.

12-04.x: Nicholas Breakspear, born near St Albans, was elected pope and took the name Adrian IV. He had earlier reorganised the Church in Scandinavia as papal legate. He remains the only Englishman to have been pope.

After eighteen years and three periods of sessions, the Council of Trent held its final session. Its decrees on Scripture, justification, the sacraments and the training of priests shaped Catholic life for the next four centuries.

Fifty Christians were burned alive at Edo, now Tokyo, by order of the shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu. Among them were the Jesuit Jerome de Angelis, the Franciscan Francis Gálvez and many Japanese lay people.

The Second Vatican Council approved its first document, the constitution on the sacred liturgy, by 2,147 votes to 4. It called the liturgy the summit and source of the Church’s life and opened the way to worship in the people’s own languages.

12-05.x: Sabas died aged ninety-three at the Great Laura he had founded in the desert between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea. The monastery, known as Mar Saba, has been lived in almost without a break ever since.

Niels Stensen, the Danish scientist who laid the foundations of geology and made discoveries in anatomy, died at Schwerin in Germany. A convert from Lutheranism, he became a priest and bishop and lived in great poverty. He was beatified in 1988.

12-06.t: Thomas Aquinas laid down his pen
12-06.x: While celebrating Mass in Naples on the feast of Saint Nicholas, Thomas Aquinas underwent an experience after which he wrote no more, leaving the Summa unfinished. He said that all he had written seemed like straw. He died three months later.

12-07.x: Ambrose, the governor of the province, was consecrated Bishop of Milan. Only days earlier he had been an unbaptised catechumen, chosen by the acclamation of the people. He became one of the four great Latin Doctors.

The French Jesuit Charles Garnier was shot during an Iroquois attack on the Petun mission village of Etharita in present-day Ontario. Wounded, he was still trying to reach a dying man when he was killed. He is one of the eight North American Martyrs.

On its last working day the Second Vatican Council issued Gaudium et spes, on the Church in the modern world, and Dignitatis humanae, its declaration on religious freedom, with decrees on the missions and the priesthood.

In a joint declaration read at the same hour in Rome and Istanbul, Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I expressed regret for the mutual excommunications of 1054 and removed them from the memory of the Church.

12-08.x: Paul Yun Ji-chung and his cousin James Kwon Sang-yeon, Korean noblemen who had embraced the faith brought by lay people from Beijing, were beheaded at Jeonju. They were the first of Korea’s many martyrs. Pope Francis beatified them in 2014.

By the bull Ineffabilis Deus, Pope Pius IX defined that the Blessed Virgin Mary, from the first moment of her conception, was preserved free from all stain of original sin by the merits of Jesus Christ.

Pope Pius IX opened the First Vatican Council in Saint Peter’s Basilica with some seven hundred bishops. It taught that God can be known by reason and by faith, and defined the primacy and infallibility of the pope.

Pope Paul VI closed the Second Vatican Council with Mass in Saint Peter’s Square. In four sessions over three years it had produced sixteen documents, and it ended with messages to rulers, workers, the sick, the young and others.

12-09.t: Our Lady appeared to Juan Diego
12-09.x: According to the traditional account, Our Lady first appeared to Juan Diego, a Nahua convert, on the hill of Tepeyac near Mexico City. Speaking in his own language, she asked that a church be built there.

Peter Fourier died at Gray in eastern France. As parish priest of Mattaincourt in Lorraine he set up a fund to help the poor, and with Blessed Alix Le Clerc founded a congregation to give free schooling to girls.

Archbishop Fulton Sheen died in his private chapel in New York, before the Blessed Sacrament. For decades his radio and television programmes had explained the faith to millions. He kept a daily holy hour throughout his priesthood, and was beatified in 2026.

12-10.x: According to tradition, the house of the Holy Family at Nazareth came to rest at Loreto in Italy on this night. The shrine built around it has drawn pilgrims ever since, and Our Lady of Loreto is now in the general calendar.

The priest Edmund Gennings and the layman Swithun Wells, in whose house he had been arrested saying Mass, were executed in London. Two more priests and three laymen died the same day. Four of the seven, Gennings and Wells among them, were canonised with the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.

12-10.t: Mother Teresa received the Nobel Peace Prize
12-10.x: In Oslo, Mother Teresa of Calcutta accepted the Nobel Peace Prize in the name of the poor. She asked that the banquet be cancelled and the money given to the hungry, and in her lecture the next day spoke in defence of unborn children.

12-11.t: Death of Pope Saint Damasus I
12-11.x: Pope Damasus I died aged about eighty. He honoured the Roman martyrs with verse inscriptions at their tombs and commissioned his secretary, Saint Jerome, to revise the Latin Gospels, the beginning of the Vulgate Bible.

12-11.t: The feast of Christ the King
12-11.x: In the encyclical Quas primas, closing the Holy Year of 1925, Pope Pius XI instituted the feast of Christ the King. He wished to remind a world turning from God that Christ’s reign extends over all peoples.

12-12.t: The image of Our Lady of Guadalupe
12-12.x: According to the traditional account, Juan Diego opened his cloak before Bishop Juan de Zumárraga. Roses fell out, and the image of Our Lady was seen upon the cloth. It is venerated today in the basilica at Guadalupe.

12-13.x: After five months as pope, the aged hermit Celestine V laid down the papacy at Naples, judging himself unequal to the office. He was canonised in 1313 and is one of very few popes to have resigned.

After years of delay, the Council of Trent opened in the cathedral of that city in the Alps, with only about thirty prelates present. Called by Pope Paul III, it answered the Reformation and renewed the Church’s life.

12-13.t: Death of Saint Jane Frances de Chantal
12-13.x: Jane Frances de Chantal died at the Visitation convent in Moulins, aged sixty-nine. A widow and mother, she founded the Order of the Visitation with Saint Francis de Sales in 1610. By her death it had over eighty houses.

12-14.t: Death of Saint John of the Cross
12-14.x: John of the Cross died at Úbeda in Andalusia, aged forty-nine, after harsh treatment by his own brethren. Reformer of Carmel with Saint Teresa, and author of the Dark Night and the Spiritual Canticle, he is a Doctor of the Church.

12-15.t: Death of Saint Maria Crocifissa di Rosa
12-15.x: Maria Crocifissa di Rosa died in Brescia, aged forty-two. She had nursed the victims of cholera and the wounded of war, and founded the Handmaids of Charity to care for the sick in hospitals. She was canonised in 1954.

12-16.x: The Empress Adelaide, widow of Otto the Great, died at the monastery she had founded at Seltz in Alsace. She had known imprisonment and exile as well as power, and used her position to support the Church and the poor.

12-16.t: First of the Martyrs of Thailand
12-16.x: Philip Siphong, a catechist who led the Catholics of Songkhon in Thailand after their priest was expelled, was shot by police. Ten days later two sisters and four companions were killed for refusing to deny Christ. All seven were beatified in 1989.

12-17.x: Sturm, a Bavarian disciple of Saint Boniface, died at Fulda, the abbey he had founded about 744 in the forests of Hesse. Fulda became a great centre of learning and mission and guards the tomb of Boniface.
Pope Innocent III approved the rule of the Order of the Most Holy Trinity, founded by Saint John of Matha to ransom Christians held captive. John himself died on this same day in 1213.

Jorge Mario Bergoglio was born in Buenos Aires, the eldest of five children of a family of Italian origin. A Jesuit and Archbishop of Buenos Aires, in 2013 he became the first pope from the Americas. He died in 2025.
