12-18.x: In his rooms at Valdocco in Turin, Saint John Bosco and seventeen companions, most of them young men he had taught, formed the Society of Saint Francis de Sales to continue his work for poor boys.

12-19.x: Pope Urban V died at Avignon. A Benedictine monk who kept his habit and simple ways as pope, he had brought the papacy back to Rome in 1367, only to return to France three years later. He was beatified in 1870.

12-20.t: Death of Saint Dominic of Silos
12-20.x: Dominic, a shepherd who became a Benedictine abbot, died at the monastery of Silos in Castile, which he had rebuilt from ruin. A century later Blessed Joan of Aza prayed at his tomb and named her son, Saint Dominic, after him.

12-20.t: Pius XI on the Catholic priesthood
12-20.x: Pope Pius XI issued the encyclical Ad catholici sacerdotii on the dignity and duties of the priesthood. It insisted that candidates be chosen and formed with great care, holiness mattering more than numbers.

12-21.x: On the fourth Sunday of Advent, the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos preached in Santo Domingo against the settlers’ cruel treatment of the native people of Hispaniola. His sermon began the long defence of their rights by Spanish friars.

The Jesuit Peter Canisius died at Fribourg in Switzerland. Through his preaching, his colleges and above all his catechisms, he did more than anyone to renew the Catholic faith in German lands. He is a Doctor of the Church.
The Vietnamese priest Andrew Dũng-Lạc was beheaded in Hanoi with his fellow priest Peter Trương Văn Thi. His name leads the list of the 117 Martyrs of Vietnam canonised by Pope John Paul II in 1988.

12-22.x: By the bull Religiosam vitam, Pope Honorius III confirmed the community that Saint Dominic had gathered at Toulouse. The Order of Preachers, devoted to study and to preaching for the salvation of souls, spread across Europe within a few years.

12-22.t: Death of Saint Frances Xavier Cabrini
12-22.x: Mother Cabrini died in Chicago, in one of the sixty-seven schools, hospitals and orphanages she had founded, most of them for Italian immigrants in the Americas. In 1946 she became the first citizen of the United States to be canonised.

12-23.x: Thorlak Thorhallsson, Bishop of Skálholt, died in Iceland. He had studied in Paris and Lincoln, founded the island’s first Augustinian house and worked to reform its clergy. Pope John Paul II declared him patron of Iceland in 1984.

Marguerite d’Youville died in Montreal. A widow left in debt, she took the poor into her home, founded the Sisters of Charity known as the Grey Nuns, and ran the city’s hospital. In 1990 she became the first Canadian-born saint.

The Franciscan friar Antônio de Sant’Anna Galvão died in São Paulo at the convent he had built, now the Monastery of Light. Known for his care of the sick, he became in 2007 the first saint born in Brazil.

12-24.x: On Christmas night at Greccio in central Italy, Saint Francis of Assisi had a manger prepared with hay, an ox and an ass, and Mass was celebrated over it. From this came the custom of the Christmas crib.
John of Kęty, priest and professor at the University of Kraków, died on Christmas Eve. He was known for his learning, his gentleness in debate and his habit of giving away what he had to the poor.

At Mass on Christmas Eve in the church of Saint Nicholas at Oberndorf near Salzburg, the carol “Silent Night” was sung for the first time. The words were by the curate, Father Joseph Mohr, and the music by the organist Franz Xaver Gruber.

The Maronite monk and hermit Charbel Makhlouf died at Annaya in Lebanon, eight days after suffering a stroke while celebrating the liturgy. Many healings have been reported at his tomb. Pope Paul VI canonised him in 1977.

12-25.x: Pope Gregory the Great wrote that at Christmas this year more than ten thousand of the English were baptised by Augustine, the monk he had sent to Canterbury. It was the first great harvest of the mission to the Anglo-Saxons.

During Christmas Mass in Saint Peter’s Basilica, Pope Leo III placed a crown on the head of Charlemagne, King of the Franks, and the people acclaimed him emperor. The act shaped relations between Church and rulers in the West for centuries.

After Midnight Mass at Lisieux, the thirteen-year-old Thérèse Martin was freed in a moment from the oversensitivity that had troubled her since her mother’s death. She called it her complete conversion. Fifteen months later she entered Carmel.
With the apostolic constitution Humanae salutis, Pope John XXIII formally summoned the Second Vatican Council to meet in 1962. He asked the whole Church to pray for a new Pentecost.

12-26.t: Birth of Saint Clement Mary Hofbauer
12-26.x: Clement Hofbauer was born at Tasswitz in Moravia, the ninth of twelve children. A baker before he became a Redemptorist, he brought his order north of the Alps and renewed Catholic life in Warsaw and Vienna.

József Mindszenty, Archbishop of Esztergom and Primate of Hungary, was arrested by the communist authorities. Tortured and sentenced to life after a show trial, he became a symbol of the Church’s resistance to tyranny.

12-27.x: The Emperor Justinian dedicated the rebuilt church of Holy Wisdom in Constantinople, raised in under six years. For nine centuries it was the greatest church of the Christian East and the cathedral of the Patriarch.

12-27.t: First revelation of the Sacred Heart
12-27.x: On the feast of Saint John, as she prayed before the Blessed Sacrament at Paray-le-Monial, the Visitation nun Margaret Mary Alacoque received the first of the great revelations in which Christ showed her his Heart burning with love for mankind.

12-27.t: John Paul II forgave his attacker
12-27.x: Pope John Paul II visited Mehmet Ali Ağca in Rebibbia prison in Rome and spoke privately with the man who had shot him in Saint Peter’s Square in 1981, assuring him of his forgiveness.

12-28.x: The abbey church of Saint Peter at Westminster, built by King Edward the Confessor, was consecrated on Holy Innocents’ Day. The king was too ill to attend, died eight days later and was buried there.

12-28.t: Death of Saint Francis de Sales
12-28.x: Francis de Sales, Bishop of Geneva, died at Lyon aged fifty-five. Through his preaching, his letters and his Introduction to the Devout Life, he taught that holiness is possible in every state of life. He is a Doctor of the Church.

12-28.t: Death of Saint Gaspar del Bufalo
12-28.x: Gaspar del Bufalo died in Rome. Exiled and imprisoned for refusing an oath of loyalty to Napoleon, he afterwards founded the Missionaries of the Precious Blood and preached missions across the Papal States. He was canonised in 1954.

12-29.x: Four knights of King Henry II killed Thomas Becket, Archbishop of Canterbury, in his cathedral at the hour of Vespers. He had defended the freedom of the Church against the king. He was canonised little more than two years later.

12-30.x: Pierre Roger de Beaufort was elected pope at Avignon and took the name Gregory XI. Urged on by Saint Catherine of Siena, he returned the papacy to Rome in 1377. He was the last French pope.

12-30.t: Holy See and Israel signed accord
12-30.x: Representatives of the Holy See and the State of Israel signed the Fundamental Agreement in Jerusalem. It led to full diplomatic relations the following year and pledged both sides to oppose antisemitism.

12-31.t: Death of Pope Saint Sylvester I
12-31.x: Pope Sylvester I died after nearly twenty-two years as Bishop of Rome. In his time Constantine gave peace to the Church, the first great basilicas were built, and the Council of Nicaea met in 325.

12-31.t: Death of Saint John Francis Regis
12-31.x: The Jesuit John Francis Regis died at Lalouvesc in the mountains of southern France, aged forty-three, having caught pneumonia while preaching a mission in the snow. He had spent himself for the rural poor.

Sister Catherine Labouré died in Paris after forty-six years of quiet service to the elderly poor. Only near the end of her life did she let her superior know that she was the sister who had received the Miraculous Medal.

Benedict XVI died at the Mater Ecclesiae monastery in the Vatican, aged ninety-five. One of the leading theologians of his time, he was pope from 2005 until he resigned in 2013. His last words were reported as “Lord, I love you.”
